metadata.title: Why Was the DRT Act Needed? 8 Years in Civil Court vs 180 Days in DRT | DRT Act Explained Ep 1
metadata.author: Court Kutchehry
metadata.shortDescription:
Episode 1 of "DRT Act Explained with Judgments" (Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993) with Adv. Dr. Vineet Kohli.
 
Before we read a single section, we must understand the problem this Act was designed to solve:
• The problem before 1993: bank recovery suits stuck in civil courts for years, security losing value, public money locked up
• The committees: Tiwari Committee (1981) and the Narasimham Committee on the Financial System (1991)
• From Ordinance to Act: the 1993 Ordinance and Act No. 51 of 1993, deemed in force from 24 June 1993 under Section 1(3); once the "RDDBFI Act", now the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
• What the Act set out to do: a specialised forum, a summary procedure, and a dedicated recovery machinery
• A practical example, and a quick test

0:17 Today's episode

For education and general awareness only. Not legal advice. Please verify every provision in the current bare act and read the full judgments before relying on them.

segments.text: Namaskar Ji.
I am Dr. V.K. Kohli,
Advocate.
Welcome to CourtKutchehry.com.
Viewers, today we begin a new series titled
DRT Act Explained with Judgments.
In this episode, we go back in time.
Before we read a single section,
we must understand the problem that this Act
was designed to solve.
Viewers, imagine a bank in the 1980s.
A borrower has defaulted on a large loan.
The bank files a suit,
a civil suit for recovery.
The suit goes through pleadings,
issues, evidence and arguments, and takes many years.
Then comes execution,
which takes many more.
By the time the bank recovers anything,
the security has lost value,
and the money lent from public deposits is
locked up.
This was the reality.
Thousands of bank recovery suits were pending in
civil courts across the country,
and crores of rupees of public money were
stuck in litigation.
The idea of special tribunals came from expert
committees.
The Tiwari Committee, set up in 1981,
examined the legal and other difficulties faced by
banks and financial institutions, and recommended special tribunals
to recover their dues quickly.
A decade later, the Narasimham Committee on the
Financial System, in 1991, made the same recommendation
as part of the reform of the banking
sector.
It said that banks could not be healthy
if they could not recover their loans.
Parliament acted in 1993.
First, the President promulgated the Recovery of Debts
Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Ordinance,
It was then replaced by an Act of
Parliament with the same name,
Act No.
Under Section 1, sub-section 3,
the Act is deemed to have come into
force on 24 January 1993,
the date of the Ordinance.
For many years, it was known by its
initials,
the RDDBFI Act.
Today, after amendments made by the Insolvency
and Bankruptcy Code, its name is the Recovery
of Debts and Bankruptcy Act,
The preamble states the object simply:
to provide for the establishment of Tribunals for
the expeditious
adjudication
and recovery
of debts due to banks and financial institutions.
Three ideas run through the entire Act.
The Debts Recovery Tribunal; a summary procedure,
free from the technicalities of the Civil Procedure
Code; and dedicated recovery machinery,
the Recovery Officers, so that the decision is
actually enforced.
Let us take an example.
a bank lends 50 lakh rupees to a
factory, secured by a mortgage of its land.
the factory defaults, and the bank files a
suit, a civil suit.
The suit is decreed only in 1995,
after 8 years of hearings.
Execution takes another five.
By then, the machinery is scrap,
the land is encroached, and interest has made
the claim far larger than the security.
Now take the same case after 1993.
The bank files an application before the DRT,
which follows a summary procedure,
must aim to decide within 180 days,
and has its own Recovery Officers to sell
the property.
That contrast, between years and months,
is the whole reason this Act exists.
Now, a quick test.
Three questions, three quick answers.
Which 1981 committee first recommended special tribunals for
banks?
Answer is:
the Tiwari Committee.
From which date is the Act deemed to
be in force?
The answer is:
24 January 1993.
What is the Act's present name?
Answer is:
the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act,
Viewers, in this episode we continue the history:
the constitutional challenge to the Act,
and the major amendments of 2013 and 2016.
This video is for education and general awareness
only, and is not legal advice.
Please verify every provision in the current bare
act, and read the full judgments before relying
on them.

with your friends, relatives,

Advocate.

The idea of special tribunals came from expert committees. The Tiwari Committee, set up in 1981, examined the legal and other difficulties faced by banks and financial institutions, and recommended special tribunals to recover their dues quickly. A decade later, the Narasimham Committee on the Financial System, in 1991, made the same recommendation as part of the reform of the banking sector. metadata.author: Tim Santoni
metadata.shortDescription:
3 Investigation Strategies for Judgment Enforcement - Debt Collection- Finding Assets

Link to the VIDEO: https://youtu.be/rDAzEvzlcbo


1. Asset and Background Investigation- real property ownership, vehicle ownership, employment, licenses, business affiliations, civil judgments, bankruptcy, liens... Record your abstract of judgment in any county where the debtor COULD own property.

2.  Locate their residence to determine feasibility of covert trash collection (evidence collection).

3. Surveillance- determine daily activities which might include employment, visits to their bank, and properties they might own or manage.  Document plates of vehicles, watercraft, RV's, and motorcycles they are driving and are observed in or around their residence.

Tim Santoni is the President & CEO of Santoni Investigations @santoniinv.  Santoni Investigations is an entrepreneurial and innovative, family owned, investigation firm that was founded over 40 years ago.  Tim is a licensed private investigator (LPI), certified private investigator (CALI) and an active and certified member of the National Association of Professional Background Screeners (NAPBS).  He works with Insurance Companies, Law Firms, Brand Owners & Business owners to help mitigate risk through comprehensive investigative services.

He has testified as an expert witness in counterfeiting, insurance fraud and a variety of other civil cases.  He has worked and supervised over 20,000 investigations.

Tim is passionate about elevating the private investigation industry and educating clients and investigators.  He is an active member of CALI, NCISS, NAPBS and regularly speaks and attends MCLE type topics for attorneys and legal professionals.

⚖️ The Role of Vietnam’s Civil Judgment Enforcement Agency in Debt Recovery | LTS LAW FIRM

In Vietnam, debt recovery does not end with a court judgment. Enforcement is handled by the Civil Judgment Enforcement Agency, and without a proactive legal strategy, many judgments remain uncollected for years—or permanently unpaid.

This video explains how enforcement really works in Vietnam and what foreign creditors must do to protect their recovery rights.

🎯 What You Will Learn in This Video:
✅ Structure and authority of the Civil Judgment Enforcement Agency
✅ The difference between winning a case and recovering money
✅ Enforcement timelines and procedural bottlenecks
✅ Asset tracing, bank freezing, and property seizure
✅ Why creditor initiative is essential
✅ Practical enforcement lessons from real cases

💼 Our Services Include:
✅ Enforcement-ready litigation strategy
✅ Judgment enforcement representation
✅ Asset tracing & bank account investigation
✅ Seizure, freezing & auction procedures
✅ Cross-border creditor support in Vietnam

📊 Trusted by multinational companies, exporters, and foreign investors.

This series of videos covers the most successful methods of collection, including obtaining an Earnings Withholding Order and Bank Levy;  Applications and Orders for Appearance and Examination; and Abstracts of Judgment.  Calculating interest on judgments, renewing judgments, and filing an Acknowledgment of Satisfaction of Judgment are also covered.
See also: 
Collecting and Resisting Judgments: Info from the Law Library, https://saclaw.org/law-101/collecting-resisting-judgments-topic/

metadata.title: Enforcing a Judgment in Ontario: How Do You Actually Get Paid? Hashmi Law Group
metadata.author: Nizam Hashmi - Hashmi Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Winning a lawsuit in Ontario does not necessarily mean the money is paid automatically.

If the judgment debtor does not pay voluntarily, the judgment creditor may need to take additional enforcement steps.

In this video, Nizam Hashmi of Hashmi Law Group explains some of the main ways a money judgment may be enforced in Ontario.

Topics discussed include:

• What happens after you win a judgment  
• Garnishment  
• Writs of seizure and sale  
• Examination in aid of execution  
• Locating a debtor’s income and assets  
• Bank accounts and wages  
• Property and land  
• Post-judgment interest  
• Enforcement costs  
• Why the economics of collection matter  

WINNING DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY MEAN GETTING PAID

A court judgment gives the creditor legal rights, but it does not guarantee that the debtor will voluntarily pay.

If payment is not made, the creditor may need to use enforcement procedures.

GARNISHMENT

Depending on the circumstances, money owed to the judgment debtor may be subject to garnishment.

This can potentially include certain wages or funds held in a bank account.

However, garnishment is subject to procedural requirements, legal limits and applicable exemptions.

Not every source of income or every dollar held by a debtor can necessarily be garnished.

WRITS OF SEIZURE AND SALE

Another enforcement tool is a writ of seizure and sale.

Depending on the circumstances, a writ may affect eligible personal property or land owned by the judgment debtor.

The effectiveness of a writ can depend on issues including ownership, priorities, exemptions, existing creditors and the particular property involved.

EXAMINATION IN AID OF EXECUTION

Before choosing an enforcement strategy, it is often important to understand what the debtor actually owns or earns.

An examination in aid of execution can be used to obtain financial information from a judgment debtor.

Depending on the circumstances, questions may address:

• Employment  
• Income  
• Bank accounts  
• Property  
• Debts  
• Expenses  
• Other financial information  

This information can help determine which enforcement method may be practical.

THE ECONOMICS OF ENFORCEMENT

A remedy may be legally available but still not make financial sense in every case.

A creditor should consider factors such as:

• The amount of the judgment  
• Assets available for enforcement  
• The debtor’s income  
• Existing creditors  
• The likely recovery  
• Enforcement costs  
• Time involved  

Post-judgment interest may also continue to accrue according to the judgment and applicable law.

WHAT IF THE DEBTOR HAS FEW ASSETS?

A judgment can be legally valid and enforceable even where immediate recovery is difficult.

The practical enforcement strategy depends heavily on the debtor’s financial circumstances and whether reachable assets or income exist.

HASHMI LAW GROUP

Civil Litigation  
Judgment Enforcement  
Debt Recovery  
Contract Disputes  
Commercial Litigation  
Garnishment and Enforcement Proceedings  

North York & Mississauga  
Serving the Greater Toronto Area and clients throughout Ontario

Website:  
https://nhashmilaw.com

If you found this video helpful, please like it, share it with someone who may benefit, and subscribe to the Hashmi Law Group YouTube channel for more practical information about Ontario civil litigation and judgment enforcement.

DISCLAIMER

This video is provided for general educational and informational purposes only. It does not constitute legal advice and does not create a lawyer-client relationship. Judgment enforcement is highly fact-specific. The availability and effectiveness of garnishment, writs, examinations and other enforcement procedures depend on the judgment, the debtor’s circumstances, applicable exemptions, priorities and procedural requirements. Obtain legal advice regarding your particular circumstances before taking, or deciding not to take, any enforcement step.

I’m Nizam Hashmi of Hashmi Law Group.
Ontario law provides several ways to enforce a money judgment.
One common method is garnishment.
Depending on the circumstances, certain wages or bank funds owed to the debtor may be subject to garnishment.

The key point is this: a judgment gives you legal rights, but collecting the money may require a separate enforcement strategy.

metadata.title: Collecting Money After A Judgment - Wage Garnishment And Bank Levy
metadata.author: Jedidiah “Jed” McKeehan
metadata.shortDescription:
In this legal training video, Knoxville attorney Jed McKeehan discusses collecting money after a judgment by means of a wage garnishment or bank levy.

Learn more about this legal topic and others at http://attorney-knoxville.com.

Follow us online:
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/JedMcKeehan/
Twitter: https://twitter.com/jedmckeehan

#knoxvilleattorney #attorneyknoxville  #insession

metadata.title: Bank Levy vs. Wage Garnishment... What's the Difference?
metadata.author: Consumer Warrior
metadata.shortDescription:
Some might think a bank levy and wage garnishment are the same thing, but they’re not, and understanding the difference can completely change how you protect your money.

Before assuming what a creditor can do, it’s crucial to understand how wage garnishment works, how a bank levy affects your bank account, and what legal options you have to stop or reduce them. 

If you’re dealing with debt or worried about creditors taking your income or savings, this is something you need to understand now.

In this video, John breaks down the key differences between wage garnishment and bank levies, how creditors legally access your assets, and why one can impact your paycheck long-term while the other can hit your bank account instantly.

metadata.shortDescription:
Won a judgment but the debtor isn't paying? 

Brady Dunlop, an attorney with Hendershot Cowart P.C., walks through the main collection options, from finding assets to court-appointed receivers.

⏱️ Chapters
0:00 – Texas judgment collection tools
0:15 – Post-judgment discovery: finding assets
0:29 – Writ of execution and sheriff's sale
0:43 – Writ of garnishment on bank accounts

Collection usually starts with post-judgment discovery, which uses formal requests to locate the debtor's non-exempt assets. From there, creditors can use:
- A writ of execution, which lets the local sheriff seize and auction non-exempt property, with the proceeds applied to the judgment.
- A writ of garnishment, which targets funds at a bank where you know the debtor has an account. Current wages are exempt, and the debtor must prove the funds qualify.
- A turnover order, which directs the debtor to hand over non-exempt assets and can be served on any bank to search for accounts.

A court-appointed receiver is usually a last resort. Receivers handle the collection work but typically take about 25% of what they collect, so the goal is to get you paid before it comes to that.

metadata.title: # What Happens If You Lose a Civil Lawsuit? Judgment & Garnishment Explained
metadata.author: Verdict
metadata.shortDescription:
What happens if you lose a civil lawsuit in America? Losing a lawsuit doesn't necessarily mean your financial problems end with the court's decision. A civil judgment can lead to wage garnishment, bank account levies, property liens, and years of financial consequences.

In this documentary-style legal explainer, discover what happens after a court judgment, how judgment creditors collect money, how post-judgment interest increases your debt, and what legal options you have if you cannot afford to pay. We also explain appeals, supersedeas bonds, default judgments, and the deadlines that could affect your next move.

Learn about wage garnishment limits, judgment liens, bank levies, debtor examinations, homestead exemptions, and assets that may be legally protected from creditors. We also explore how long civil judgments last, how bankruptcy may affect certain judgments, and the famous McDonald's hot coffee case, including the $33.5 million verdict that became part of a much larger legal story.

If you've been sued, lost a civil case, or simply want to understand how the American legal system works, this video explains what happens next — from the first court judgment to the long-term consequences.

**CHAPTERS / TIMESTAMPS:**

00:00 The Loss You Never Saw Coming: Default Judgments
01:59 Verdict vs. Judgment: The Paper That Changes Everything
03:56 The Bill: Damages, Court Costs and Attorney Fees
06:09 Post-Judgment Interest: The Meter That Never Stops
08:10 28 Days: Post-Trial Motions and the Hot Coffee Case
10:31 Appealing a Civil Judgment: Deadlines and Odds
12:50 The Bond Problem: Collection During Your Appeal
14:49 Wage Garnishment, Bank Levies and Judgment Liens
17:55 Debtor Exams and Exemptions: What They Can't Take
21:06 How Long a Judgment Lasts: The $117 Million Story
24:09 Bankruptcy: The Reset Button for Judgments
27:26 Injunctions, Contempt and Non-Money Judgments
30:59 The Smart Loser's Playbook: First 30 Days to 20 Years

**LEGAL DISCLAIMER:**
This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Laws, exemptions, collection procedures, interest rates, and appeal deadlines vary by state and individual circumstances. Consult a qualified attorney for advice about your specific legal situation.

The judgment goes dormant if the creditor lets 10 years pass without issuing an execution. But a dormant judgment can be revived within 2² years after that. Illinois allows enforcement for 7 years at a time with revival possible, generally up to 20 years from entry. And judgments travel. If you move to another state to escape one, the winner can domesticate it. Under the Uniform Enforcement of Foreign Judgments Act, adopted in the overwhelming majority of states, an authenticated copy of your home state judgment gets filed in your new state and the new state's garnishment and lien machinery takes over. The Constitution's full faith and credit clause is the engine under that. State courts must honor each other's judgments. Moving is not a defense. It is a change of venue for the creditor. Now let me show you the long shadow at its longest because it involves the most famous civil loser in modern American history. In February 1997, a California civil jury found O.J. Simpson liable for the wrongful deaths connected to the Goldman and Brown families and awarded $33.5 million, $8.5 million in compensatory damages to the Goldman family and $25 million in punitive damages. Simpson paid only a small fraction in his lifetime. He lived largely on protected ground. His NFL pension was shielded by ERISA type protections, and he moved to Florida where that unlimited homestead law guarded his home. Creditors took what they could reach, memorabilia, some assets, but the bulk of the judgment went uncollected, growing at California's 10% simple interest year after year. When Simpson died in April 2024, 27 years after the judgment, the Goldman family filed a claim against his estate for more than $117 million, the original 33.5 plus decades of interest. In November 2025, the estate's executor accepted the claim at just under $58 million. And then comes the final deflating fact. The estate's total assets appear to be somewhere between half a million and a million dollars. An accepted claim is not a payment. The judgment outlived the debtor, grew to triple its size, won every legal fight, and may still collect pennies on the dollar. That story teaches the two truths of this whole subject at once. A judgment can pursue you for decades and beyond the grave, and what actually gets collected is decided less by the size of the number than by the map of exemptions we just walked through, which is why some losers reach for the one legal tool that can stop the entire machinery at once. Bankruptcy. The moment a bankruptcy petition is filed, something remarkable happens. The automatic stay under Section 362 of the Bankruptcy Code freezes virtually all collection, garnishments halt, levies stop, lien enforcement pauses, and the underlying civil case itself is put on ice. It is the fastest known way to stop an active wage garnishment. Money taken shortly before the filing can sometimes even be recovered. There are two main consumer chapters. Chapter 17 is liquidation. A trustee sells any non-exempt assets. In most consumer cases, there are none beyond the exemptions, and the eligible debts are discharged usually within about three to four months. To qualify, you must pass the means test. If your recent income sits above your state's median for your household size, a formula of expense allowances decides whether chapter 7 is available or whether you are pushed into chapter 13 instead. Chapter 13 is the repayment plan. You keep your property and pay some or all of what you owe over three to five years under court supervision with the remaining eligible balance discharged when the plan is completed. Can bankruptcy erase a judgment? Usually yes. If the judgment is an ordinary money judgment, breach of contract, negligence, a consumer debt, the labeled judgment does not protect it. What matters is the conduct underneath it because section 523 of the code lists the debts that survive. Debts obtained by fraud survive. Debts for willful and malicious injury survive. Domestic support obligations survive. Most taxes survive. Debts for death or personal injury caused by drunk driving survive. If your judgment rests on one of those foundations, bankruptcy will not wash it away. And for some categories, the creditor must sue in the bankruptcy court by a deadline or the debt is discharged anyway. There is one more piece of fine print and it matters enormously to homeowners. Even when a debt is discharged, a lien can ride through bankruptcy as a charge on your property. But section 522F gives the debtor a counter move. A judicial lien can be avoided, wiped out to the extent it impairs an exemption like a judgment lien eating into your protected home equity. And remember that 1.7 million IRA cap and the homestead limits we discussed. Bankruptcy has its own ceiling for people who poured money into a mansion in a protective state shortly before filing. Equity acquired within about three years and four months before filing, technically 1,215 days, is capped at $214,000. Congress built that trap on purpose after watching exactly the exemption games described earlier in this video. Bankruptcy is not a free escape either. A Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for up to 10 years. Remember, it is now the only public record that routinely appears there. Civil judgments themselves were removed from the Big Three bureaus reports back in 2017 and 2018, though they remain only public in court records, title searches, and background checks. Still, for a loser facing a large, ordinary, unpayable judgment, bankruptcy is often the door marked exit. It is not the only door though. Some losses cannot be paid off at all because the judgment was never really about money. Not every civil judgment is a check. Courts can order you to do things or to stop doing things, and losing that kind of case puts your behavior, not just your bank account, under the court's command. An injunction is an order, stop the infringement, end the nuisance, honor the non-compete. In contract cases, a court can order specific performance, perform the deal itself, classically for real estate and unique goods instead of paying damages. A declaratory judgment can strip away a legal position you've depended on, a ruling that a patent is invalid or that an insurance company owes no coverage with consequences far beyond any single payment. Disobeying these orders is where the one real threat of jail in civil law lives, contempt of court. Civil contempt is coercive, fines or jail until you comply. As judges put it, you hold the keys to your own cell. Criminal contempt punishes past disobedience with a fixed sanction. This is the precise boundary of the old rule. America does not imprison people for debt. It imprisons people, occasionally, for defying a judge. For businesses, losing can be existential in quieter ways. A court can place the company in receivership, handing control to a court-appointed outsider. Deadlock and oppression suits can end in court-ordered dissolution. Licenses the business needs can be jeopardized, and a large judgment on the books can trigger defaults in the company's own loan agreements. Cross defaults so the bank calls its loans before the judgment creditor has collected a single dollar. Preclusion finishes the job. Claim and issue preclusion mean the loss is final law between the parties, usable again in related cases. You cannot simply relitigate your way out. Now, against all of this, the machinery, the interest, the decades, there remains one ordinary, unglamorous exit that ends more of these stories than any courtroom drama. A deal. Post-judgment settlement is standard practice. Winners discount. A lump sum today in certain money can beat years of garnishment fights and exemption claims. Payment plans get written down, sometimes as formal court orders. Whatever is agreed must be in writing with the exact payoff terms spelled out. And when the money is paid in full or in the agreed amount, the creditor must file the document that officially ends the story, the satisfaction of judgment. That filing is not paperwork vanity. It is what clears the judgment liens off your property's title and proves to every future lender and title company that the debt is over. A paid judgment with no satisfaction filed can cloud your life for years. Losers should chase that paper like it is money because it is. There is also one legal rescue for the judgment that should never have existed. Under Rule 60B in federal court and state equivalents, a court can relieve you from a judgment from mistake or excusable neglect for newly discovered evidence or for the other side's fraud, generally within one year. For a void judgment, one entered without jurisdiction or without proper service within a reasonable time with no fixed cap. This the weapon against the worst defaults, the cases where the process server lied, the papers went to a stranger's address, the defendant never knew. That story, the shadow epidemic from the opening of this video is exactly who this rule exists for. So, you have lost. The paper exists. What do you actually do and in what order? Everything in this video compresses into a timeline. Here it is. In the first 30 days, you stop the bleeding. The judgment is entered, the interest clock is running. In federal court, execution is automatically paused for 30 days. That window is for planning, not relaxing. By day 28, your post-trial motions must be filed in federal court. Remember, that is the battlefield where a 2.7 million dollar award became 480,000. By day 30, your notice of appeal is due. And immediately, not eventually, you decide the bond question. Can you post security to freeze collection during the appeal or will the winner be collecting while you fight? At the same time, you map your exemptions, home, benefits, retirement, and you do not under any circumstances start moving or hiding assets. Post-judgment transfers invite fraudulent transfer lawsuits and can be unwound on top of everything else. And you open settlement talks early while the winner still prefers fast certain money to years of enforcement work. In the first 6 months, the machinery arrives in its usual order. The lien is recorded, the debtor examination puts your finances under oath, the garnishment or the bank levy lands. Your job in this phase is precision. Claim every exemption you have in writing on deadline. If the judgment is large, ordinary, and truly unpayable, this is also when a serious bankruptcy consultation belongs on the calendar because the automatic stay is the only tool that stops everything at once and its lien avoidance rules may strip the judgment lien off your exempt home. In the long term, years 1 through 20, respect the math. At 10% interest, the balance doubles in a decade. Creditors who calendar their renewals can keep a judgment alive through successive enforcement periods with interest folded in at each renewal, and they can follow you across state lines. If you pay, pay in a way that ends it, written terms and the satisfaction of judgment filed and the liens released. If you truly cannot pay and you qualify, a bankruptcy discharge ends most ordinary money judgments permanently, whatever the state clock says. And hold on to the two truths from the Simpson story because they are the whole subject in one frame. A judgment can be enormous, durable, and undefeated and still collect almost nothing if the debtor's assets live behind exemption walls. The verdict is the headline, the exemptions, the deadlines, and the paperwork are the outcome. What happens if you lose a civil lawsuit? A process happens, measured in 28-day fuses and 30-day clocks, in liens and levies and quiet interest compounding in the dark. It is a process with real teeth and real defenses, and almost every turn in it rewards the person who moves first and punishes the person who freezes. The worst loss is not the judgment itself, it is the default, the fight that never happened, the deadline that passed in silence, the envelope that was never opened. Because in American civil courts, losing is survivable, disappearing is what makes it permanent.

In this fifth video in Benjy Law Corporation's California Judgment Enforcement Series, attorney Bob Benjy discusses utilization of the writ of execution tool to involuntarily take money from a judgment debtor's bank account (and take and sell the contents of a judgment debtor's safe deposit box). 

If you find this video of interest, you are encouraged to both hit the like button and the subscribe button and also to share the video with others you believe might benefit from viewing it.  Additional videos in the series will be posted on interim basis in the coming weeks and months.

Bob Benjy has earned a AV Preeminent peer review rating from Martindale-Hubbell and has been honored with a SuperLawyer title for 2018 and 2019.  Bob is primarily a litigator and specializes in the areas of business, real estate, finance and collections matters.

This brief, summary educational video is produced by Benjy Law Corporation and its founder, Bob Benjy, for informational and legal marketing purposes only.  It is not intended to establish any attorney-client relationship with any viewers, nor to be relied upon as any form of legal advice.

metadata.title: Wage Garnishment in Georgia - How Much Can They Take and How Do You Stop It?
metadata.author: Law Office of Jeffrey B. Kelly
metadata.shortDescription:
Is a wage garnishment taking a chunk of your paycheck in Georgia? In this video, Georgia bankruptcy attorney Jeff Kelly answers the four questions people ask most when a garnishment hits: How much can they take? How did this get to my employer without me knowing? Will I lose my job? And how fast can a Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 bankruptcy filing make it stop?

HOW MUCH CAN THEY TAKE FROM YOUR PAYCHECK?
For an ordinary debt like a credit card, medical bill, or personal loan, Georgia law caps a wage garnishment at 25 percent of your disposable earnings. Disposable earnings are not exactly the same as take-home pay. They are what is left after the deductions the law requires, such as income taxes, Social Security, and Medicare. Voluntary deductions like health insurance or retirement contributions are not subtracted first, so the garnishment can feel bigger than a quarter of your check.

Here is what that looks like: if your disposable earnings are 800 dollars a week, a creditor can take 200 dollars every week. That is more than 10,000 dollars a year leaving your paycheck before you ever see it. Lower-income workers have an extra layer of protection, and if your disposable earnings fall below a floor tied to the minimum wage, a regular creditor cannot garnish anything at all.

Child support, alimony, federal student loans, and tax debts follow different garnishment rules. This video focuses on the most common situation: a regular creditor who sued you and won.

HOW DID THE GARNISHMENT GET TO MY EMPLOYER WITHOUT ME KNOWING?
A creditor cannot just call your employer and start taking money. In Georgia, a wage garnishment comes at the end of a court process, and it usually unfolds like this:
1. You fall behind, and the account is sold to a debt buyer or sent to a collection law firm.
2. You are sued, usually in magistrate court or state court in your county.
3. You are served. The papers may be left at your home with someone who lives there, like a teenager, a roommate, or an ex, and they get lost in the mail pile.
4. You have 30 days to answer. If you do not, the creditor can get a default judgment with interest, court costs, and often attorney fees added.
5. The clerk issues a FIFA (writ of fieri facias), which is recorded on the general execution docket and acts as a lien on property you own in that county.
6. The creditor serves a garnishment on your employer. You are supposed to receive notice and an exemption claim form, but many people never open it.
If you were never properly served with the lawsuit, that is something an attorney needs to review.

WILL A GARNISHMENT COST ME MY JOB?
Jeff explains the protection you have against being fired over a garnishment for one debt, why that protection weakens when multiple garnishments pile up, why your employer cannot ignore a garnishment, and why quitting and changing jobs does not make a judgment go away.

HOW FAST DOES BANKRUPTCY STOP A WAGE GARNISHMENT?
The moment a bankruptcy case is filed, the automatic stay goes into effect and orders creditors to stop collecting, including wage garnishments. Once the creditor's attorney and your employer's payroll department are notified, the very next paycheck is usually clean. Depending on the amount and your situation, money garnished in roughly the 90 days before filing can sometimes be recovered.

Chapter 7: The garnishment stops at filing, and for most ordinary debts, your personal responsibility for the judgment is wiped out at discharge. The garnishment does not come back.

Chapter 13: The garnishment stops at filing, and your debts are handled together through one payment to a trustee, based on what you can afford, over three to five years. Chapter 13 is often the better fit if you are also behind on a house or car you want to keep.

WHAT TO DO THIS WEEK
Open every piece of mail from a court or law firm. Gather your recent pay stubs and any court papers. Do not quit your job, and do not take out a high-interest loan to pay off the garnishment. Talk to a bankruptcy attorney before your next payday, not after.

ABOUT JEFF KELLY
Jeff Kelly has practiced consumer bankruptcy law in Georgia since 1998, helping everyday Georgia families break free from debt through Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 bankruptcy. The Law Office of Jeffrey B. Kelly, P.C. has offices in Rome, Marietta, Cartersville, and Dallas, Georgia, and serves clients throughout the Northern District of Georgia, including the Rome, Atlanta, Gainesville, and Newnan divisions.

Pursuant to the United States Bankruptcy Code, we are a debt relief agency. We help people obtain relief from their creditors by filing bankruptcy.

Nothing in this video or post is intended as legal advice. If you want legal advice for your specific case, you need to speak directly to an attorney.

metadata.title: Judgment Lien: Definition, Examples, Vs. Property Lien
metadata.author: Simple Explain
metadata.shortDescription:
A judgment lien is a court ruling that allows a creditor to take possession of a debtor's property if they fail to fulfill their obligations. These liens can be attached to personal and real property, and debtors can potentially avoid them through repayment or bankruptcy. Unlike property liens, judgment liens are imposed without the debtor's consent, and they are intended to force debtors to pay off their creditors.

segments.text: Today, we will talk about judgment
liens, including what they are, how they
work, what debtors can do, examples of
judgment liens, and how they differ from
property liens.
A judgment lien is a court ruling that
gives a creditor the right to take
possession of a debtor's property if the
debtor fails to fulfill their
contractual obligations.
For example, if you owe money to a
creditor and don't pay, they can sue you
for the balance.
If the court rules against you, the
creditor can file a judgment lien
against you.
This means the creditor can access your
assets, such as your personal property,
real estate, or business to satisfy the
judgment.
If a court enters a judgment against a
debtor, a lien is automatically created
on any real estate the debtor owns in
some states.
In most states, the judgment creditor
must record the lien via county or state
filing.
Once the lien is filed, it becomes
attached to the debtor's property,
whether personal like cars or real
estate like homes or land.
However, a drawback of liens on personal
property is that a large portion of
someone's personal property has no
title, so they are not officially
recorded against that property.
Debtors can satisfy or avoid a lien
through a few ways.
The first and most obvious option is to
repay the debt.
If they pay off their obligation, the
creditor will remove the lien by filing
a release.
Debtors can also avoid a non-consensual
lien in bankruptcy under certain
conditions.
For example, if one person injures
another through negligence and insurance
does not cover the damaged party's
reparations, a judgment lien can be
placed against the negligent person's
property.
Another example is a judge placing a
lien on a debtor's car for non-payment
of a car loan.
Unlike judgment liens, property liens
are permitted by the debtor who
voluntarily gives up the right to their
property.
They are considered consensual and are
often used by lenders as a form of
security or collateral when lending
large sums of money.
A statutory lien is a type of lien that
is based on legal statutes rather than
common law or a contractual agreement.
Judgment liens are imposed by courts to
force debtors to pay off their
creditors.
When a debtor receives a judgment lien,
it's usually best to pay off the debt if
possible.
Here are three key takeaways.
One, a judgment lien is a court ruling
that gives a creditor the right to take
possession of a debtor's property if the
debtor fails to fulfill their
contractual obligations.
Two, judgment liens are non-consensual
because they are attached to property
without the owner's consent or
agreement.
Three, these liens can be attached to
real or personal property or, if the
debtor has none at the time of judgment,
to future acquisitions.
Hope this would help. Thanks for
watching.

segments.text: once a party prevails in a lawsuit and
obtains a monetary judgment the next
step is to collect that judgment while
it would be nice if judgment debtors
simply wrote checks to cover judgments
the day that they were entered real life
does not often work that way in a
different presentation we discussed the
steps that are advisable after obtaining
a judgment together and determine
whether collection activities make sense
in this presentation we will look at
some specific methods that are available
once the decision has been made to
pursue collections
these formal collection methods may be
necessary once it becomes apparent that
the judgment debtor will not or cannot
pay the judgment an alternative that is
always open to the creditor is to try to
negotiate a settlement that allows the
debtor to pay less than the full
judgment giving the judgment debtor a
discount to ensure payments may save
resources in the long run moreover the
debtor and creditor may be able to agree
on an installment plan to pay off the
debt or the debtor can be encouraged to
seek other forms of financial assistance
such as a loan to pay off the debts the
most familiar method of post judgment
collection is wage garnishments wage
garnishment is a legal procedure in
which a judge orders an employer to
withhold a portion of that debtors
earnings and then use that portion to
pay back the judgment creditor under
this method each paycheck a debtor earns
helps to pay back the debt owed under
the judgment protecting the creditors
interests while protecting the rights of
the debtor against overly burdensome
collection actions wage garnishments are
subject to limitations under title 3 of
the Consumer Credit Protection Act which
dictates that the amount that may be
garnished cannot exceed the lesser of
25% of the employee's disposable
earnings or the amount by which those
earnings are greater than 30 times the
federal minimum wage disposable earnings
are the amounts left over after Social
Security and income taxes are withheld
this limitation on the amount that can
be garnished however may not apply to
certain types of debt such as child
support or spousal support federal tax
debt and student loans subject to
collection by the United States
Department of Education these exceptions
may grant a creditor a larger portion of
the debtors disposable earnings
however garnishment may not be effective
in all situations it may take a great
deal of time to pay back a high value
judgment on a low income garnishment is
even less effective when the debtor is
unemployed if there is no income on
which to collect a garnishment yields no
rewards as any portion of 0 is
inevitable
zero in that case a judgment creditor
must turn to other alternatives a second
method of debt collection is the
judgment lien which allows the judgment
creditor to attach the debt to real
property owned by the debtor within the
territorial jurisdiction in which the
judgment was obtained once the lien is
attached it will prevent a judgment
debtor from selling the property without
first satisfying the unpaid judgment
state law covers both the method and
duration of judgment liens and judgment
liens may need to be renewed before
expiration a downside to this method of
collection is that it may take a long
time to collect on a judgment lien as
the property must first be transferred a
judgment creditor cannot foreclose on
the property he may only collect his
debt out of the proceeds of the sale of
the property if the owner chooses not to
sell or transfer the property for 20
years no money will be collected during
that time while this method often takes
longer to collect on a debt in most
states statutory interest accrues the
entire time the debt is unpaid in this
way the judgment creditors rights are at
least somewhat protected from purposeful
delay by the imposition of increasing
debt upon the judgment debtor this
increased debt acts as a deterrent
against purposeful avoidance of the
judgment lien as when the property is
eventually sold the debt will be repaid
with interest from the date of the
judgment
a far less common technique to collect
on a judgment is a levy in a levy a
local sheriff is instructed to seize a
certain portion of the judgment debtors
personal property such as a car jewelry
television etc the personal property is
then sold and the proceeds of the sale
can be used to pay the debtors judgment
the sale is typically done by public
auction following which the local
sheriff pays the costs of conducting the
auction and uses the remaining proceeds
from the sale to pay the debt levies are
not permissible in every case and are
usually subject to very strict
guidelines such as specific notice
requirements broadly defined exempt
property that cannot be levied auction
guidelines and differing state laws as
to seizure of property the days of
Dickenson Ian debtors prisons were in
people such as pip and Great
Expectations
are imprisoned for failing to pay a debt
are long over still debtors can be sent
to prison for failure to abide by a
court order this is common in the case
of failure to pay child support
wherein criminal contempt actions are
used to imprison parents who fail to pay
court-ordered child support in 2011 the
Supreme Court reaffirmed the
constitutionality of this practice
though it required that states provide
certain safeguards to ensure that people
are not imprisoned wrongfully on these
grounds failure to make payments in
other types of cases where the defendant
is clearly able to pay but chooses not
to can also theoretically lead to
contempt of court charges this is
exceedingly rare though contempt of
court charges in cases involving
ordinary civil debts do more frequently
occur where the defendant ignores court
orders to turn over documents answer
questions or appear for debtors
examinations or lie under questioning
regarding assets or income
even when a judgment has been secured
and it's been determined that collection
actions are worthwhile determining which
collection actions to pursue and
pursuing them are skill intensive tasks
this presentation has provided an

videos.full_text: once a party prevails in a lawsuit and obtains a monetary judgment the next step is to collect that judgment while it would be nice if judgment debtors simply wrote checks to cover judgments the day that they were entered real life does not often work that way in a different presentation we discussed the steps that are advisable after obtaining a judgment together and determine whether collection activities make sense in this presentation we will look at some specific methods that are available once the decision has been made to pursue collections these formal collection methods may be necessary once it becomes apparent that the judgment debtor will not or cannot pay the judgment an alternative that is always open to the creditor is to try to negotiate a settlement that allows the debtor to pay less than the full judgment giving the judgment debtor a discount to ensure payments may save resources in the long run moreover the debtor and creditor may be able to agree on an installment plan to pay off the debt or the debtor can be encouraged to seek other forms of financial assistance such as a loan to pay off the debts the most familiar method of post judgment collection is wage garnishments wage garnishment is a legal procedure in which a judge orders an employer to withhold a portion of that debtors earnings and then use that portion to pay back the judgment creditor under this method each paycheck a debtor earns helps to pay back the debt owed under the judgment protecting the creditors interests while protecting the rights of the debtor against overly burdensome collection actions wage garnishments are subject to limitations under title 3 of the Consumer Credit Protection Act which dictates that the amount that may be garnished cannot exceed the lesser of 25% of the employee's disposable earnings or the amount by which those earnings are greater than 30 times the federal minimum wage disposable earnings are the amounts left over after Social Security and income taxes are withheld this limitation on the amount that can be garnished however may not apply to certain types of debt such as child support or spousal support federal tax debt and student loans subject to collection by the United States Department of Education these exceptions may grant a creditor a larger portion of the debtors disposable earnings however garnishment may not be effective in all situations it may take a great deal of time to pay back a high value judgment on a low income garnishment is even less effective when the debtor is unemployed if there is no income on which to collect a garnishment yields no rewards as any portion of 0 is inevitable zero in that case a judgment creditor must turn to other alternatives a second method of debt collection is the judgment lien which allows the judgment creditor to attach the debt to real property owned by the debtor within the territorial jurisdiction in which the judgment was obtained once the lien is attached it will prevent a judgment debtor from selling the property without first satisfying the unpaid judgment state law covers both the method and duration of judgment liens and judgment liens may need to be renewed before expiration a downside to this method of collection is that it may take a long time to collect on a judgment lien as the property must first be transferred a judgment creditor cannot foreclose on the property he may only collect his debt out of the proceeds of the sale of the property if the owner chooses not to sell or transfer the property for 20 years no money will be collected during that time while this method often takes longer to collect on a debt in most states statutory interest accrues the entire time the debt is unpaid in this way the judgment creditors rights are at least somewhat protected from purposeful delay by the imposition of increasing debt upon the judgment debtor this increased debt acts as a deterrent against purposeful avoidance of the judgment lien as when the property is eventually sold the debt will be repaid with interest from the date of the judgment a far less common technique to collect on a judgment is a levy in a levy a local sheriff is instructed to seize a certain portion of the judgment debtors personal property such as a car jewelry television etc the personal property is then sold and the proceeds of the sale can be used to pay the debtors judgment the sale is typically done by public auction following which the local sheriff pays the costs of conducting the auction and uses the remaining proceeds from the sale to pay the debt levies are not permissible in every case and are usually subject to very strict guidelines such as specific notice requirements broadly defined exempt property that cannot be levied auction guidelines and differing state laws as to seizure of property the days of Dickenson Ian debtors prisons were in people such as pip and Great Expectations are imprisoned for failing to pay a debt are long over still debtors can be sent to prison for failure to abide by a court order this is common in the case of failure to pay child support wherein criminal contempt actions are used to imprison parents who fail to pay court-ordered child support in 2011 the Supreme Court reaffirmed the constitutionality of this practice though it required that states provide certain safeguards to ensure that people are not imprisoned wrongfully on these grounds failure to make payments in other types of cases where the defendant is clearly able to pay but chooses not to can also theoretically lead to contempt of court charges this is exceedingly rare though contempt of court charges in cases involving ordinary civil debts do more frequently occur where the defendant ignores court orders to turn over documents answer questions or appear for debtors examinations or lie under questioning regarding assets or income even when a judgment has been secured and it's been determined that collection actions are worthwhile determining which collection actions to pursue and pursuing them are skill intensive tasks this presentation has provided an overview of some of the options available to judgment creditors

segments.text: A debtor examination is only as
productive as the preparation that goes
into it. Walking into a debtor
examination without an independent
investigation already complete, relying
solely on the debtor's voluntary
disclosures under oath, misses the most
valuable use of the examination. Here's
the professional approach to preparing
for a debtor examination. Step one,
conduct a comprehensive pre-examination
asset investigation. Before the
examination takes place, commission a
professional skip trace and asset
investigation that independently
identifies all real estate the debtor
owns or has recently transferred, all
vehicle registrations, all business
entities the debtor is associated with
across all 50 states, UCC lien records,
professional license records, court
records in all states, and any other
public records relevant to the debtor's
financial position. This independent
investigation gives you two things:
information the debtor may not disclose,
and a framework for cross-examining the
debtor when their disclosures are
incomplete or inconsistent. Step two,
review all prior litigation involving
the debtor. Financial disclosures,
deposition testimony, and court filings
from prior cases, divorce proceedings,
bankruptcy filings, prior collections
matters, often contain the debtor's own
sworn statements about assets and
income. Inconsistencies between prior
sworn statements and current testimony
are powerful examination tools.
Step three, prepare a systematic
examination script. Don't rely on
improvisational questioning. Prepare a
written examination outline that covers
every asset category. Real property,
current and transferred, vehicles, bank
accounts, every institution, business
interests, every entity, income, every
source, receivables, everyone who owes
the debtor money, pending litigation,
any claims where the debtor is a
plaintiff, and recent transfers. Step
four, have documents ready.
If the examination order requires the
debtor to produce documents, tax
returns, bank statements, financial
records, review those documents
carefully before the examination and
prepare to ask about specific entries.
Step five, know the contempt procedure.
If the debtor is evasive, unresponsive,
or provides obviously false testimony,
know how to immediately pursue contempt
remedies to enforce the examination
order. People Locator Skip Tracing
provides the pre-examination asset
investigation that makes debtor
examinations productive. Visit
peoplelocatorskiptracing.com
to place your order.

the attorney for the plaintiff will

Creditor must file a motion to compel

segments.text: A debtor examination is one of the most
powerful but underutilized tools
available to judgment creditors. It
compels the debtor to appear in court,
testify under oath, and answer detailed
questions about their income, assets,
bank accounts, and financial
circumstances. Here's everything you
need to know to use this tool
effectively.
The debtor examination goes by different
names in different states. In
California, it's called an order for
examination. In New York, it's a
post-judgment information subpoena or a
deposition in supplementary proceedings.
In other states, it may be called
supplementary proceedings, creditor's
examination, or judgment debtor
interrogatories. Despite the different
names, the core process is similar
everywhere. To initiate a debtor
examination, the judgment creditor files
a motion or application with the court
the judgment, requesting an order
requiring the debtor to appear. The
court issues the order, which must then
be personally served on the debtor. This
is why current address information from
a professional skip trace is a
prerequisite. You can't serve the order
without knowing where to find the
debtor. Once the order is served, the
debtor must appear at the specified date
and time for the examination. Failure to
appear can result in a bench warrant and
contempt findings. At the examination,
the creditor's attorney, or the creditor
directly in some courts, asks the debtor
questions under oath about their
financial circumstances. The scope is
broad: bank accounts and financial
institutions, employment and income,
real estate and personal property,
vehicles, business interests, retirement
accounts, inheritance rights, accounts
receivable, pending litigation, and any
assets transferred in the recent past.
The examination is conducted on the
record. False statements are perjury, a
crime with serious consequences. This
creates a powerful incentive for debtors
to disclose honestly, even assets they
had been concealing. Banks and employers
can also be ordered to appear for
examination. This allows direct
questioning of financial institutions
about account balances and direct
questioning of employers about
compensation and benefits. At People
Locator Skip Tracing, we provide the
current address information necessary to
effectuate service of examination
orders, along with pre-examination asset
investigation that gives your attorney a
comprehensive briefing before walking
into the examination. Visit
peoplelocatorskiptracing.com
to place your asset investigation order
today.

metadata.title: Regulation F: New Debt Collection Laws You Need to Know Even if You're not in Debt
metadata.author: SeniorLiving.Org
metadata.shortDescription:
What is Regulation F? New debt collection laws affect you, even if you're not currently in debt. When a debt collector calls, not only should you know the rules that govern them, but also realize that your actions could affect whether you have to pay any money. 

Time Stamps
0:00 You need to know about debt collection even if you’re not in debt
0:23 Introduction to HELPS Nonprofit Law Firm and Attorney Kaisa Janzen
0:40 How new debt collection laws protect you
1:36 Recent changes to the laws regarding debt collection
2:10 Anyone could receive a debt collection for debt that that they never owed
3:30 The original debt collection law began in 1978 before modern-day technology
4:17 How Regulation F protects you being contacted by debt collectors via text unless you approve
5:36 How the new 7-in-7 rule protects you from unwanted debt collection phone calls
8:01 What to do if you’re getting too many debt collector calls or texts
10:25 Debt collectors need to send you a validation notice within five days of contact with a tear-off sheet
11:55 What has to be on a debt validation notice
13:41 Don’t ignore a debt validation notice, but dispute it
14:32 Debt collectors can’t post anything public on your social media
16:02 Debt collectors can’t put things on your credit report without contacting you first 
17:48 Other new rules debt collectors must follow
19:00 Why you shouldn’t send any money to a debt collector for an old debt
20:30 Does Regulation F apply to all debt collectors? 
22:00 Debt collectors will not inform seniors of their rights
22:19 How to contact the HELPS Nonprofit Law Firm for free legal help

The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act was enacted in 1978, but gets tweaked occasionally. The latest round of changes, known as Regulation F, gives new rules around 
cell phones, email, social media and more modern innovations. For example,  Regulation F prohibits any debt collector from making more than 7 phone calls to a consumer in 7 days, if a consumer cannot be contacted. If the consumer can be contacted, and a phone conversation occurs, the debt collector cannot attempt to call the consumer again until seven days have passed from the day of the conversation. 

Whether you're in debt, or have never borrowed a cent, you need to know the recent changes in the laws regarding debt collection. Why? Because debt collectors may come after you even if it wasn't your debt to begin with! Just sharing the same name as someone else may get you harassed by debt collectors, and seniors can be especially vulnerable to debt collector intimidation. 

Kaisa Janzen is the Assistant Director of the HELPS Nonprofit Law Firm which helps low-income seniors and others who are struggling financially. In this video, the attorney will explain how new laws protect you, including:

How often can debt collectors call?
How your credit report is protected
How your social media is protected 
How your email is protected
What is the 7 in 7 rule?

You'll also learn why you shouldn't ignore a debt collector, what not to say to them, why you shouldn't send them even a nickel without knowing the consequences of your actions, and where you can get free legal help. 

Jeff Hoyt is SeniorLiving.org’s Editor-in-Chief.

To learn why seniors don't need to worry about old debts, watch https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FDlyud-vG90

For how to deal with debt collectors, watch https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b7Xg5O0dJAY

Learn how to master the debt collection process by watching https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aw78_lSLjRk

To learn how seniors can avoid paying taxes, watch https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xv7Om8SAIAM

Subscribe to SeniorLiving.org on YouTube:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCIYQwu7wEpLyijISnF5Z6eA?sub_confirmation=1 

For more tips for seniors:  https://www.seniorliving.org/

If you're interested in joining the hundreds of thousands of families who've found senior living communities on SeniorLiving.org, read the reviews on our website: https://www.seniorliving.org/housing/

To contact the HELPS Nonprofit Law Firm, call 1-855-435-7787 or visit helpsishere.org.

metadata.author: Alabama Consumer Protection Lawyers

Today we wanted to give you an overview of what to expect when you're dealing with a FDCPA lawsuit against an abusive debt collector. 

We cover all that happens from the beginning of the lawsuit to the trial, and everything in between. 

We'd be happy to delve in further and elaborate more on this process if you're interested. 

Just let us know in the comments.

Thanks for watching!

John G. Watts
Watts & Herring, LLC
Representing consumers across Alabama
205-879-2447
https://www.alabamaconsumer.com/
https://www.alabamaconsumer.com/contact-us/  (to send us a message)

metadata.title: Debt Collectors: Know Your Rights Before You Pay a Dollar 🛡️
metadata.author: WealthCurve
metadata.shortDescription:
A debt collector is calling about a debt you don't recognize — and your first instinct is to pay it just to make the calls stop. Don't. Federal law gives you real rights, and most people never use them. In this video: who the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act covers (third-party collectors, not original creditors), the validation notice every collector must send within 5 days of first contact, your 30-day window to demand proof in writing, the things collectors are never allowed to do, the time-barred debt trap hidden in old debts, the short validation letter that makes them prove it, and what to do if they break the law — including complaints to the CFPB and your right to sue within one year.

Chapters:
00:00 - A collector is calling — don't pay yet
00:57 - Who the law covers: FDCPA and Regulation F
02:00 - The validation notice: 5 days
02:56 - Your 30-day window to demand proof
03:50 - What collectors can never do
04:46 - Time-barred debt: the hidden trap
05:49 - The validation letter (copy this)
06:49 - If they break the law: your 3 moves
07:50 - Your checklist

⚠️ Educational content only - not legal or financial advice. Rules vary by state.
🤖 This video uses AI-generated voiceover and visuals.

🔔 Follow WealthCurve for daily money tips!

📺 Channel: https://www.youtube.com/@WealthCurveTV
Hashtags: #DebtCollectors #FDCPA #ConsumerRights #KnowYourRights #PersonalFinance #WealthCurve

metadata.title: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA): Definition and Rules
metadata.author: Simple Explain
metadata.shortDescription:
The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) is a federal law that limits the actions of third-party debt collectors who are attempting to collect debts on behalf of another person or entity. It creates a structure within which debt collectors are allowed to work in an attempt to make debt collection a fair and nonaggressive process. The law covers how and when debt collectors can contact debtors, as well as what constitutes harassment or violations of the law. If a debt collector violates the FDCPA, the debtor can sue them for damages and legal fees.

metadata.title: Debt Collector Rights: What They Can and Can't Do
metadata.author: Night Ferry
metadata.shortDescription:
Debt collectors, explained: in the US, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) and the CFPB's Regulation F generally cover third-party debt collectors (collection agencies, collection lawyers and usually debt buyers), not most original creditors collecting their own debts; state laws vary and some cover original creditors. We follow an invented card debt as it's charged off, sold and placed with a collector, then read its validation notice: who's collecting, for whom, how the amount was built up from a reference date, and the deadline. A written dispute sent within the validation period (it can arrive later) makes the collector, once it receives it, pause collecting the debt, or the disputed part, until it sends verification; a written request for the original creditor's name and address works the same way. In the example, Memorial Day moves the assumed receipt date, so the printed deadline is June 26.

Then the limits: more than seven counted calls about one debt within seven days, or another counted call within seven days after a phone conversation about it, is presumed to violate the law (calls only, generally per debt, some calls excluded, and rebuttable); no contact before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. your time unless you agree; no contact at work once they know it isn't allowed; no lying, fake lawyers or arrest threats; and an opt-out in every email or text. Collectors may contact you, report to credit bureaus after speaking with you, or after mailing or messaging you and waiting a reasonable time for a bounce-back, and sue within the time limit. We cover the two clocks for old debt (a state statute of limitations vs the generally seven-year credit-report clock), why in some states a payment can restart the lawsuit clock, what happens if you're sued, federal garnishment limits and the automatic bank protection for recent direct-deposited federal benefits, fake-collector warning signs, and the FDCPA's one-year window to sue a collector that broke the law, for actual damages plus up to $1,000 in additional damages per individual lawsuit and, if successful, costs and attorney's fees (you may still owe the debt). Legal information, not legal advice: every example is illustrative.

Chapters

0:34 How a debt reaches a collector
1:26 The validation notice and disputes
3:16 What debt collectors can and can't do
5:18 Old debt: two different clocks
6:30 If a debt collector sues you
7:35 Fake debt collectors and your options

Key sources
- Regulation F, 12 CFR part 1006 (eCFR): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1006
- FDCPA, 15 U.S.C. 1692k: civil liability: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1692k

- CFPB: What is a debt validation notice?: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-debt-validation-notice-and-how-do-i-respond-en-1695/

segments.text: Your phone rings: a debt collector, about a debt you don't recognize.
At the CFPB, a US consumer finance regulator,
debts people say they don't owe have been the top debt-collection complaint issue
every year since 2013.
In 2024, in 60% of those the CFPB analyzed,
people said the debt wasn't theirs.
You'll see the letter that can pause collection,
and the call rules.
So what can debt collectors do, and what can't they?
Why would a stranger collect your debt?
Take Dana, an invented example.
Her Lantern Bank card first missed a payment on August 20th,
Banks generally write card debt off their books,
or charge it off, at about 180 days past due;
That's accounting, not forgiveness: she still owes $2,340.
Lantern sold it to a debt buyer, which placed it with Ridgeline,
a collection agency.
That handoff matters.
In the US, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act,
or FDCPA, and the CFPB's rule, Regulation F,
generally cover third-party debt collectors:
collection agencies, collection lawyers and usually debt buyers.
Not, generally, a creditor collecting its own debt,
or business debts.
Most states add their own laws, and some cover original creditors.
Ridgeline's first contact is a letter, mailed May 19th:
a validation notice.
Collectors generally must give this information at first contact,
in writing or orally, or send it within 5 days.
It names the collector, the creditor now, and the one on the itemization date,
a reference date the collector picks.
Then the math: $2,340 on the charge-off date,
minus a $45 credit and a $100 payment, leaves $2,195.
And a deadline.
When is that deadline?
Not simply 30 days after the letter.
A collector may assume the notice arrived 5 days after mailing,
skipping weekends and federal holidays.
Memorial Day makes that May 27th.
The deadline is 30 calendar days later: June 26th.
The printed date counts, and a collector can set a later one.
A debt collector's first letter has a deadline that matters.
Under the CFPB's Regulation F, if a consumer sends a written dispute by then,
the collector, once it receives it, must stop collecting the debt,
or the disputed part, until it sends verification,
like a copy of the bill.
It can arrive later and still count.
A written request for the original creditor's name and address works the same way.
A phone call alone doesn't.
In this invented example, Dana's validation period starts May 19th,
when the notice is mailed.
It's assumed received May 27th, so the deadline is June 26th.
On June 10th, she mails back its tear-off form by certified mail,
disputing the debt and requesting the original creditor's details.
It arrives June 15th, and collection must pause until Ridgeline sends both:
here, June 29th.
How many calls is too many?
In this invented example, a collector calls Dana about one debt,
starting Monday, June 1st.
Under Regulation F, the federal debt collection rule,
more than 7 calls about a debt within 7 days is presumed to break the law.
Rings and voicemails count.
Thursday's ringing call makes 6; a busy signal that day doesn't count.
Friday's call is the 7th.
Saturday's, the 8th.
A second trigger: after a phone conversation about the debt,
another counted call about it within 7 days,
counting that day as day 1, is presumed a violation.
Dana's talk on June 9th puts a June 12th call over the line.
These are presumptions: 7 calls in one day could still be harassment.
Texts and emails aren't counted, but can't harass either,
and each must offer a simple opt-out.
Ridgeline's first call reached Dana at 7:30 in the morning,
her time.
Collectors can't contact you before 8 in the morning or after 9 at night,
your time, unless you agree, or at other times or places you say are inconvenient.
Nor at work, once they know your employer forbids it.
Saying you can't take personal calls there is enough.
A collector generally can't discuss your debt with your boss,
friends or most relatives; it can usually contact them only to find you.
It can't pose as a lawyer or a government agency,
threaten arrest, or threaten action it can't legally take or doesn't intend to,
lie about what you owe, or add interest or fees the agreement or law doesn't allow.
So what can they do?
Plenty: call, write, email, text or send private social-media messages,
within those limits.
Report the debt to credit bureaus, once they've talked with you about it,
or mailed or messaged you and waited a reasonable time for a bounce-back;
14 days counts.
And sue, within the time limit.
But not post about it publicly, or ignore an opt-out.
Can a debt be too old to sue over, yet still on your credit report?
Yes.
The lawsuit clock, the statute of limitations,
depends on state law and the type of debt: 3 to 6 years in most states,
longer in some.
The credit-report clock is federal: generally 7 years,
starting 180 days after the first missed payment of the delinquency that led to
collection.
In this invented example, Dana's debt first went delinquent on August 20th,
2025, and was never brought current.
Say her state's limit is 4 years from then.
After about August 20th, 2029, it's time-barred:
a collector must not sue or threaten to sue,
though in most states it may still ask for payment.
But by the bureaus' usual practice, it can stay on her report until about August
Is paying a little on an old debt harmless?
Not always.
In some states, a payment, or admitting the debt in writing,
can restart the lawsuit clock.
If Dana lived in one, a payment in October 2029 would start 4 new years,
to about October 2033.
Her credit-report clock stays tied to the missed payment that began the delinquency.
What if a collector sues?
Pew's 2020 report found that over the prior decade,
in the courts with data, more than 70% of debt collection lawsuits ended in default
judgments: rulings made when the person sued doesn't respond.
The CFPB says to respond by the date in the court papers;
deadlines vary.
Without a response, a default judgment can add costs,
interest and attorney fees, as allowed.
For ordinary debts, a private collector generally needs a court judgment before it
can garnish, or take money from, wages or a bank account;
depending on state law, courts can sometimes order limited freezes or attachments
before judgment.
For ordinary debts, federal law caps wage garnishment at a quarter of weekly
disposable earnings, or less for low earners.
At today's $7.25 federal minimum wage, nothing can be garnished from $217.50
a week or less.
And banks must automatically protect 2 months of qualifying direct-deposited federal
benefits, like Social Security, SSI or VA benefits,
up to the balance.
Other exempt money may need to be claimed.
Back to that unfamiliar debt: some callers aren't real collectors.
FTC warning signs: they won't give a mailing address or phone number,
or they threaten arrest or reporting you to the police.
Scammers may insist on gift cards, wire transfers,
crypto or a payment app.
But real collectors may call about unfamiliar debts too,
if they were sold.
The FTC suggests sharing nothing personal or financial until validation information
arrives.
The CFPB and FTC suggest disputing in writing,
by certified mail with a return receipt, and keeping records.
Problems can be reported to the CFPB, the FTC or a state attorney general.
Federal law also gives people 1 year from a violation to sue a collector:
for actual damages, up to $1,000 more per lawsuit,
and, if they win, costs and lawyer's fees.
The debt may still be owed.
So, in 3 lines.
A written dispute sent by the notice's deadline pauses collection,
once received, until verification is sent.
More than 7 counted calls about one debt in 7 days,
or another within 7 days after a phone conversation,
is presumed illegal.
And collectors must not sue or threaten to sue over time-barred debt,
though in some states a payment can restart that clock.
Thanks for riding the Night Ferry.

metadata.title: Case Decision FDCPA Definition of Debt Collector of Debt Buyer --  Barbato v Crown Asset
metadata.author: Alabama Consumer Protection Lawyers
metadata.shortDescription:
This is a very important decision that helps consumers when dealing with debt buyers -- it says under the FDCPA that debt buyers are considered debt collectors and subject to the FDCPA.

The decision is Barbato v Greystone Alliance, 960 F.3d 260 (3rd Cir. 2019) -- the google scholar link is here:  https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12917476254464533173&q=916+F.+3d+260&hl=en&as_sdt=203&as_ylo=2019

We go over most of the opinion in detail -- so it is a long video.  If you have no interest in the FDCPA (Fair Debt Collection Practices Act) then definitely skip this one.  :)

But if you are interested in seeing a “cutting edge” argument by debt buyers get shot down, then read the opinion and if you find any value in my commentary, watch the video.  :)

Let me know if you like these and thanks for watching!

John

John G. Watts
Watts & Herring, LLC
Representing consumers across Alabama
205-879-2447
http://www.alabamaconsumer.com/

metadata.title: Web Scraping for Law Firms - STOP manually tracking court dates and dockets
metadata.author: Martin Kravchenko
metadata.shortDescription:
As a boutique law firm, time is your most precious resource. 

Every minute spent on tedious administrative tasks is a minute not spent on billable work or growing your practice.

But what if I told you there was a way to reclaim countless hours of lost productivity using a powerful technique called web scraping? 

Even better - you can do it without writing a single line of code!

Web scraping allows you to extract structured data from any website into convenient formats like CSV and Excel. 

Here are 3 ways boutique law firms can use web scraping to their advantage:

1️⃣ Monitor court dates & dockets - Easily track and extract upcoming court dates, case details and docket entries from court websites. Stay on top of your cases without manual checking.

2️⃣ Keep tabs on the competition - Automatically monitor your competitors' websites for any updates or changes to their services, pricing, or personnel. Always know what they're up to!

3️⃣ Capture the latest legal news & rulings - Set up web scraping to pull the latest legal news, rulings and regulatory changes from key websites. Stay informed with zero effort.

The best part? You can do all this using no-code tools like Octoparse. 

In the video below, I walk through exactly how to use Octoparse to scrape patent data from the US patent database - no coding required!

With a little creativity, you can adapt this for any web scraping use case relevant to your firm.

Implement even one of these web scraping ideas and you'll give your boutique firm an instant productivity boost. 

Go try it out!

Disclaimer: Be sure to review the terms of service of any website you scrape. Some sites prohibit automated scraping which could be against their TOS.

---

If you're a boutique law firm owner struggling to keep up with admin, I post on how to use Automation and AI systems to make your firm human-less. 🛎️

Ready to work smarter, and not harder? DM me "Automation" for more details. 🔝

==================================

I'm Martin Kravchenko, CTO at a Law Firm Growth company dedicated to helping law firms like yours save time, increase productivity, and scale effectively using legal tech and automation. 

⚖️Want to learn how to grow your law firm?
Visit Swans (formerly known as "Automation for Lawyers"): https://swans.co/ 

📚Join our FREE online Legal Tech community: https://www.skool.com/automation-for-lawyers-2634/about (only for law firm owners and managers)

Find me on
Facebook:   https://www.facebook.com/martin.kravchenko.0/
LinkedIn:  https://www.linkedin.com/in/martinkravchenko/
TikTok:  https://www.tiktok.com/@martin.kravchenko
