metadata.title: How to Defeat Your Employer's Motion for Summary Judgement at EEOC - Employment Discrimination
metadata.author: Fight Employment Discrimination
metadata.shortDescription:
An employer's motion for summary judgement is one of the unhappy surprises that await you, once your case is finally assigned to an EEOC judge.   Most of us don't expect it, and don't realize that it's a strategy that a lot of employers use to beat back employee discrimination claims, and deprive us of our day in court. 

Before you can win your discrimination case, you'll have to stop your employer's motion.  Here's how I stopped NASA's Motion for Summary Judgement, and went on to win my employment discrimination  claim at EEOC.   

These are my practical tips for nailing your response to your employer's motion for SJ, put in easy-to-understand language, in the hope of helping others fight smart, hang in & win their EEOC cases.   

I am not an employment attorney,  just an employee who filed a discrimination claim against NASA and won my case, and maximum damages, in an EEOC court.  

My claim against NASA was on the basis of disability discrimination, but the practical tips in this video can help anyone who is facing a potential Summary Judgement in an employment discrimination or harassment claim at EEOC Administrative.

I am not an attorney, just an employee who fought discrimination through the EEOC and won my case against employment discrimination at NASA.  

Workplace discrimination is wrong.  Beating it is a hard fight.


NOTE:  I AM NOT AN ATTORNEY, JUST AN EMPLOYEE WHO WON AT EEOC!  
For an attorney's perspective on beating Motions for Summary Judgement, I like these channels.  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MBy0eCtzTWc



Here's an attorney who's excellent at explaining law topics to normal people:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OZ9HpY7_eFg&t=192s

For a simple, easy-to-understand overview of Summary Judgement, this is as simple as it gets.    
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hMhIyh2WjjY

---- All opinions are my own. Not LEGAL advice. Just me sharing my perspective as an employee who went through the EEOC claims process & won. I am not an expert at all things EEOC. While I do my best to be factual in my observations, viewers should assume that all observations or statements are ALLEGEDLY. *Never trust your fate to a YouTube content creator. Do your own research, pilot your own vessel. *

--- Background photo on thumb courtesy of searchable NASA Image Library: https://images.nasa.gov/

metadata.title: Debt Collection 101: Tips for Successful Skiptracing at Scale
metadata.author: Arbeit U
metadata.shortDescription:
Skiptracing is one of the most important parts of your debt collection process, and finding the data is just as important as knowing what to do with it. 

We wanted to speak to an expert about what skiptracing services are available, how to find those services and how to make sure you are using the data to it's fullest potential. 

Luckily, we met Chris Ball of Belvista Software. Belvista Software, LLC was founded in 2019 with mission to help businesses realize the full potential of their technology investments - one of which is skiptracing. 

Chris answered all our questions about skiptracing at scale and how agencies can maximize their productivity and effectiveness with the skiptracing investments they make. 

If you'd like to skip to a topic, use the timestamps below:

What Skiptracing Services are Currently Available and How Can You Find Them? [1:28]
What are Some Elements to Differentiate Services and Green Lights to Unique or Effective Services? [2:20]
What Are Some Matching Criteria that Agents Can Use to Identify Consumers Correctly? [3:31]
How Can an Agency Ensure the Data Gets in Front of the Right People? [4:14]
Are there Ways to Automate the Skiptracing Process? [6:08]
What are Some KPIs that Agencies Can Look to to Measure the Effectiveness of Skiptracing Efforts? [7:28]

About Our Guest

Chris Ball has spent his entire career in the debt collection industry. It was his first job out of college, and he has been supporting and implementing technology, best practices and processes for the industry ever since. He founded Belvista Software, a consulting and software development firm for the industry, in December of 2019. With his business, he helps agencies of all sizes solve their technology problems. 

To learn more about Belvista Software, click here: https://belvistasoftware.com/about/

metadata.title: How to Enforce a Foreign Judgment
metadata.author: Snellings Law LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
How to Enforce a Foreign Judgment

A foreign judgment is a judgment entered into in any jurisdiction but your own. It can be a judgment entered into in a different state or even a different country. Generally, a state court only has power to address matters within its boundaries. However, there are several ways that a state court may be able to enforce a foreign judgment.

1. Money Judgments From Other States

The U.S. Constitution provides that judgments from one state should be given full faith and credit in other states. This means that a judgment entered into in one state should essentially have effect nationwide. However, for a state court to enforce a foreign judgment from another state, the home state will have to "domesticate" the judgment. The process of domestication entails the creditor filing the judgment in the home state, and then the judgment will be treated as if a court in that state made the judgment. After the filing, the judgment will then be served on the debtor and the home state court can enforce the judgment.

2. Non-Monetary Judgments From Other States

It can be much more complicated to enforce judgments from foreign jurisdictions that have do with non-monetary concerns. In many cases, you may need to file an independent civil action in your home state and seek a new judgment. But while you may need to file a new lawsuit, you should know that the foreign state's ruling is usually given great deference so long as that state had proper jurisdiction over the matter and there is no indication of fraud.

3. Money Judgments From Foreign Countries

The U.S. is not obligated to recognize any judgments rendered in a foreign country. Just as foreign countries do not have to recognize a monetary judgment made in the U.S. However, some states do have laws that provide for recognition of foreign judgments. You will want to talk to an attorney in your jurisdiction to learn the laws in your state. If your state does recognize monetary judgments from other countries, the creditor typically will need to bring an action in the home state so that the state court can domesticate the order.

metadata.author: Florida Trust, Real Estate, Probate, & Foreclosure
metadata.shortDescription:
⚖️ WEIDNER LAW | Florida Appellate Oral Argument Series

You won a judgment in another state — but can Florida block it because the statute of limitations has run? This oral argument examines one of the most misunderstood intersections in Florida law: foreign judgment enforcement and time limitations. Essential viewing for anyone dealing with out-of-state judgments or domestic judgment collection.

📋 CASE NO.: 2D13-3355 | Florida 2nd District Court of Appeal
📅 DATE: 2015

🏛️ THE LEGAL ISSUES:
• Florida's Enforcement of Foreign Judgments Act
• Statute of limitations defenses to foreign judgment domestication
• Full faith and credit — constitutional vs. procedural protections
• What Florida courts do when sister-state judgments are stale

👁️ WATCH FOR: The panel's dissection of whether the limitations period runs from the original judgment date or domestication — a crucial distinction that trips up many attorneys.

🔔 Subscribe | Weidner Law — Florida's appellate court, unfiltered
🌐 mattweidnerlaw.com | St. Petersburg, Florida | 727-954-8752

#ForeignJudgment #StatuteOfLimitations #FloridaLaw #AppellateCourt #DebtCollection #OralArgument #WeidnerLaw #CivilLitigation #JudgmentEnforcement #FloridaAppellate

metadata.title: How To Enforce Foreign Judgments in the USA & How US based Agencies Can Reach Offshore Activity   Of
metadata.author: OffshoreAlert
metadata.shortDescription:
Obtaining a judgment in a British Commonwealth jurisdiction, whether in the United Kingdom or one of its offshore territories, is no easy feat. The sad truth is that wining the case might have been the easy part. Enforcing a judgment when there are few or no assets in the jurisdiction issuing the writ can involve complex cross-border litigation.

Execution of a judgment is even more difficult when assets, or individuals subject to the judgment, are in the United States, where a web of federal and fifty different state laws can stymie even the most tenacious judgment-holder.

This session will explore the process and methods to enforce foreign judgments in the U.S., and impart practical tips to do so quickly and efficiently. It will also show how U.S.-based agencies can reach offshore activity.

Speakers:

- Jon Sablone, Partner, Nixon Peabody
- Robert Fisher, Counsel, Nixon Peabody

This session was recorded on April 30, 2019 at The OffshoreAlert Conference on Financial Intelligence & Investigations which took place at the Miami Beach EDITION hotel in Miami Beach, Florida.

To learn more, visit: https://www.offshorealert.com/conference/miami/

segments.text: i had a very interesting question raised
in a live stream about enforcing a
foreign judgment in the united kingdom
now whilst this subject is far too vast
to go into in any great detail
i did think it was worth providing
something of an overview
for those that are interested but first
of all if you're new to me i'm a
barrister who helps you understand law
so make sure you hit that subscribe
button and perhaps
one of your questions will find its way
into a video very soon
so of course the game and the objective
of any civil litigation is to enforce a
judgment
if you are successful whether that's a
money judgment
or whether it is an order of the court
prohibiting someone else or another
company from doing something
or ordering that they do so but the
question raised is what do you do with a
judgment that you've obtained in a
foreign jurisdiction
now for the purposes of this video i'm
going to talk about money judgments
predominantly because there are several
different types of judgments such as
divorce settlements
which i can cover in another video as a
starting point there is a difference
between getting a judgment recognized
and then getting a judgment enforced but
getting it recognized is usually the
first step in this process
once a judgment is recognized it really
ought to prevent a party from
re-litigating it in the hopes of a
better decision or
redefending it in the hopes of a better
decision whereas
enforcement of a judgment quite a part
is taking some
actual step in order to enforce that
judgment if you hold a judgment in your
favor you become a judgment
creditor until that judgment has been
fulfilled and you have been paid
if you've had a judgment against you you
become a judgment
debtor in other words you owe the
judgment creditor a debt
under the judgment as a judgment
creditor you can take these positive
steps against the judgment debtor
in order to settle your judgment debt
this may very well be by
seizing the judgment debtors assets such
as property
or even freezing money in a bank account
or obtaining an attachment to earnings
which is a deduction from money earned
in a salary
paid by the employer an attachment to
earnings for example would be deducted
before the salaries paid to the judgment
debtor
however before that happens as i said
you need to get the judgment
recognized no judgment can be enforced
unless of course
it has been recognized first and whilst
there are certain principles apply
in recognizing a judgment wherever it's
come from there aren't any special
procedures for this
like there are most certainly with
enforcing a judgment so with so many
different places and so many different
systems let's talk about how we begin
to think about getting a judgment
recognized and then moving on to
enforcement steps
and this is broken down in what we call
a regime so there are broadly four
different regimes under which we can
seek to enforce a foreign judgment in
england and wales this will depend on
from where the judgment originates
and the date the proceedings commenced
so firstly we have the uk regime it
should go without saying that judgments
from england and wales can be enforced
in england and wales with no particular
recognition
it is a recognized judgment because that
is where it has been
issued so outside of england and wales
we have the rest of the uk regime which
is of course
scotland and northern ireland next and
very slightly tricky we have the
european regime
this will apply to proceedings that were
issued before the 31st of december
2020 and just to note that this regime
will not apply to
cases issued later those judgments that
originate from proceedings that were
issued
after that date will come under the
common law regime which encompasses the
united states
then of course we have judgments from
most of the other commonwealth states
which is the
statutory regime and aside from these
four principal regimes we also have the
hague convention on the choice of court
agreements and again until the 31st of
december 2020 there was a short list of
countries to which this would ordinarily
apply to
so a very broad outline of how you would
set about enforcing a judgment from one
of those regimes would be as follows
as you'll remember from the outset of
the video the typical starting point
would be to get a judgment
recognized and that's the case for
scotland and northern ireland you would
go back to the original court issuing
the judgment and get a certificate
and with a few twists and caveats you
can then apply to the high court to
register the judgment
looking at eu cases that were instigated
before the 31st of december 2020
you are entitled to enforce the judgment
as though it were an
english judgment in the english courts
the judgment creditor can use all of the
normal procedures and methods of
enforcement which i'm going to come back
to
after talking about the regimes as for
cases that fall under the common law
regime which includes cases instigated
after the 31st of december 2020 in the
eu
and united states for example this is a
little bit more complicated for example
to be enforceable at common law a
judgment must be for a definitive sum
of money so for example an injunction
ordered by a court in an eu
state after this date would no longer be
enforceable in
england there are also some complex
rules about jurisdiction and consent
between
territories so typically enforcement of
a foreign judgment under common law will
require
fresh proceedings although the judgment
creditor
may be able to obtain summary judgment
on the basis that there has already been
a judgment
in his or her favor although this is
going to require further steps before
the usual steps will be open for
enforcement as to enforcement of
judgments from commonwealth and some
other countries under the statutory
regime there are several acts and
statutory instruments that cover
different countries and
again broadly speaking it needs to be
for a money judgment for a definitive
sum
and it needs broadly to start with a
recognition or certification of the
judgment and then following
various steps so again this is a very
complex area so that would be your
starting point but i would urge you to
seek
for more legal advice depending on your
specific circumstances
as to the types of enforcement once
you've passed these hurdles of getting a
judgment recognized and or
certified and following those procedures
depending on where your judgment is from
typically you will have similar types of
enforcement available to you
which would be third-party debt orders
which is for example
when your judgement debtor has a bank
account and you have the details
you can apply to have those funds frozen
and paid over to you although before
that happens the judgment deto will have
an opportunity
to argue at court as to why that
shouldn't happen
again that's a subject for another video
on each of these enforcement areas
there are also rits and warrants of
control and there are charging orders
which can apply to
properties so as i said each of these
areas can warrant an in-depth video but
i just wanted to give a very broad
overview as to how we would go about
looking at enforcing a foreign judgment
because it is extremely complicated so
with that said i hope you found this
video useful make sure you drop your
questions and comments in the box below
make sure you check out black belt
secrets if you want to hear my stories
how i became a barrister
why i do what i do and hit that
subscribe button here
so you don't miss out on new videos in
the meantime thanks for watching i'll
see you next time

More Best Asset Protection Strategies and Wealth Preservation Method: https://www.assetprotectiontraining.com/country-automatically-enforce-judgments/



Why use an offshore asset protection trust, an offshore LLC or an offshore bank account?  Simple: Because rulings from US courts aren't worth the paper they are written on in other countries.  To enforce a US judgment in another country the "creditor" has to file another lawsuit (very expensive and time-consuming) and win it (more expensive and time-consuming) .....  if this becomes a risk the protected person just moves his assets to an account in another country (simple, inexpensive and quick) which starts the process all over again.

A solid asset protection plan simply makes it legally and financially unwise to pursue protected funds.

Remember, lawyers, trying to collect money is like common burglars: they want the easy pickings.  Good protection removes their economic incentive to litigate and they go after easier unprotected funds.  

Here it is in a nutshell: If you have a team of trained german shepherds protecting your home and your neighbors have nothing, the burglars are going to hit your neighbor's house.  It is the same with asset protection

metadata.shortDescription:
mike@irs-matters.com    954-328-3501


The normal IRS statute of limitation period is 10 years  on collecting back taxes.


But beware, there are many events that can happen that extend the 10 year statute of limitations.


You must pull an official IRS transcript to find out officially when the statute  is over.


Things like offers in compromise, collection due processes, and bankruptcy extends the iris statute of limitations.

metadata.title: Does Statute of Limitations Stop a Collections Suit
metadata.author: Richardson Law Offices
metadata.shortDescription:
Creditors do not have an unlimited amount of time to sue you to collect the money. If they wait too long to do it, they'll be out of luck. 

 Why? Because New Jersey has a statute limitations that prevents creditors from bringing collection lawsuits after six years. The statutes exist because, after a while, memories fade and documents can get lost or destroyed. This can make it rather difficult for people to either bring a suit or defend themselves against one. 

 When Does the 6 Years Start to Run? 

 The six year starts to run from the date the creditor has the right to see you. In other words, six years from when you default on the agreement to pay the debt. This can be as early as 30 days past the due date for a payment, or six months after the last payment, and the creditor is required to  charge off the debt . 

 The easiest way to do this is to look on your credit report where the debt appears and find the date of charge off. Has it been more than six years since that date? If so, you may have a defense against the lawsuit, should the creditor bring one. 

 When Does It Stop? 

 If the creditor brings suit and successfully gets a judgment against you within that six year period of time, then the statute of limitations is no longer an issue. I have had people call me complaining that their bank was levied upon or their wages garnished on a judgment that was more than six years old. Once suit is brought and the judgment is entered, the clock stops ticking. 

 The clock can also stop and start. Suppose you filed a bankruptcy, and that bankruptcy was dismissed 3 months later without a discharge. The clock stopped ticking for those three months, because the creditor was unable to bring suit against you to collect because of the automatic stay in the bankruptcy. 

 Then the third way the clock can stop is if the creditor simply fails to bring suit within the six year period, and the time runs out. 

 Creditor Sued After Statute of Limitations Ran? 

 So what do you do if the creditor brings a lawsuit after the statute of limitations has passed? Well, the court will not reject the lawsuit on that basis. You must file an answer asserting the statute of limitation's as a defense, and make a motion to dismiss the lawsuit. If you do not, then the creditor will succeed in getting a judgment against you! 

 Sometimes the creditor will try and trick you. If it has been six years since you made your last payment, chances are that the creditor sold the debt to a debt buyer, such as Midland Funding, LVNV Funding, Cavalry Portfolio, or New Century Financial. These debt buyers can try and reset the clock to the date they purchased the debt. This will not hold up if you challenge it. They can't reset the clock. 

 So What Do I Do? 

 If a creditor sues you past the statute of limitations, then you need to take action now! Doing nothing will just result in a judgment being entered against you, your bank account being levied, and/or your wages being garnished. 

 If the suit is for over $10,000, you realize that you need to take action and need a lawyer to assist you, and are ready to hire one, then call my office immediately at 856-432-4113 to schedule an appointment to meet with me.

segments.text: Sued by a debt collector. Here are tips on how to win without paying practically anything. Here
with Consumer Warrior John Skiba. John, good to see you. Hey, Phil. Good to be here with you. So,
John, you’re sued by a debt collector. What are the simple things every consumer can do
without hiring an attorney just to get out and sometimes pay practically nothing? Yeah,
you know, it’s a good question and it’s a huge issue. Debt buyers—these debt companies
that buy debt and sue people—file lawsuits in gigantic volume. The typical large debt
buyer files over 500,000 lawsuits a year throughout the country,
and there are many of them. There are also smaller debt buyers, so a lot of people will
see themselves get impacted by this when they get served with a lawsuit. What I thought we
could do today is just talk about a few tips and strategies that I have used in my 23 years
of doing this. I’ve done over 400 trials against original creditors and debt buyers in these debt
collection lawsuits. I thought we could touch on some of the things that I’ve seen not only in my
own practice but also what I’ve seen consumers who represent themselves do to really prevail.
The first thing I see—and this is going to sound dumb because it’s so simple—is
not some grand legal strategy, not something only lawyers can do, but simply just showing
up and participating in the process. About 95% of people who get sued by a debt collector
don’t respond. They don’t file an answer. If you don’t file an answer,
the game’s over. You’ll get a judgment, and then you’re facing wage garnishment or a bank levy,
which can force you into bankruptcy. Nothing causes bankruptcy filings more
than wage garnishment. Statistics show that 70% of the United States lives paycheck to paycheck,
and if all of a sudden someone takes a quarter of your check, that creates a disaster quickly.
Bankruptcy can stop that, but if we want to avoid that altogether, participating in the process and
filing the answer on time—whether you’re doing it yourself or hiring an attorney—is essential.
I’ll admit that I have won a lot of cases simply by showing up on time to court hearings and making
sure that I’m filing documents correctly. I’ve done trials where I show up early, the attorney
for the debt collector is late, and the court just throws it out. Courts run tight ships—they have
to. The volume of cases they deal with means if someone doesn’t show up or participate,
it’s usually the end of the road for that party. I’ve seen consumers who file their answer,
show up early for pretrial conferences, and even drive to the courthouse the day before
to make sure they know where to park, where to check in, and how to get through security.
In the post-COVID world, you also need to know how to use the Zoom platform. Most courts in Arizona,
where I practice, handle everything virtually now. It’s rare that I go to court in person anymore.
Understanding how to use these platforms and complying with deadlines is critical.
Many consumers who represent themselves don’t meet those deadlines, don’t show up,
and don’t file required documents, and then the case is over. Debt collectors and their attorneys
are counting on that—they know the system, and you don’t. So, the first step is simple:
show up, be on time, be a few minutes early, whether on Zoom or in person.
The second thing I recommend—and an approach I’ve used in my practice and
seen many consumers use—is to push the case out of the court system into private arbitration.
Not every case is eligible for this, but most are. You’ll know if it is by reviewing the terms
and conditions of your credit card agreement, which the creditor will eventually provide. If
there’s an arbitration clause—and there usually is—you can file a motion asking the court to
move the case into arbitration. Arbitration is less formal and managed by private companies,
the biggest being the American Arbitration Association (AAA).
There are a couple of benefits. First, the rules in arbitration are relaxed.
It’s simpler for self-represented people to navigate. In court, the rules of procedure
and evidence can trip you up. Arbitration, by contrast, is much less formal. I once did
an arbitration where the arbitrator showed up in jeans and a T-shirt via Zoom. Second,
creditors generally don’t want to go into arbitration because it’s expensive and outside
their usual process. Most large debt collection law firms have just a few attorneys handling
thousands of cases in a streamlined system. Arbitration throws a wrench in that machine.
It’s also expensive for them. The consumer’s filing fee with AAA is about $200,
but the creditor has to pay between $2,500 and $5,000 upfront, depending on the case size.
If you’re being sued for $3,500, you can see why the creditor won’t want to pay that much to chase
it. Usually, they’ll dismiss the lawsuit or agree to a mutual walk-away settlement.
Here’s how it works: once you’re sued, you respond to the lawsuit. After they provide
the agreement, check for an arbitration clause. If there
is one, file a motion asking the court to move the case into arbitration. If the judge grants it,
the case leaves the court system. You can then file your claim with AAA online.
A great resource for this is the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). Their
website has a database of almost every credit card agreement ever issued. You
can download them for free if you need a copy of your terms and conditions.
Why do creditors even include arbitration clauses? They put them there because
it benefits them by reducing the risk of class-action lawsuits—not
because it helps consumers. But you can still use it. My only caveat: pursue arbitration in
good faith. File with AAA, pay your filing fee, and be ready to proceed. If the creditor refuses
to pay their fee, AAA will close the case, and the court will often dismiss the lawsuit.
The third option—the “nuclear option”—is bankruptcy. Nobody wants to file,
but sometimes it’s the best solution, especially if you’re facing multiple lawsuits
or large balances. Many people think it’s just bad luck when multiple lawsuits hit at once, but
it’s often coordinated. Credit bureaus sell something called a trigger report to creditors,
alerting them to changes in your credit that suggest you might be collectible again—like
buying a car or house. That’s why lawsuits often arrive all at once.
Bankruptcy can stop all lawsuits, garnishments,
and collections immediately and wipe out most unsecured debt. A Chapter 7 typically
takes four to five months. There’s a recovery period, but it’s often faster and more effective
than trying to settle debts individually or through debt consolidation programs.
If you’re embarrassed about bankruptcy, remember that over a million
people file every year. It’s not abuse of the system—it’s a safety
net for people who’ve had job loss, medical issues, or other hardships. Bankruptcy
is even mentioned in the U.S. Constitution because it’s essential to a functioning economy.
So, to recap:
File your Answer and show up on time.
Consider arbitration—it’s often cheaper and easier.
Explore bankruptcy if multiple lawsuits or overwhelming debt make repayment impossible.
It’s about knowing your options, staying involved, and not letting debt collectors win by default.

And so if it had been more than six years since you stopped making payments on it and then they filed their lawsuit, then I can go in and I can ask the court to dismiss it. Now how do you do that? In most jurisdictions you can file what's called a motion to dismiss. This is a written motion that's filed with the court and it outlines to the court what the statute of limitations is, the reason why they violated the statute of limitations, and why their case should be dismissed. Sometimes it's done through what's called a motion for summary judgment, but often, particularly if you're representing yourself, a motion to dismiss will suffice that you submit to the court. This is a pretty huge deal, if you can get this, 'cause not only will it get the case thrown out, it made entitle you to compensation under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, the FDCPA. This states that credit creditors and debt collectors cannot sue you for an amount that you don't owe. And if the statute of limitations has expired and they sued you anyway, they may be opening themselves up to liability. So looking at the statute of limitations, that's the first way that you can get rid of this case without having to actually go through trial. That can all be done through paperwork. So the second thing, though, let's say that they're within the statute of limitations, so you're wondering what other defenses or strategies or techniques you can use to get this case thrown out. One of them is that in virtually every single credit card agreement, and I'm talking about the terms and conditions that they mail out when you open up a credit card, there's a provision in there for private arbitration. And a private arbitration agreement essentially says, look, if there's a dispute between the parties, either party can elect to have this decided by a private arbitrator rather than going through the court process. Now nine times out of 10, actually, I'm going to say almost 100% of the time, the creditor is not going to use the private arbitration clause. They don't want to go through private arbitration, and there's a reason for that, and the main reason is it's really expensive to do it. Their whole goal is to get a judgment against you with spending as little amount of money and time as possible, and then garnish your wages or go after a bank account. That's what their end game is and their whole business model is. But they put this private arbitration clause in there and you, as a party to that contract, can actually invoke it as well, even after a lawsuit is filed. So if there's a lawsuit that's been filed and you see the terms and conditions for the particular credit cards that they're suing you on, and if they haven't provided those to you, you can look those up online. Just put in the year that the card was open, what type of card it was, and you're going to see that there's different depositories online where you're able to download copies of that. Look at the language in the private arbitration clause. This is all the fine print that nobody ever reads when they sign off on these things. And it likely says that you can ask the court to dismiss the case and allow the parties to participate in private arbitration. So that's done by filing a motion to compel private arbitration. You attach a copy of the arbitration clause to that and say, "Look, judge, "this says that either party can request this. "I'm requesting private arbitration." So now you may ask yourself, well, why would I do that? It's just going to kick me out of court and then I've got to deal with this in arbitration. I can tell you in most instances that the creditor is not going to participate. They're the ones that have the claims against you, so they're going to be the ones that are going to have to file the arbitration claim with the private arbitration company. It's usually filed with what's called AAA, the American Arbitration Association. And here's the reason why they're not going to file. The fees on this are very, very high. It could cost them literally more than they're suing you for to be able to try to go through that process. There's an initial filing fee, the arbitrator has to be paid, and then there's some other fees associated with it. So in my experience, if the court compels private arbitration, usually the case is done. The creditor is not going to pursue it. They're going to put you in a different pile and they're going to go onto the next one. So private arbitration is the other way that you can try to resolve this. Now the third and final way is settlement. Now this may be adjusting what you're defining as winning for your debt collection lawsuit. To me, if you can settle this for a low dollar amount, that's still a win in your category. If you can come in, if they're suing you for $5,000 and you can sell this for $800 or $1,000 dollars, that's still a win. Because if someone has said to you before they filed the lawsuit, "Hey, if you pay them $800, this whole thing goes away," you would have jumped on that because that's a pretty good deal. So you can still reach out to the creditor, you can try to settle it, you can offer different proposals. In every jurisdiction under the rules of evidence, settlement discussions are not admissible in court. So if you call them up and say, "Hey, I'll offer you $500 to get this thing to go away," they can't then run into the judge and say, "Hey look, judge, they already offered $500. "Clearly they owe it." They can't do that. So there's some benefit in trying to see if there's some middle ground that can be reached, and generally start lower than the total amount that you're able to pay 'cause no matter what you offer, they're going to come back with some type of counter offer. So those are the really three ways that you can avoid trial altogether and still come out in a positive situation if you're facing a debt collection lawsuit. So again, the first one is to look to see if the statute of limitations has expired. Again, take a look at those notes that I have below the video here, that's going to go through each state statute of limitations. Next you can look at to see if there's a private arbitration clause. Look at the terms and conditions for that particular credit card. And the third is look for different settlement options. I have other videos on my YouTube channel that can walk you through each of these processes individually so that you can see how they are in a little more detail. If you have any other questions, feel free to check out the other videos. I appreciate you watching today.

metadata.title: 7 mistakes when testifying in a debt collection trial
metadata.author: Alabama Consumer Protection Lawyers
metadata.shortDescription:
https://www.alabamaconsumer.com/2014/01/7-mistakes-debt-collection-lawsuit/

Watch this video if you are interested in learning what the 7 common mistakes are and how to avoid them while testifying in a debt collection trial.

1.  Guessing instead of testifying based on personal knowledge.
2.  Answering a question without fullying hearing it.
3.  Answering a question without understanding the question as a whole or individual words in the question.
4.  Answering a question without first taking a moment to think about the truthful answer.
5.  Answering more than is asked -- instead only answer the question actually asked.
6.  Trying to outsmart the collection lawyer.
7.  Having the wrong courtroom appearance including dress, showing up late, not being respectful, etc.

Thanks for watching!

John

John G. Watts
Watts & Herring, LLC
Representing consumers across Alabama

metadata.title: What a New Bill in Congress Means for Collection Attorney Litigation | Ep. 271
metadata.author: Receivables Info | Debt Collection News
metadata.shortDescription:
What happens when a new bill in Congress aims to fix long-standing regulatory conflicts for collection attorneys?

In this episode, Adam Parks sits down with Liz Terry and Michael Stillman of NCBA to unpack why lawmakers are revisiting how litigation versus debt collection requirements are regulated. They walk through the real compliance challenges law firms face today, what the proposed legislation is designed to clarify, and how NCBA’s regulatory advocacy role is shaping the conversation in Washington.

If you manage legal collections, oversee compliance, or rely on litigation strategy, this conversation matters. Listen in, subscribe, and get the context you need to understand how this bill could impact attorney oversight and compliance going forward.


Podcast Website:
https://receivablespodcast.com/videos/dual-regulation-collection-attorneys-ncba

Guest Website:
https://www.creditorsbar.org/ (https://www.creditorsbar.org/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) 

Liz Terry LinkedIn:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/elizabethcterry/

Michael Stillman LinkedIn:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/michael-stillman-5692789/

So, in one of the examples I I like to use, and it's pretty simple, but let's say someone from my office took spoke with consumer A yesterday and on the phone with them, they were trying to work it out or what have you, and my person before terminating the call asked the consumer, do we have permission to contact you within the next seven days again? metadata.title: Bankruptcy Claims Trading
metadata.author: The National Law Review
metadata.shortDescription:
Claims trading in bankruptcy cases has advanced and grown in sophistication swiftly in recent history. For example, the recent spate of digital asset-related filings (FTX, Celsius) has expanded the concept of what kinds of claims, and on what terms, can be traded. Companies and their advisors should be prepared before wading into these waters. How will a claim be treated once transferred? What steps should a company acquiring a claim take to ensure the claim is paid? How should a claim be valued? What kind of documentation will be needed to properly transfer the claim? If a dispute arises regarding the claim, how should the acquiring company defend itself? This webinar focuses on understanding these issues and addressing best practices for advanced reorganization practitioners and advisors working on the cutting edge of bankruptcy transactions.

metadata.title: Advanced Bankruptcy Transactions: Bankruptcy Claims Trading
metadata.author: The National Law Review
metadata.shortDescription:
Claims trading in bankruptcy cases has advanced and grown in sophistication swiftly in recent history. For example, the recent spate of digital asset-related filings (FTX, Celsius) has expanded the concept of what kinds of claims, and on what terms, can be traded. Companies and their advisors should be prepared before wading into these waters. How will a claim be treated once transferred? What steps should a company acquiring a claim take to ensure the claim is paid? How should a claim be valued? What kind of documentation will be needed to properly transfer the claim? If a dispute arises regarding the claim, how should the acquiring company defend itself? This webinar focuses on understanding these issues and addressing best practices for advanced reorganization practitioners and advisors working on the cutting edge of bankruptcy transactions.

Download the free slide deck (PDF) here: 
https://financial-poise-video-webinars.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/2026/ADVANCED_BANKRUPTCY_TRANSACTIONS_/2-Bankruptcy-Claims-Trading/2-Bankruptcy+Claims+Trading.pdf

One is just a a purely economic view is people that are are you're buying it at a discount. So, whether it's a a hedge fund of some kind, whether it's just a a claims trading company, any other sort of investment vehicle that someone may have, it's a purely economic decision. So I think to Joe's, you know, there there is this is a very competitive market. It can be very complex at times and you need to really have the right guide. >> So so David, let me stay with you for a minute because, you know, we were talking about the need for a lawyer, which is obviously critical. And this claims purchase and sale agreement. Can you walk me through what you think a standard claims purchase and sale agreement in order to do its job would have? And what what ultimately is the purpose for those provisions? And then ultimately, how negotiable are those provisions? >> Well, I I think you need to start with what the market what the buying market is going to expect. And the buying market is going to expect that they're buying a class of claim recovery and that they're not taking the unique seller risk of a claim, right? When you have a bond indenture or you have a loan credit agreement, wherever you are in the bonds, wherever you are in that bank debt, [clears throat] the buyer's able to review that instrument and understand exactly what rights and obligations they have vis-à-vis the debtor. Each claim might be unique, right? And and and that is not a unique risk that most buyers are willing to take. So as a seller, you need to understand that the expectation of the market is that you're going to be making reps and warranties and providing indemnity around we go back to our plumber, that that million dollar plumber's claim is going to be recognized as a million dollar general unsecured claim. That being said, as your claim becomes allowed, as cases mature, as the market becomes more competitive, there are sometimes when you can sell it more of on an as-is basis with basic representations and warranties, not no representations, but basic representations and warranties. And because that claim has been allowed by the bankruptcy court in fine by final order, that there may be certain opportunities to buy that claim without the seller guaranteeing the the notional amount. But ultimately, I think you know, the expectation, I'd love to hear if others have different views, the expectation of the market is that you're buying a class a classified claim. >> Any anybody else? I'll throw it out to the group. Anybody else have any, you know, views on that and expectations? >> Look, there's very standard documents today, much much more standard than, you know, we've ever seen and shorter documents. And folks like our firm and and and David and Matt, we we've you know, we've revised those documents many times over the years. But what I'd say is if you're a seller, you want as little reps as possible. If you're a buyer, you want as much as possible, you know, just being blunt. The question is as a buyer, if you're in a competitive auction, you need to ask yourself, is the counterparty valuable to you? If if something goes wrong, can I go after them? Um are they creditworthy? Um because at the end of the day, why does a small vendor sell their claim? Because they need money. Presumably they're not like as creditworthy as, you know, you would otherwise hope. So those are the issues in a nutshell. >> Interesting. So and and maybe you guys I'll be a little unfair about the question and I'll throw it open to the group, but you know, have there been cases where the agreements have been challenged and actually held up in courts of law? >> Yes. There have been. Um and you know, it's usually when there's disparate information from the buyer and the seller or there's been a change in the market. And you know, um there's a recent case. It's not in a bankruptcy, um but I'll I'll cite it. Oak Tree Capital Management sued BJ's Wholesale Club on a 21 on a $29 million it's called AIPA tax refund claim that they were buying for $20 million and at the time that the deal was negotiated, um BJ's had no sense of when payments would start. And after the deal was and that's 70 cents on the dollar, by the way. After the deal was negotiated, um the administration announced that payments were going to start. So that's a kind of very so something changed in the environment. BJ said, hey, we never consummated this deal. There wasn't a meeting of the minds, but there likely was, right? Um and Oaktree said going to sue you for you know, 9 million bucks, BJs. >> Wow. And do we know the ending to that story or at this point is it still pending? >> Well, the the the ending is this is that neither party is in the [clears throat] position they expected to be when they entered into the trade and now they're paying lawyers and they're going sideways and BJs BJs does not have the liquidity that they expected to have. And I will tell you, this is a story that we see over and over with claims sellers that don't get the right counsel up front, don't understand that a agreement to agree is binding and that um they need to understand and and be counseled, you know, at the term sheet stage on on what they're they're agreeing to. And so I I you know, what what we always say to our selling clients is if you wind up in this situation where you're now litigating over uh you know, the enforceability of a trade, that's not what you start. That's not what you came here for. It's not what you came here for as a buyer. It's not what you came here for as a seller. And if parties are properly advised, a lot of those issues can be avoided. >> Okay. So Joe, let me turn back to you. Let's let's just briefly touch in touch on the the question on some specific examples. And in this specific example, we're talking about the good faith of the entity acquiring the claims. Scenario one, for example, to protect the position, a lender goes out into the market and buys unsecured claims for the purpose of blocking reorganization, not because they think it's a great investment. Is that permitted? >> So there is um a good faith standard um that um courts have um employed or or or ruled that um you need to um acquire claims in in good faith. And um there is some case law there um um both ways, by the way, because um we used to see in the claims world people acquiring claims for the purpose of proposing a plan or um you know or or owning the asset. We see that much much less now. >> Okay. And and and the same thing, David, would go to you. I'm a competitor. Uh I'm Best Buy, and I want to you know I don't want Circuit City in my market anymore. I'll buy those claims just to create chaos and potentially put them out of business. Uh is that a good Is that a good Is that a plausible business strategy for Best Buy? >> Probably not. But you know you may have You may be able to have standing you know when you when you buy a claim and you become a creditor and you transfer visa be 3001, you have standing as a party in interest. But what that means if you're one of thousands of general unsecured um creditors, what that means visa be your ability to influence a a plan um is really going to depend on the size, the timing of your entry into the case um and how you're viewed by other parties. >> Um Cliff, I want to give a referral of the so Enron Bartman, which is uh a BAP decision um in 2025 BAP number 246019 there was an interesting um the court held that good faith under section 363M of the bankruptcy code can be implied from the absence of bad faith evidence that you didn't have to give affirmative proof of good faith. Obviously the dissent disagreed with that, but I think you know as David said earlier if you're litigating these issues jeez a lot of money better be at stake and two you know that's not what either party you know really bargain for at the outset. >> So so we have to that point and and I and I don't know the year, but if you go back there's a Bear Stearns Hitachi dispute uh probably 20 years ago the case and and and what the outcome of the case is they they there was preliminary emails traded back and forth where Hitachi was selling a vendor claim to Bear Stearns and they had agreed um on price and the notional amount of the claim and subject to docs. And what the court ultimately said was what was required of the parties and Hitachi said there's nothing here and Bear Stearns sued and the parties were sent back and the court said what was required was a negotiation in good faith. And so what you'll see in many trade claim confirms these days is that the parties agree that they're going to negotiate towards settlement in good faith uh towards a type two New York law uh agreement. The the issue becomes and one that I'm fascinated with and will spend another two hours on at another time is what is good faith? Right? As Joe as Joe said, and what did the addition, what are those? And that's really where you get stuck with people like me litigating these issues, and that's not why you came to the party. Right? So while it's fun for me, it's not fun for a buyer or a seller, and why it's more important to do the work and make sure we have a clean trade upfront for all parties. >> Understood. And you know, Matt, let me let me just turn to you because [clears throat] Joe said something that peaked my curiosity, and it's sort of on on the line of something that I think I'd like you to weigh in on, and that is, when are these agreements binding? Joe had said an agreement to an agree is binding. So, you know, if I'm talking to a claims buyer, am I already sudden bound? Where does the line there? >> Uh, it depends. That's the best answer, right? It depends on what's the I mean, you're going to apply the same analysis to a claims trading agreement as you do to any other any other agreement under under state statutes, right? What what are the material terms and were they discussed? If they were, even if there's language that says this is subject to final final approval or subject to final documentation, if you talked about the price and you talked about some indemnification and you talked about when the closing was going to be, you're probably there. And and the difficulty in bankruptcy cases is the speed at which things tend to move. You know, you want to if you're early in the case and you want to minimize your risk as a seller, you you want to get this thing done fast. And so maybe you're shooting emails back and forth with terms, and and every email says, you know, subject to final documentation, things fall through. Well, maybe you've got a deal you already made via email, right? So it's it's the the law of the state's going to apply and it's going to the same way it does to any other contract. >> Interesting. So, I'm going to leave actually where I know we're running up on the time frame. So, I'm going to leave you with one question for Joe and then we can all talk about it as really was fascinating for me and that is I'm an insider to a company and I want to sell my claim to someone. My my first question, Joe, is is that if it's an unsecured claim, is there a some sort of a taint on it because it's an insider claim that shouldn't be sold? What are what are you getting when you buy my insider claim? >> Yeah, I mean that's a that's a risky trade. Um you know, obviously insiders have a fiduciary duty, a higher they're viewed in a with a higher lens and um to the extent that they're let's say they had uh a claim for um you know an employment contract or something like that that they're looking to monetize on. Um you know, you always have to ask yourself when a third party reviews these claims are they going to be um you know objective about it or are they going to somehow look to subordinate that claim? David, what do you think? >> You're on mute, David. >> Look, I I think you you have to do the work, right? You you have to do the work and you have to look at the different parties and the angles that are being taken in a case and this goes back to the question you asked Joe about the documentation and can you clean everything you need to know from a docket um and what's filed with the court and there's a lot of public information that's out there, but what type of plan is coming, who's the dip lender, who are going to be the sponsors for a reorganization. But you have to expect that if you have insider risk um on a claim that it could be attacked and that's why it's important to have indemnities. And it's important to know know specifically with those types of claims your counterparty credit risk and will that be available if that claim is slow to pay compared to others. >> [clears throat] >> Well, I I thank all of you for your time and your expertise. I can tell you I would be able to spend another hour just asking questions from you and and hearing what your responses are. So thank you very much. I thought this was certainly very and educational and hopefully somewhat enjoyable. And at this point I'm going to close. We are here to answer any questions and we can be contacted through the deck which has the information. Thank you all very much. It's greatly appreciated. We'll talk soon.

metadata.author: Capital Decode
metadata.shortDescription:
THE WALL STREET JOURNEY — An Investment Banking Story

EPISODE 23 — WHEN THINGS BREAK

“When a company runs out of room, every claim matters.”

NovaTech is no longer simply trying to grow.

Debt payments are approaching.
Liquidity is tightening.
Creditors are getting nervous.

And the analyst is about to enter one of the most complex areas of investment banking:

Financial Restructuring.

This episode explores:

• Causes of Financial Distress
• Liquidity Problems
• Debt Covenants & Defaults
• Refinancing & Raising Capital
• Out-of-Court Restructuring
• In-Court Restructuring
• Debtor vs. Creditor Side
• Chapter 7 Liquidation
• Chapter 11 Reorganization
• Absolute Priority Rule
• Recovery Waterfall
• Pre-Packaged Bankruptcy
• Plan of Reorganization
• Impaired Classes
• Automatic Stay
• DIP Financing
• Super-Priority Claims
• Priming
• Thirteen-Week Cash Flow Model
• Operational Restructuring
• Working Capital Management
• Asset Restructuring
• Going-Concern Valuation
• Liquidation Analysis
• Distressed Valuation
• Distressed Debt
• Secured vs. Unsecured Claims
• Recovery Analysis
• Fulcrum Security
• Debt-to-Control
• Debt-for-Equity Restructuring

Follow the analyst as she investigates NovaTech's financial distress and discovers that restructuring is not simply about determining what a company is worth.

It is about determining:

Who gets paid?
How much do they recover?
Can the business survive?
Which claims have priority?
And where does the value break?

From the thirteen-week cash flow model to the restructuring plan, from Chapter 11 to DIP financing, and from creditor negotiations to the fulcrum security, the analyst begins to see the company from an entirely different perspective.

Because when there isn't enough value for everyone, the capital structure becomes a map of who stands where.

THE WALL STREET JOURNEY
An Investment Banking Story

Episode 23 — WHEN THINGS BREAK

CHAPTER 6 — THE INDUSTRY
Financial Restructuring

Same business.
Different questions.
A much tougher reality.

Next Episode:

EPISODE 24 — PROPERTY & PRIVATE EQUITY
REIT + REPE

segments.text: All right, let's jump straight into this
explainer and rejoin our analyst right
where we left off. She's just mastered
all the nuances of valuing healthy
companies. But opening the very next
file on her desk, yeah, everything
changes. This is the Novatec file and it
is stamped urgent. Just glancing at the
numbers, cash is tightening dangerously.
There are some massive debt maturities
looming and creditors, well, they're
getting incredibly anxious. Novatech is
facing severe financial distress, which
means all those traditional rules we've
learned so far, we are throwing them
right out the window. So, approaching
this exactly like her previous M&A
deals, the analyst looks at these
deteriorating numbers and asks the
instinctive question, how much is
Novatech actually worth? She naturally
wants to run a DCF, look at some
comparables, and figure out the
company's going concerned value. I mean,
it makes total sense, right? It's
exactly what she's been trained to do.
But stepping into the restructuring
advisory group, we quickly learn that is
absolutely not the starting point
anymore. The senior banker leans over
and completely shifts her paradigm. In
the gritty world of financial
restructuring, survival and capital
recovery override literally every
traditional valuation metric. Think
about it. When a company is teetering on
the brink, it really doesn't matter if
your complex DCF model says it's going
to be worth a billion dollars in 5
years, especially if it simply can't pay
its suppliers by next Tuesday. To
actually fix the problem, we first need
to diagnose exactly what pushed Novatech
to the edge. There are a handful of
common catalyst for this kind of
distress. Very often, it's a severe
liquidity problem that leads to a missed
interest or principal payment. Or maybe
it was a failed leverage buyout that
just left the company way too
overlevered. But sometimes it's not even
directly about debt like missing
payments to vendors or violating
technical debt covenants which can
actually trigger forced liquidations.
For Novatech, it's a brutal combination.
An unexpected drop in financial
performance colliding headon with high
leverage. Now the analyst points out
that Novatek stock price has absolutely
plummeted. But the banker makes a
crucial crucial distinction here. And
honestly, this is a massive takeaway for
any investor. A falling share price by
itself cannot force a company into
bankruptcy. If Novatech can scrape
together the cash to keep making its
debt payments, it survives regardless of
what the stock ticker is screaming.
Actual legal financial distress is
strictly defined by the inability to
service debt or comply with covenants.
Though, to be fair, a tanking stock does
make raising new capital basically
impossible. This dynamic sets up a
really fascinating battlefield. You see,
the restructuring landscape is split
into two distinctly waring camps. On one
side, you have the debtor. In our story,
Novatech, desperately trying to fix the
business, execute a turnaround, and just
stay alive. On the exact opposite side,
you have the creditors. These are the
lenders and bond holders whose only goal
is to maximize the recovery of their
capital. As a restructuring banker, you
could advise either side. And depending
on who you represent, your entire
strategy is going to look radically
different. In this case, our analyst is
in the trenches advising the debtor.
Before anyone rushes straight to the
bankruptcy courts, the analyst has to
evaluate their survival alternatives.
Can Novatech just organically replace
its old debt with a brand new issue?
Well, highly unlikely. New lenders
usually won't touch a distressed asset
with a 10-ft pole. Okay, could they
raise additional equity? Good luck
pulling that off when your stock is
cratering. So the most practical
alternative left on the table is trying
to reach a private agreement with
existing lenders to renegotiate those
debt terms completely out of court. So
the big decision right now is weighing
an outofc court fix against a formal
bankruptcy. And out of court
restructuring is faster. It's way
cheaper and crucially it avoids the
nasty public headlines that might scare
away Novate's remaining customers.
However, in court restructuring, meaning
formal bankruptcy, brings some immense
legal superpowers. A judge oversees the
whole process. Changes can be legally
forced on dissenting creditors. Terrible
leases can be torn up and the company
gets access to very special emergency
financing. Our analyst attempts to model
a slick outofc court deal for Novatech,
but it hits a brick wall almost
immediately. Why? Because of a massive
hurdle known as the holdout problem. In
an outofc court restructuring, all the
creditors generally have to agree to the
new terms. But what happens is a few
rogue bond holders realize that if
everyone else takes a haircut, meaning
they accept less than what they're owed,
the company might just survive. So these
holdouts stubbornly refuse to
participate. They demand 100% of their
money back, basically hoping all the
other creditors will just take the hit
for them. Because those holdouts
completely paralyze the private deal,
Novatech has no choice. They are forced
to officially file for bankruptcy. But
there's a huge immediate benefit to this
filing, securing what's called the
automatic stay. This is a critical legal
injunction. Think of it as hitting a
giant pause button on the bleeding. It
legally prohibits any creditor from
initiating legal action, foreclosing on
assets, or evicting the company. It
finally gives Novatech the breathing
room it needs to keep its daily
operations running while they figure out
a permanent fix. Now that we're inside
the court, the road splits in two. The
analyst contrasts a chapter 7 complete
liquidation against a chapter 11
reorganization. Under chapter 7, it's
game over. The business shuts down. The
management team is kicked out and a
trustee comes in to sell off the assets
piece by piece. Novatech obviously opts
for chapter 11. In chapter 11, the
current management team actually stays
in place. They act as the debtor in
possession so they can try to fix the
underlying operations and hopefully
reemerge as a healthy company. Here's
the thing, though. Chapter 11 can turn
into a chaotic multi-year nightmare if
you're starting from scratch. That's a
scenario known in the industry as a
free-fall bankruptcy. Nobody wants that.
To avoid it, Novateex advisers push hard
for what's called a prepackaged
bankruptcy or a prepack. This means the
major stakeholders have already hashed
out and agreed on the restructuring plan
before the official paperwork is even
filed. This dramatically accelerates the
timeline, sometimes letting a company
emerge from bankruptcy in just a matter
of months. Ultimately, exiting
bankruptcy requires a court-approved
plan of reorganization or a PO. This is
a massive legal and financial document
that spells out exactly what happens to
every single dollar of assets,
liabilities, and equity. Most
importantly, it categorizes which
classes of creditors are impaired.
Impaired simply means they are not
getting 100% of their money back. And
here is the kicker. Only these impaired
classes actually get to vote on whether
to accept the company's proposed future.
So, picture this. The analyst is sitting
in a really tense restructuring meeting.
The entire capital structure is
projected up on a screen and everyone is
facing the harsh mathematical reality of
distress. There is simply not enough
value left in Novatech to pay everyone
back. The senior banker looks around the
room and asks the defining question of
financial restructuring. If the pie
shrinks, who gets a slice and who gets
completely wiped out? The answer to that
question lies in the recovery waterfall.
It's a strict hierarchy that dictates
exactly how the remaining money flows.
At the very top, you have super priority
and pre-etition secured claims. They are
first in line. Next come administrative
claims. These cover the massive legal
and advisory fees of the bankruptcy
process itself. Then priority unsecured
followed by general unsecured claims
which includes trade vendors and regular
bond holders. And sitting way down at
the very bottom, equity. If you ever
hold common stock in a bankrupt company,
this right here is exactly why your
investment almost always goes to zero.
This entire vertical stack is governed
by the absolute priority rule. It is an
unbreakable legal principle in
bankruptcy and it ensures that value
only trickles down to a lower class if
the class directly above it has been
made 100% whole. No exceptions. You
literally cannot pay a general unsecured
creditor a single dime until the secured
creditors have recovered every penny of
their principal and interest. So as the
analyst does the math and follows this
waterfall down, she hits a pivotal point
known as the fulcrum security. This is
the exact tier in the capital structure
where the money just runs out. Because
this specific class of debt holders
won't receive their full cash recovery,
they are usually compensated in a
totally different way. They take over
ownership of the newly restructured
Novatech. The old equity is wiped out
and this specific debt converts into the
new controlling equity. Okay, let's zoom
in on the immediate liquidity crisis
because the clock is ticking. The
analyst builds out a 13-week cash flow
model. We start at week one with their
current cash balance. By week four, some
massive operating payments and debt
service hit the books. And then by week
six, the model is flashing red.
Novatek's liquidity drops to absolute
zero. Without a drastic immediate
intervention, they won't even make it
halfway to their target horizon of week
13. To survive past that terrifying week
six and literally just keep the lights
on, Novate desperately needs DTOR in
possession or DIP financing. This is an
injection of fresh capital brought into
the business strictly to keep operations
running during the bankruptcy process.
But there's a catch. DIP financing is
highly specialized and it's only
accessible because the company is under
the formal legal protection of the
bankruptcy court. Now, you might be
wondering, lending millions to a
bankrupt company sounds incredibly
risky. Why would anyone ever do it?
Well, because these new DIP lenders
demand super priority status. Through a
legal maneuver called priming, the
bankruptcy court allows these new
lenders to completely jump the line.
They leapfrog even the existing senior
secured debt, placing themselves at the
absolute top of the recovery waterfall.
Sure, they take on risk, but they
practically guarantee they are the very
first ones getting paid back. With that
dip lifeline finally secured, Novateex
management can take a breath and execute
an operational restructuring because
honestly, fixing the balance sheet means
absolutely nothing if the underlying
business is still fundamentally broken.
This phase requires aggressive cost
cutting, squeezing way better terms out
of working capital, making strategic
headcount reductions and selling off any
unproductive non-core assets so they can
refocus strictly on what actually
generates revenue. Ultimately, to get
the judge and the skeptical creditors to
approve this massive turnaround plan,
our analyst has to help Novatech pass
what's called the best interest test.
She builds out highly conservative
projections using steep discount rates
to account for all this distress to
prove a very specific point. She has to
mathematically prove that Novatech is
ultimately worth more alive as an
operating going concern than it would be
dead and sold for parts in a chapter 7
liquidation. The math holds up. The
court gives its approval and those
Fulcrum security holders take control of
the company. Which leaves us with one
final incredibly high stakes question
for these new equity owners.
Congratulations. You survived the
financial restructuring. You cleared the
debt and you satisfied the waterfall.
But after the severe brand damage of
bankruptcy and a constantly shifting
industry landscape, can you actually win
back your customers and make this
company thrive again? That is the true
test of a turnaround. Thanks for tuning
in to this explainer. I hope it gave you
a solid look at what really happens
behind closed doors when things break.

Nobody wants that. To avoid it, Novateex advisers push hard for what's called a prepackaged bankruptcy or a prepack. This means the major stakeholders have already hashed out and agreed on the restructuring plan before the official paperwork is even filed. This dramatically accelerates the timeline, sometimes letting a company emerge from bankruptcy in just a matter of months. Ultimately, exiting bankruptcy requires a court-approved plan of reorganization or a PO. This is a massive legal and financial document that spells out exactly what happens to every single dollar of assets, liabilities, and equity. Most importantly, it categorizes which classes of creditors are impaired. Impaired simply means they are not getting 100% of their money back. And here is the kicker. Only these impaired classes actually get to vote on whether to accept the company's proposed future. So, picture this. The analyst is sitting in a really tense restructuring meeting. The entire capital structure is projected up on a screen and everyone is facing the harsh mathematical reality of distress. There is simply not enough value left in Novatech to pay everyone back. The senior banker looks around the room and asks the defining question of financial restructuring. If the pie shrinks, who gets a slice and who gets completely wiped out? The answer to that question lies in the recovery waterfall. It's a strict hierarchy that dictates exactly how the remaining money flows. At the very top, you have super priority and pre-etition secured claims. They are first in line. Next come administrative claims. These cover the massive legal and advisory fees of the bankruptcy process itself. Then priority unsecured followed by general unsecured claims which includes trade vendors and regular bond holders. And sitting way down at the very bottom, equity. If you ever hold common stock in a bankrupt company, this right here is exactly why your investment almost always goes to zero. This entire vertical stack is governed by the absolute priority rule. It is an unbreakable legal principle in bankruptcy and it ensures that value only trickles down to a lower class if the class directly above it has been made 100% whole. No exceptions. You literally cannot pay a general unsecured creditor a single dime until the secured creditors have recovered every penny of their principal and interest. So as the analyst does the math and follows this waterfall down, she hits a pivotal point known as the fulcrum security. This is the exact tier in the capital structure where the money just runs out. Because this specific class of debt holders won't receive their full cash recovery, they are usually compensated in a totally different way. They take over ownership of the newly restructured Novatech. The old equity is wiped out and this specific debt converts into the new controlling equity. Okay, let's zoom in on the immediate liquidity crisis because the clock is ticking. The analyst builds out a 13-week cash flow model. We start at week one with their current cash balance. Without a drastic immediate intervention, they won't even make it halfway to their target horizon of week 13. To survive past that terrifying week six and literally just keep the lights on, Novate desperately needs DTOR in possession or DIP financing. This is an injection of fresh capital brought into the business strictly to keep operations running during the bankruptcy process. But there's a catch. DIP financing is highly specialized and it's only accessible because the company is under the formal legal protection of the bankruptcy court. Now, you might be wondering, lending millions to a bankrupt company sounds incredibly risky. Why would anyone ever do it? Well, because these new DIP lenders demand super priority status. Through a legal maneuver called priming, the bankruptcy court allows these new lenders to completely jump the line. They leapfrog even the existing senior secured debt, placing themselves at the absolute top of the recovery waterfall. Sure, they take on risk, but they practically guarantee they are the very first ones getting paid back. metadata.title: Purchasing Assets in Bankruptcy
metadata.author: The National Law Review
metadata.shortDescription:
Buying assets out of a bankruptcy proceeding presents unique benefits and challenges for the buyer. Companies considering acquiring assets out of bankruptcy must understand more than the simple concept of acquiring the target assets “free and clear,” under the Bankruptcy Code. As such, professionals advising these companies must understand and be able to counsel their clients regarding various matters, such as the benefits and drawbacks of serving as a “stalking horse,” asset purchaser; drafting and negotiating the terms of an asset purchase agreement, and sale order with the bankrupt debtor and other parties involved in the bankruptcy proceedings; strategies for acquiring assets at auction or by alternative means; and seeking bankruptcy court approval of a proposed transaction. This webinar focuses on understanding these concepts and addressing best practices for advanced reorganization practitioners and advisors.

Learning Objectives:
-Understanding the basics of bankruptcy asset purchases
-Evaluating the role of a “Stalking Horse” asset purchaser
-Drafting and negotiating key legal documents
-Mastering auction and alternative acquisition strategies
-Navigating the bankruptcy court approval processes
-Applying best practices in advanced reorganization scenarios
-Implementing effective tactics for advising clients on bankruptcy asset purchases, focusing on strategic, legal, and practical challenges in advanced reorganization cases
