early only if, on the day it
cancels, it already holds a reasonable
written technical reason to
believe no repair could work
in that time. A test report can be
enough, but only if it explains why a
repair couldn't work.
Without that justification, the full
$7,600,000 comes due. You read that
twice, because a rule
that specific is only as good as the
dates it gets tested against. Then you
find the test report,
stamped failed, dated March 5th. The
cancellation is dated March 10th.
14 days would have run out on March
19th. At first you assume
it's another coding mistake,
because that's where you've found money
before. An email footer
mentions a supervised retest,
but the attachment isn't in the contract
archive, so you stop
theorizing and follow the paper.
The red stamp isn't the only
document with a date on it.
Someone booked a second test before
Wyndham Peak walked out.
By the summer of 2024 you hand Nolan Vey
a discrepancy chart,
Aster's shipment numbers lined up against
Tolliver's old testing register,
five days in March nobody has explained,
and he reads it with a pen uncapped in
his hand, never writing a word.
Then he authorizes a supervised review,
meaning a chair, a guard, and
a cleared paper copy of
everything from that March.
Tomas Ibarra, the old production
supervisor, meets you at the test bay
doorway in a work jacket with a small
burn mark near the cuff and
points at the stained
concrete where the rig stood.
"Gauge dropped like a stone," he says.
"Operator signed it.
That was a real failure."
Your theory dies there, and you write on
the top line of your notes, in pen,
that you were wrong.
Then you find a blue rework card in
Aster's own shipping file,
stapled to the packing
slip for the replacement seal.
The box marked technical approval carries
initials dated March 7th
from Wyndham Peak's qualified lead test
engineer, who had reviewed the March 5th
pressure curve and approved a supervised
seal replacement and
a retest on March 14th
with the customer watching.
"That's an engineer's box," Tomas says.
"Nobody initials it to
say a date got booked.
They initial it to say go ahead and try.
Doesn't mean it would have passed."
The seal was picked,
staged and never installed.
Procurement canceled on March 10th, in one
paragraph on letterhead, and
you read the whole file as support for a
single thing, the ordinary 14 days.
You hand Nolan a packet and he forwards
it to estate counsel, promising nothing.
Mireya Teague squares a stack of paper on
her desk once before she
tells you the bad news.
"You own a claim, not the
contract, and not the lawsuit.
You can find the evidence.
You can't pull the trigger."
The estate starts investigating anyway.
By winter, somebody offers
to buy your position for cash.
The offer arrives on a Monday in early
2025, from a specialist
buyer that has seen the
trustee's investigation and started
pricing the chance that you're right.
$160,000, wired within the
week, good until Friday at 5.
You take the number to a diner counter
and do the arithmetic on
the back of the receipt.
Your claim is $2.8
million out of $7.2 million
in ordinary claims,
roughly 39% of the pool.
If the lawsuit nets $2 million after
costs your share is about $778,000,
and if it nets $3.6
million your share is $1,400,000.
Scenarios, not promises, and you know it.
But somewhere between the eggs and the
check you stop comparing
the offer to the $2,400 you paid
and start comparing it to
the numbers on the receipt.
"You'd be turning down more than 66 times
your money," Mireya says that afternoon.
"Even if you're right about everything,
that's a great result."
"It's a lower version of the one I've
already counted," you say,
and hear how that sounds
as it leaves your mouth.
You picture a new scanner, a cleared
backlog, weekends with the phone off.
You let Friday pass anyway.
Four days later the old scanner jams in
the middle of a paid rush job,
and instead of replacing it you spend
the night feeding torn pages through by
hand while you build
another evidence packet, and a repeat
client who was waiting
pulls a $1,600
assignment the next morning.
That isn't an expense. It's
work that used to be yours.
You have exposed a sure
$160,000 to the risk of zero,
and the next report doesn't question
whether the test failed.
It questions whether the repair you bet
on could ever have worked.
The second reversal arrives in November,
in a demonstration
video the estate's consultant
forwards without comment. Wyndham Peak's
expert has cut open an
exemplar valve and is holding
a laser dot on a weld collar. The seal
was never the problem, he says, the
casting underneath it
was, and a new seal and a routine retest
might never have made that
assembly safe. You watch
it twice at your desk, with unpaid
invoices stacked around the jammed
scanner like sandbags.
If Wyndham Peak's reasons hold up, your
claim is worth nothing,
and a report written years
later makes that frighteningly easy to
believe. The estate's own
consultant won't promise the
seal swap would have cured it. Then Nolan
calls. "They've offered
$900,000. Gross. The cost of the
case and the wind down has already passed
that, so there'd be nothing
left for your class." Nothing.
The same word you started with, only now
you've paid for it. The
offer you turned down is gone,
your outlay is heading toward $20,800,
and the client who left hasn't returned.
Mireya offers no rescue. "You proved the
date," she says. "You
haven't proved the repair."
That night, alone, you spread the blue
card beside the expert's report.
This morning the card looked weak, a plan
on a scrap of carbon
paper. Now two pages disagree,
and you've spent your whole working life
listening for pages that disagree.
Your own rosy math talked
you out of the sure money,
and the engineering may have made it the
most expensive mistake of your life.
Somewhere past two in the morning, with
the blue card and the
expert's report still side by side
on the table by the window, the question
finally arrives in plain
words. If fixing it was obviously
futile, why did Wyndham Peak's own
engineer sign off on trying? You lay the
blue approval beside
the cancellation letter. Three days
separate them. Then you do what you
skipped last year and go
through Nolan's cleared copy of that
March, every page between those dates,
looking for the engineer's
second thought, a memo calling the repair
hopeless, anything explaining why the
trial no longer mattered.
There's a purchase order, a shipping
notice, and one
paragraph from procurement.
Nothing from the engineer who approved
the repair. Tolliver never got
its nine days. Last year you
read those initials as support for the
ordinary 14 days and
nothing more. Now you see them for
what they are, Wyndham Peak's own
engineer saying yes to a repair three
days before Wyndham Peak
said no. Maybe the expert is right, but
the contract doesn't ask
who diagnosed the defect
best in 2026. It asks what they had in
writing on March 10th. You carry two
pages into Nolan's office
and set them side by side. "I'm not asking
you to prove it worked,"
you say. "I'm asking them to
explain why they signed off on trying it
and then canceled before it
happened." "Engineers schedule
tests they expect to fail all the time,"
Nolan says. "Initials aren't a
lawsuit." "No. They're a question.
It's the exact question the contract
asks." He takes a long time to answer. He
still thinks Wyndham
Peak might win, but might is the whole
point, he says, because a defense that
might win is a defense
somebody has to pay to make go away, and
he carries your two pages
to the estate's lawyers.
No new email appears and no retest
passes. It's the same blue
card from 2024, and only what it
means has changed. Without your
reconstruction, the estate
was closer to taking $900,000
and calling it a result. Now someone has
to ask Wyndham Peak the
same question out loud.
You're back in the room with the red
page. The mediator turns to you first.
"Walk me through March, in order." You
do, and every answer is dull on purpose.
The expert's argument is real and the
machine may have been
unsafe from the start,
and the estate doesn't claim otherwise.
Then counsel sets three pages in a row,
the failed test, the March 7th approval,
the March 10th cancellation.
"I'm not asking whether the repair would
have worked," the mediator says to
Wyndham Peak's side.
"I'm asking what you had in writing on
March 10th, not what
anyone learned years later,
when your own engineer had approved a
trial three days before."
The room goes still. Across the table a
junior lawyer slides a
page toward the senior one,
someone whispers, and someone starts
doing arithmetic on a legal pad.
You can guess the number. $7,600,000 if
the exception fails,
against months of testimony to find out.
Nobody on either side is sure.
The offer comes back at $2.7 million,
triple the $900,000
they offered last year,
and you do the receipt math
before you can stop yourself.
After $1.4 million in costs, $1.3 million
is left for the class,
and your share is just over
$500,000, more than three times what you
refused. "That's the last
number we will ever say,"
Wyndham Peak's lawyer tells the mediator.
Nolan says no. He counters near the full
guarantee, and in the corridor he stops
beside you. "If their
expert holds, we get nothing,"
he says quietly. "Not $900,000. Nothing."
Then he asks you to step out.
It's the diner decision again, a good
number refused for a
better one already counted,
and this time it isn't yours to make.
You wait three hours in a hallway,
catching fragments through the doors.
When Nolan comes out he
stands beside you until
the elevator opens. "Five million," he
says. "No admission, no
ruling on whether a repaired
machine would have passed." You nod,
because there is nothing else your face
can do. Five million.
Now the only question is what's left.
Mireya calls with the final numbers and
reads them slowly, the way
she reads everything that
matters. "Five million dollars came in
from Wyndham Peak," she
says. "$1.4 million paid for
the case and the estate. That leaves $3.6
million for the creditors, who
are owed $7.2 million between
them." Everyone in the class gets 50 cents
on the dollar, so your
claim of $2.8 million pays
$1,400,000. The wire lands on a
Thursday morning in
September. You read the balance before
the sender's name, $1,400,000 in
an account that has never
held more than a few thousand,
and then you count the places twice, the
way you'd check a column, and lay the
original receipt for
$2,400 beside the screen. It doesn't feel
like money yet. It's before
taxes, and it isn't all profit.
After the $20,800 you spent,
you're left with $1,379,200.
You think about Gwen, whose signature
still sits on the transfer
an inch from the old estimate.
She wasn't wrong. A closing company
needed $2,400 more
than it needed a maybe,
and someone who kept the claim might have
collected nothing. You
almost did, and refusing
$160,000 wasn't smart just because it
worked out. You lay the
original sheet beside the deposit,
the one with a single word in the
recovery column. Closed and reconciled
were never the same thing.
You spent your working life putting final
numbers on unfinished things,
and this time you almost did it again.
You order a new scanner
before lunch. The old one jams on
the first page of the next client's
invoice, and you feed it
through by hand one last time.

metadata.shortDescription:
The claims bar date in bankruptcy is a critical deadline for creditors—and understanding it is essential for everyone involved in a case. Attorney David Ienna from Fairmax Law explains what it is, how it works in Chapter 7 and Chapter 13, and why it matters. Don’t miss this important update.

At Fairmax Law, our mission is to provide our clients with top-tier legal guidance on all things bankruptcy. With our team of dedicated professionals, we're here to help you navigate the complexities of the financial world.

📞 Contact Us:
For a consultation or to learn more about our services, please visit our website at www.fairmaxlaw.com or call us at 888-fairmax.

🔔 Subscribe to our channel for more informative videos on legal topics and insights!

👍 If you found this video helpful, please give it a thumbs up, share it with friends, and drop your questions or feedback in the comments below.

Don't Let These 10 Mistakes Blow Up Your Bankruptcy Case
Filing bankruptcy is a fresh start—but only if you avoid these critical pitfalls. In this video, Georgia bankruptcy attorney Jeff Kelly breaks down the top 10 reasons perfectly good Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 cases get derailed, dismissed, or worse.
The 10 Mistakes:

Failure to disclose an asset (perjury risk)
Not telling the truth at your 341 hearing
Not reading your bankruptcy petition before signing
Paying loans back to friends/family right before filing
Running up credit cards 60+ days before filing
Unrecorded quit claim deeds from divorce
Forgetting about inherited money
Draining your 401k or IRA before bankruptcy
Behaving badly at your 341 meeting of creditors
Filing Chapter 7 when you should file Chapter 13 (the most common and costly mistake)

Bankruptcy protections only work if you file smart. Learn what not to do—and how an experienced attorney can keep your case on track.
About Jeff Kelly:
Jeff Kelly is a consumer bankruptcy attorney practicing in Georgia since 1998. His firm has filed over 10,000 bankruptcy cases throughout the Northern District of Georgia, serving the Rome, Gainesville, Atlanta, and Newnan divisions. If you're struggling with debt and considering bankruptcy, understanding these mistakes could save your home, your car, and thousands of dollars.
Resources:
📖 Free Chapter 7 & 13 Guide: kellycanhelp.com

🎥 More Bankruptcy Education: Visit the Kelly Can Help YouTube channel for dozens of videos on Georgia bankruptcy law
Office Locations: Rome, GA | Marietta, GA | Dallas, GA | Cartersville, GA

We are a debt relief agency. We help people obtain relief from their creditors by filing bankruptcy.

This free lesson from North Texas Paralegal Institute covers what unauthorized practice of law is, who owns what, how to answer that question, the five-part hand-off note, the bright UPL lines, the supervision rules and what "done" means.

segments.text: A scared client asks you, what should I
do? It's the most common trap. If your
answer changes what they do, it's
advice. Here's how paralegals handle it.
Family law clients call because they are
scared and want you to tell them what to
do. You are not licensed to give legal
advice. Unauthorized practice of law
means doing work that requires a law
license when you do not have one.
Advising someone about their situation,
choosing the legal path, speaking for
the client as their lawyer, or making
the lawyer's business decisions, like
accepting a case or setting a fee.
You organize, draft from instructions,
calendar, gather, track, and flag. The
attorney owns legal judgment, strategy,
advice, what to plead or settle, and
anything that needs a lawyer's signature
or license. You may explain the firm's
process and share facts already in the
file. You may not tell a client what
they should do. If your answer depends
on this client's facts and changes what
they do, it is advice. Pass it to the
attorney. When Marcus asks when his
hearing is and whether to bring his
girlfriend, only the hearing date is
already in the file.
When a client asks what they should do,
that is the most common trap. If you and
the attorney have not talked about it,
tell them you need to check with the
attorney because every situation is
different and tell them when they will
hear back. Then send the question. If
you have already talked, pass along the
plan and say it came from the attorney.
Do not present it as your own idea or
add to it. For a safety emergency,
follow your firm's emergency process and
get the attorney right away.
Pass every legal question in a short
handoff note the attorney can read in 30
seconds. Use five parts in this order.
What the client said in their own words
where you can, what you already from the
file, what you can finish today without
legal advice, what waits for attorney
judgment, and one confirmed question.
Then calendar a reminder so you keep the
callback you promised. A note that only
says John called is not enough.
Some lines are always bright.
Questioning a witness at a deposition is
practicing law. If the attorney is late,
refuse and wait. Drafting a deed for a
friend without supervision is
unauthorized practice, even with no fee.
If a neighbor with court forms asks
which remedies to seek, decline and
point them to a lawyer or legal aid. At
a clinic, you may gather facts, but the
attorney decides qualification and gives
the advice. A paralegal may not set
fees, accept cases, or appear in court
for a client.
Rule 503 requires the supervising lawyer
to make reasonable efforts to keep your
conduct in line with the lawyer's
duties. Rule 504 bars a non-lawyer from
owning part of, directing, or serving as
an officer of a law firm.
Done is not I sent something. Done is
the right document in the right folder
with the right name, a matching calendar
entry, a short note the attorney can
trust, and a clear next ask if something
is blocked. Before a document leaves the
office, full account numbers and social
security numbers come off. A later
section teaches the redaction steps. Do
not fill silence with legal conclusions
or advise friends and family off the
clock.
This is section one of NTPI's Family Law
Lifecycle Workflows course. Get the full
course at ntpi.training.

segments.text: Your neighbor asks you, can you draft my
lease on the side? Helpful favor or
unauthorized practice. In Texas, it's a
class A misdemeanor. Here's where the
paralegal line is.
You work inside a lawyer's license.
Texas government code section 81.101
treats the practice of law as work
reserved to a licensed lawyer, advice on
legal rights, preparing instruments that
affect those rights, and representing
someone in a proceeding. Texas penal
code section 38.123
makes unauthorized practice a class A
misdemeanor. Disciplinary rule 5.03
makes the supervising lawyer responsible
for your conduct.
Three tasks stay with the lawyer. You do
not tell a prospect the firm has taken
the case, and you do not sign the
representation agreement. You do not
quote a contingency percentage, an
hourly rate, or a discount. You do not
evaluate whether a claim is strong.
Gathering facts is allowed. Deciding
what those facts mean legally is not.
On a first meeting, say three things
before you take the story. You are not a
lawyer. The meeting is to collect facts
for a lawyer to evaluate, and the firm
has not accepted the matter. Do not
predict an outcome or quote a fee. If a
neighbor asks you to prepare a
residential lease on the side, decline.
You do not have a supervising lawyer on
that request.
When the person asks a legal question in
the middle of intake, write the question
word for word. You may explain a form
the court requires, such as that a sworn
inventory has blanks the client will
complete. You may not answer whether a
premarital retirement account must be
listed. Book time with the lawyer and
tell the client the lawyer will answer.
You may call the client and read a
recommendation the lawyer has made, then
record the client's decision. Say that
the recommendation is the lawyer's. Do
not add your own reading or a prediction
about what a judge would do. If the
client asks a new question, stop and
take it back to the lawyer.
You may not stand when the case is
called and ask the judge for a reset.
You may tell a coordinator off the
record that the lawyer is in another
court. At a deposition under rule 199,
you do not question the witness or state
objections. You mark exhibits, keep
notes, and speak quietly to the
examining lawyer about facts that still
need a question.
Preparing a will, a testamentary trust,
or a deed is the practice of law. You
may assemble the draft from the lawyer's
instructions and build the signature
packet. A lawyer reviews the text and
approves the terms before anyone asks
the client to sign. You do not present
the packet as ready because you finished
typing it.
On firm letters and email, your name
sits above a non-lawyer title, paralegal
or legal assistant. A blank title or a
title such as senior associate or trial
counsel tells the reader you are a
lawyer. A specialty credential may
appear on the card, but not a lawyer
title.
This is section one of NTPI's ethics and
professional responsibility course. Get
the full course at NTPI.training.

Book time with the lawyer and tell the client the lawyer will answer. You may call the client and read a recommendation the lawyer has made, then record the client's decision. Say that the recommendation is the lawyer's. Do not add your own reading or a prediction about what a judge would do. If the client asks a new question, stop and take it back to the lawyer. You may not stand when the case is called and ask the judge for a reset. You may tell a coordinator off the record that the lawyer is in another court. At a deposition under rule 199, you do not question the witness or state objections. You mark exhibits, keep notes, and speak quietly to the examining lawyer about facts that still need a question. Preparing a will, a testamentary trust, or a deed is the practice of law. You may assemble the draft from the lawyer's instructions and build the signature packet. A lawyer reviews the text and approves the terms before anyone asks the client to sign. You do not present the packet as ready because you finished typing it. On firm letters and email, your name sits above a non-lawyer title, paralegal or legal assistant. A blank title or a title such as senior associate or trial counsel tells the reader you are a lawyer. A specialty credential may appear on the card, but not a lawyer title. This is section one of NTPI's ethics and professional responsibility course. Get the full course at NTPI.training.

metadata.shortDescription:
91 Civil Procedure flashcards for 1L review: the constitutional provisions, statutes, Federal Rules and doctrines you need, read aloud with each term and definition on screen. Play it while you commute, cook or review before class.

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:04 Constitutional Provisions & Core Foundations
1:40 Subject Matter Jurisdiction: Federal Question (28 U.S.C. § 1331)
3:29 Subject Matter Jurisdiction: Diversity of Citizenship (28 U.S.C. § 1332)
6:09 Subject Matter Jurisdiction: Supplemental Jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. § 1367)
9:46 Subject Matter Jurisdiction: Removal Jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. §§ 1441–1447)
11:07 Personal Jurisdiction: Traditional Bases & Long-Arm Statutes
12:48 Personal Jurisdiction: Minimum Contacts & Modern Standards
14:27 Civil Procedure: Key Terms & Essential Doctrines

How to study with it: say the definition out loud before the card flips, then check yourself.

Practice writing it: the free Essay Coach grades your Civ Pro essays in F-IRAC → https://lawfrogrnesq.com/pages/essay-coach
More study guides: https://lawfrogrnesq.com

Closing Address & Judgment | Week 14 | Civil Litigation | Nigerian Law School Bar Part II
Welcome to Week 14 of our Nigerian Law School Bar Part II Civil Litigation Series.
Closing Address and Judgment represent the final and most decisive stages of every civil trial. A well-delivered closing address allows counsel to persuasively summarize the evidence and applicable law, while a properly reasoned judgment reflects the court's determination of the rights and obligations of the parties. These topics are among the most important and frequently tested in the Nigerian Law School Bar Final Examinations.
In this comprehensive lecture, O. O. Stevens, Esq. provides a practical and examination-focused explanation of Closing Address and Judgment under Nigerian Civil Procedure, guiding students through the principles, procedures, and advocacy techniques expected of every legal practitioner.

This lesson is specifically designed for Nigerian Law School Bar Part II students, law graduates, and legal practitioners seeking to master Civil Litigation Practice in Nigeria and prepare effectively for the Bar Final Examinations.

In This Lecture You Will Learn
✅ Meaning and Purpose of a Closing Address
✅ Structure of an Effective Final Written Address
✅ Oral Adoption of Final Addresses
✅ Summarising Evidence Before the Court
✅ Analysis and Application of Relevant Law
✅ Citing Judicial Authorities
✅ Burden and Standard of Proof
✅ Evaluation of Evidence by the Court
✅ Writing and Delivery of Judgment
✅ Components of a Valid Judgment
✅ Ratio Decidendi and Obiter Dicta
✅ Reliefs Granted by the Court
✅ Costs and Consequential Orders
✅ Relevant High Court Civil Procedure Rules
✅ Important Nigerian Case Law
✅ Practical Bar Examination Tips

A thorough understanding of Closing Address and Judgment is essential for every aspiring legal practitioner because these stages determine how evidence is analysed, legal arguments are presented, and disputes are finally resolved by the court. This topic is consistently examined in the Nigerian Law School Bar Final Examinations and is fundamental to effective courtroom advocacy.
This lecture forms part of our complete Civil Litigation Course, carefully developed to equip Nigerian Law School students with the practical knowledge and advocacy skills required to excel in the Bar Part II Programme and successfully qualify for the Call to the Nigerian Bar.

Whether you are revising for examinations, preparing for tutorials, or improving your understanding of Nigerian Civil Procedure, this lesson provides clear explanations, practical insights, and examination-focused guidance to help you succeed.
This Civil Litigation Series Covers
Introduction to Civil Litigation
Overview and Sources of Civil Litigation
Parties to a Suit
Preliminary Conditions Before Commencement of Action
Commencement of Action in the High Court
Interlocutory Applications
Summary Judgment
Undefended List Procedure
Pleadings
Pre-Trial Issues and Trial Proceedings
Trial Preparation and Examination of Witnesses
Closing Address & Judgment
Appeals
Enforcement of Judgments
Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR)
Bar Final Revision Classes
Lecturer:
O. O. Stevens, Esq.

If this lecture contributes to your preparation for the Nigerian Law School Bar Final Examinations, please Like, Comment, Share, and Subscribe. Your support helps us continue providing high-quality educational content for Nigerian Law School students preparing for the Call to the Nigerian Bar.

metadata.shortDescription:
Friday, October 12, 2018
MDL at 50 

The Center on Civil Justice hosted MDL at 50, commemorating the 50th anniversary of the 1968 Multidistrict Litigation Statute. This conference was co-hosted by the Center on Civil Justice at NYU Law School and the Liman and Solomon Centers at Yale Law School. 

Moderator: 
• Troy McKenzie '00, Professor, NYU School of Law

Panelists: 
• Andrew Bradt, Professor, University of California Berkeley Law School
• Robin Effron, Professor, Brooklyn Law School
• Teddy Rave, Professor, University of Houston Law Center
• Linda Silberman, Professor, NYU School of Law
• Adam Steinman, Professor, University of Alabama School of Law

The very fact that these cases are aggregated I think may simultaneously undermine these norms, undermine the differences between these cases. So when a single federal judge has to apply 50 different sets of state law to a massive litigation, some smoothing out around the edges seems inevitable. And this is not to say that choice of law doesn't matter. Choice of law certainly matters. - I hope so. (laughter) - When an MDL judge is deciding a summary judgment motion in a particular case, or instructing the jury in a bellwether trial, it's gonna decide that motion or instruct the jury according to the law that the transferor court would apply to that case. But there are plenty of opportunities for shortcuts, and grouping different states' approaches into broad categories, and things like consolidated complaints, or in deciding common issues on general causation. And as we heard in the last panel, when judges are deciding, sometimes the most important motions in the case is the Daubert motions. Those are decided according to our federal standard, and that's going to apply to all of the cases. And the judges in the last panel told us that very often state law is not factoring into their consideration in those motions. And really, you know, state law is not that different. There are a couple of different approaches, maybe three baskets of approaches that you can put together. I think they'll figure it out. I can't fault judges or the lawyers handling these cases for trying to do that. This is a massive problem if you have to apply 50 different sets of law. And any ways to simplify I think our inevitable and not necessarily a bad thing. Probably the biggest opportunity for smoothing out differences in state law comes at the point of settlement. And John Wood eluded to this in the last panel too where he says it's not the fact that these cases are in federal court that's smoothing out state law, it's the fact that all of these cases settle. So I think many of the people in this room know more about the content of MDL settlements than I do. Most MDL settlements are confidential. But at least in the publicly available mass settlements that have emerged out of MDLs, they rarely make any sort of fine grain distinction among plaintiffs based on the choice of law rules that would apply to their cases. So I've looked at the 12 publicly available non-class master settlement agreements in product liability MDLs, and out of those 12, none of them appeared to take differences in the applicable state law into account in setting the recovery amounts. The recovery grids didn't factor in things like the plaintiff's state of residence, or the place of injury, or anything else that might go into a choice of law analysis. So, what we end up here with is a system that formally accounts for differences in state law but in practice smooths out some of those differences. And the more mass tort cases, like product liability cases, are channeled into federal MDLs and out of state courts the more we're going to see developments in product liability law are driven by federal judges, federal judges who are faced with, I think, sort of an inevitable pressure towards simplification and uniformity that state court judges don't feel in these cases. And when all of the action is in federal court, it's not quite but it's starting to sound close to something like a federal common law, as Sam Azakharoff pointed out almost a decade ago in relationship to capital. Fourth and finally, channeling more cases into MDL is going to concentrate more power in the hands of MDL judges and the lawyers who control this litigation. Now as I said, there are huge benefits to aggregating cases in a single forum and empowering lead lawyers can help plaintiffs coordinate their efforts and prevent strategic holdouts, prevent the state court lawyers from throwing a wrench into things. But there are also risks whenever power is consolidated. So in MDLs, individual plaintiffs often have very little control over their cases for as long as they're consolidated. And as Andrew said, there's no way for them to opt out. And the incentives of the lead lawyers, who are the ones who make the most important decisions, might not always line up perfectly with the interests of each individual plaintiff. And so we end up with a similar type of principal agent problem that we saw in class actions but without many of the formal protections that are built into the class action rules. And one consequences of the Bristol-Myers decision in making it harder to file state court litigation is that it eliminates one potential competitive check by making it harder for competing lawyers to set up other aggregations in state courts. Now as I said, there are advantages to that but also, I think, some potential disadvantages. So with more power concentrated in the hands of MDL lead lawyers, I think it becomes even more important for federal judges, MDL judges, to manage the litigation with an eye towards protecting the individual plaintiffs and importantly, making sure that they have the information that they need to make informed decisions about settlements and to monitor their lawyers. And with that... - Thank you, Teddy. I just wanted to translate something. You said smoothing out of state law. I think what you meant in English was running roughshod over state law. Is that right? (laughter) - No, I think smoothing is what I mean. - Okay, I'll tell the translator then. - I think it's... It's not disregard for state law, right. - It's general common law. It's not federal common law, it's general common law. - So, I don't want to go that far. I don't want to say that federal judges are back in the Swift era where they're thinking what is the right way to approach this problem. There's still the reference to state law but there's just pressure towards simplification. I think it was Judge Kennelly who said in the last panel, you know, you can put it into like three baskets. That's not Swift, that's not general common law. It's just a practical problem that we're trying to find some way to get a handle on. And it's all gonna settle anyway, and in the settlement they're not gonna account for it. - But it doesn't say you ignore it. I mean, in the class action context, they have figured out ways of subclassing and looking at these issues in groups, and there's no reason that that can't occur in this context as well, but it doesn't mean running roughshod over choice of law. - Adam, would you like to respond? - Sure, yeah, just one thought. Maybe it's not running roughshod, it's running smoothshod. - I'll take it. - So, it's been great to be a part of this conference. It's been really enjoyable so far. This is timely, interesting stuff. I thought the discussion this morning of testosterone and male energy was a good followup to Kanye's comments at the White House. (laughter) But in terms of my designated duties here responding, I don't have much to object to Robin's provocative comments, but I will just offer a few thoughts on some of those pre-BMS cases. And one thing I guess I'll say is even though cases like Mcintyre have left things in a bit of a muddle, I guess I want to emphasize it's not necessarily a more restrictive muddle, or a muddle that has to be one that constricts the scope of personal jurisdiction. And here of course the saving grace is that Justice Kennedy's plurality opinion did not get five votes, and so as a result, if we're looking for any kind of law or guidance, and there's admittedly a lot of deep, unresolved questions about how we deal with opinions that don't have, or decisions that don't have a majority opinion, but, you know, if there's law anywhere, it's gotta be in the Breyer/Alito concurrence. And that opinion is premised on a very narrow reading of the factual record in this case. And among other things, Breyer indicated that personal jurisdiction might have been fine if there had been, in the record, evidence of a market in the state of New Jersey, or evidence of New Jersey customers attending trade shows where the British defendant was promoting its products. That's consistent with the view that a defendant who benefits from a market in the forum state should be subject to personal jurisdiction when the product causes injury there, and that's the old line from World-Wide Volkswagen, that it's proper if the defendant delivers its products into the stream of commerce with the expectation that they'll be purchased by consumers in the forum state. A majority of justices endorsed that idea back in 1980 and we still don't have a majority of justices rejecting that idea today. Turning to the sort of general jurisdiction cases, the ones that enshrine this essentially at home test, you know, I agree with Robin that they do work a significant doctrinal change in terms of where corporation can be subject to general jurisdiction. And it's interesting, of course, that some of the justices who might ordinarily favor greater access to judicial remedies have supported this change. It's been Justice Ginsberg by and large leading the charge on this new definition of general jurisdiction. And one reason for this I think might be the fundamental irrationality of general jurisdiction. I mean, to say there is general jurisdiction over a defendant is to say this lawsuit can proceed in this forum even if there is no reason on God's green earth why this forum should be hearing this case. And, you know, it's the same reason why transient, or tag jurisdiction, is controversial, because what difference should it make that the defendant happens to be served with process while they're physically present in the forum state. There's just no good reason. And I think one of the key questions going forward is, well what if there is a good reason for a case to be proceeding in a particular forum? And I think that's what's underlying some of the questions that arise in the wake of the Bristol-Myers decision and some of the topics that Linda addressed. I think one of the doctrinal issues where litigants will battle this out, especially in the context of litigation, is where exactly this line is between specific jurisdiction and general jurisdiction, and what should we understand as driving the distinction between these two categories. And, you know, the test, to the extent we have one, is, well there has to be an affiliation between the forum and the underlying controversy. And this of course would include cases where the lawsuit arises out of or relates to the defendant's context with the forum, but that's not necessarily the only kind of affiliation that can count. Bristol-Myers is, of course, the only Supreme Court decision to squarely address that question. But even it didn't provide a clarifying theory for what should be guiding courts going forward. One way we might tackle this issue, one way courts and litigants might tackle this issue, is to examine the practical reasons why a particular forum should be hearing a particular dispute, not because that sort of functional analysis would override minimum contacts and all those basic requirements but because they can inform whether the case has the required affiliation with the forum state to justify looking at the case through a specific jurisdiction lens. And I think that's what's oddly missing from the majority opinion in Bristol-Myers. Alito writes in the majority opinion, of course, that it's not enough that California plaintiffs and non-California plaintiffs suffered the same injuries. But again, there was no consideration of the practical value of aggregating related claims arising from the same underlying conduct. Now, it may be that the actual litigation in Bristol-Myers didn't present a particularly strong case in terms of why you really needed multi-state aggregation. It didn't seem like these were low value claims that might require broad multi-state aggregation to make them economically viable. But suppose multi-state aggregation was necessary to make even in-state plaintiffs claims economically viable. That's a stronger interest that might create a more meaningful affiliation with the forum state, and maybe that's one way to think about some of the issues Andrew addressed regarding personal jurisdiction in the MDL court. It's the importance of being able to facilitate aggregation that creates the necessary affiliation with respect to the broader bolus of claims. And I think finally this is one way we might conceptualize pendent personal jurisdiction. It's sort of part of that wider category of cases where a defendant has the basic level of minimum contact with the forum state and there are practical, dispute-related reasons for having the availability of judicial remedies against that defendant for that defendant's course of conduct can be adjudicated in that forum. And we've certainly let courts get away with a heck of a lot more than that in the context of subject matter jurisdiction. In the context of supplemental jurisdiction we don't treat each plaintiff's claim as an independent unit that must independently qualify for subject matter jurisdiction. Article III of the Constitution permits all of the plaintiffs to come into federal court potentially even if some of those individual claims don't have an independent basis as long as they arise from a common nucleus of operative fact. And in a statute like the Multiforum, Multiparty Trial Jurisdiction Act, you can even have a case where there's not even a semblance of subject matter jurisdiction, there's not even minimal diversity, but you could remove it to federal court because there's other litigation going on that's related for which there would be at least minimal diversity. So again, that similar logic potentially might apply in the personal jurisdiction context. And I'll just close with one point about Robin's final observation about formalism, and that's just to clarify that, you know, formalism doesn't necessarily have to be restrictive. I think Burnham is a great of example of that. Justice Scalia, noted formalist, says, let's just have a rule that says every time you get served with process you're subject to jurisdiction. It's a very formalist interpretation but it's a very broad interpretation. So one way to think about these problems going forward if we assume that the powers that be are gonna take a formalist approach is whether they might be formalist approaches that are more expansive rather than more restrictive. - I am going to choose not to take up more time responding other than to respond (laughter) to Andrew and Teddy about personal jurisdiction in the world of MDL. And Andrew in particular, I find attractive on one level the idea that maybe we should look at the transferee court. The difficulty I have there though is the basic assumption that the transfer should not affect any change of substance or change of a claim or defense. And personal jurisdiction is a defense. I mean obviously, as the court said in Schutz, personal jurisdiction is not just about defendants but it is typically raised as a defense. And if we start looking at the transferee court, then you really are transforming, in some sense, claims and defenses when you transfer from court A to the MDL court. And I just wanted your brief response to that thought. - Yeah, that's not an unreasonable point. - It's the best I can hope for, not unreasonable. - Not unreasonable, that's different from reasonable. I would say, the way that I would think about this is to say you've got to have personal jurisdiction under the usual rules in the transferor court. Then after the transfer there should be personal jurisdiction in the transferee court but measured by a different test that is measured by the test of whether or not it's reasonable under the Fifth Amendment. And what Adam says I think is the direction I'm going, that there's a national interest in efficiently resolving nationwide disputes that's captured in the MDL statute. And the most cases sort of hearkening back to Melane, which is something that Judith has written about recently, is this notion as a practical matter, that interest is going to outweigh the individual inconveniences to the parties in these cases. And so, if you look at MDL that way, sort of a realistic assessment of what it's doing, I think it does pass constitutional muster but not to deprive the defendant of a defense that there's no personal jurisdiction in the transferor court. Not only would it not deprive the defendant of that defense in the MDL court, it also ensures that if and when the case gets remanded, or if the case is gonna be decided on a dispositive motion, or tried as a bellwether trial in the MDL courts, we know what choice of law rules are supposed to apply for that case. - Yeah, but Ted is smoothing those over, if you recall. - Well, you do and you don't. I think the smoothing over is not running roughshod because there are places where state choice of law matters. And it matters in these circumstances where a judge actually has to apply it in individual cases, not instances where the judge stays with idea, oh my god, I've got to apply it 7,000 times. I'm applying it in this summary judgment motion, this bellwether trial. - So I think we have about a few minutes left for questions. Abbe has a question. - [Abbe] Hi, Abbe Gluck. I have a couple of comments and a question. So, just in light of the testosterone comment, I feel compelled to say that the attorney who helped the at home standard, my husband, is at home with the child. (laughter) So I think that we've made major progress here, so I can't resist that. I have a sort of a question comment for Teddy, and for Andrew actually. So, with the smoothing out thing about the state interest, I think it's more than just state law. And this is a preview of tomorrow's 9:00 AM panel, so please wake up at 8:45 to come to our 9:00 AM panel. But thinking about when states bring cases, there's more than just state law at stake. There's state interests, there's the attorney general obligation to stop a particular kind of harm in a state. So there's more than just the choice of law question but the particular considerations that might be unique, or different, when a governmental actor in a state brings a case and they sort of get bullied into the MDL. So I would just point that out and tantalize you all for the coffee that will be served tomorrow, 8:45. - In other words, it's not just private versus private in these cases. - [Abbe] Yeah, I think that it's not just a matter of the law, it's the whole stateyness and everything that could be going on. The other question for you guys, you know, I was surprised. I sort of thought that Robin, we were gonna go there. Surprised that in talking about where the personal jurisdiction were going, there isn't more talk of federalism per se, versus nationalism, which is also sort of an implicit theme of what this panel's been about. You know, Mcintyre, that line, Kennedy's line, the sovereign by sovereign analysis versus Ginsburg, the argument that, you know, the argument whether personal jurisdiction is really about Tenth Amendment, or is it about Fifth Amendment. So in thinking about the nationalism versus federalism debate, I think that's sort of an underlying theme. The last question I have for all of you was I thought Andrew, you were gonna go and start talking about plaintiff due process rights. And I heard it implicitly but it wasn't the most explicit part of your remarks. And so, isn't it possible that some of this MDL discussion is gonna start flipping the considerations a little bit into getting us thinking not so much about the defendant's due process rights when it comes to jurisdiction, but possibly some of the plaintiff's due process rights, especially the ones that are being pulled across the nation or being pulled from state to federal court. You know, could that open up a different area of argument, constitutional argument. - So, Robin, then Andrew. - So... Yeah, I agree. I was sort of leaving the nationwide service of process question for later. It definitely put pressure on that. Just like we've seen more interest in the registration statutes, there's now tons of articles and people advocating for various forms of nationwide service of process. Some people have been writing about it in the context of how it would happen only in federal courts. Other people have been making broader arguments, sort of the Ginsburg argument, that it is possible to think of New Jersey as just belonging to United States. But I just want to throw in something not MDL related that I think is important to point out, which is that I think there's a little bit of wanting to have cake and eating it too when it comes to subject matter jurisdiction and personal jurisdiction. And a good example is the Defend Trade Secrets Act that was passed a couple years ago in which all of the interests who lined up in favor of Goodyear and J. Mcintyre for this really restrictive form of jurisdiction over foreign defendants came to Congress and said, we have a huge problem. Everyone overseas is stealing our trade secrets and the only way we can solve this problem is to have a federal forum for state trade secret law claims but we're not gonna add anything about personal jurisdiction to the statute. And it made no sense to me, and the only sense I could make out of it was that there was an urgency to sort of talk about the need to address conduct by foreign defendants but really stopping short of enabling our courts to actually hear claims that would address them. So I think that there's now this game where we can sort of set things up where it looks like maybe we can hold foreign defendants accountable, but when actual litigation materializes it's not really gonna happen unless Congress gets serious about nationwide service of process. - I'll say two things quickly. First, I think the MDL statute really is an exercise is having your cake and eating it too, though I've never understood why you'd want to have cake if you weren't going to eat it. But putting that aside, I mean, the goal of the drafters of the MDL statute was to nationalize the power of the federal courts and to centralize that power. But by making the transfer only limited, it keeps that federalism patina available. It was very important to the plaintiff's bar at the time that the MDL statute was being drafted that the Van Dusen versus Barrack rule applied because they did not want to lose the choice of law benefits that would attach to where they filed their cases. And so that was sort of the price of the plaintiff's bar getting behind the MDL statute. So it's got both. It's got this nationalizing impulse while also trying to retain the rudiments of federalism there and how that shakes out I think is a real question. I agree with you with respect to plaintiffs. I'm more explicit about this in the paper, but I think that the issues for plaintiffs are actually perhaps even more important than issues for defendants. I mean, defendants in these cases, is it really inconvenient to deal with a nationwide MDL wherever it has to go? I'm not so sure about that. But if you're an individual plaintiff and you file your case, then it gets sent off someplace else where it might not have been brought, it's gonna be prosecuted by a lawyer that you didn't pick and it may eventually only come back to you in the form of a settlement offer. That seems to be a pretty major loss of control. And you're even worse off than an absentee in class action. The Schutz rationale of consent seems to be to be a pretty thin read on which to base jurisdiction. And you don't have the right to opt out. And the judge isn't required to determine that your representation is adequate. And so if you're a plaintiff in an MDL, you may actually find yourself in a somewhat worse position. - Can I just throw in something here? I mean, all of these things that happened with the MDL, I mean, it's not at all clear to me that at the time of the original MDL, anybody thought that all of these things were gonna happen at the MDL. I mean, the language of the MDL is pretrial. And one might think about things like dispositive versus non-dispositive motions being made in the MDL. I know that that's all sort of water under the bridge, it's all happened. But when you go back and talk about things like Lexicon and things that the transferee court is not supposed to do, one at least pauses a moment to ask about the powers of the MDL, whether that's trying the case here in the MDL ocean, or sending it back, or bellwether trials. - I think Judith has a question. - Yeah, I think this is probably the last question. - [Judith] Hi, Judith Resnik. So, who wants to be in federal court why seems to be relevant to this. And in one era, I'm trying to remember the Starquist? What's the tuna fish? - StarKist. - [Judith] StarKist, thank you. So there's the case where the defendants are trying to stay out of federal court, and fighting, and then all of a sudden they say, gee, federal court is a good place to be so let's change our view of how to read 28 U.S.C. 1332 diversity. And so here we are looking at who wants to be where why, and we haven't much talked about the minimal diversity statute that is pending in Congress with some people thinking it may well be enacted. And so we're looking now to the rush to federal courts to aggregate, to disaggregate because of the assumption that either through preemption of federal law, of state claims, or through interpretation, or through mandated arbitration, or through views of the negativity of aggregation, a new group of federal judges and some of the older, some sitting federal judges who have been there for longer will come together to say you can't proceed in these amalgams, invoking whether it's due process or federally. Not attentive to federalism because the minimal due process. The minimal diversity statute is remarkably tone deaf to that. But rather looking at trying to reshape, to deshape, to disaggregate and disenable adjudication. So it seems like that the doctrinal discussion has to get intersected with what's the periodicity, when is the doctrine being made, not just by what person, but with what gestalt, about what imaginary, about what the federal and state courts are going to do. So it's a question for the various commentators about how that makes you think or how we should understand your comments in light of that. - Yeah, and I think that's something that we're gonna have to wait and see how it shakes out. So in the Bristol-Myers case it's very clear who wants to be in federal court. The defendant wants to be in federal court and is desperate to get to federal court. And after Bristol-Myers it seems like plaintiffs... - Why? - Why, because as Andrew said, they view the California state courts as the lowest common denominator. They're gonna have unfair plaintiff-friendly judges in California and they want out at all costs. They wanted to be in the MDL in New Jersey and the plaintiffs had structured the case to avoid removal of CAFA by breaking it up so it was groups of 99 and not 100 so it doesn't trigger the mass action. - But is the comparison between federal or is the comparison we know the judge in California state court and we know the MDL judge, we want to be before the MDL judge, or is it federal state? Is it judge A, judge B, or is it federal court, state court? - I believe, and Andrew, correct me if I'm wrong, I believe in Bristol-Myers it was federal court versus state court because they didn't know who the MDL judge was at that point. But that's also going to factor into the calculus. You might be quite content as a plaintiff to file in the defendant's home state in state court under general jurisdiction if you don't like the MDL judge. So it could affect the timing. I think one thing that's interesting about the federal court/state court choice here is before Bristol-Myers it was very clear that defendants usually wanted to be in federal court. And one of the reasons, one of the effects of CAFA, you could almost say that CAFA was designed to fail. It's designed to get these class actions into federal court where if they're nationwide they're gonna face a predominance inquiry that if multiple state's laws are gonna apply to them they're gonna have to do some fancy subclassing or they're not gonna be certified. MDL puts these cases into federal... Or Bristol-Myers, it is channeling these cases into MDL, which is actually designed to handle them. And this goes back to the idea that it's a smoothing out of differences in state laws. It's not riding roughshod over state law. Choice of law rules, choice of law rules matter and apply in MDL. It's just there's a pressure towards uniformity. Okay, well, I know what article we're writing together, Teddy. We are plum out of time. Please join me in thanking our panel. (applause)

Want the rest of this video? Unlock the full lesson — plus 200+ videos, outlines, study aids, and more — for just $29/month: https://www.studicata.com

00:00 What Is Justiciability?
An overview of Article III’s case or controversy requirement and its importance in limiting federal court jurisdiction.

02:01 Why “Hypotheticals” Don’t Belong in Federal Court
Federal courts can only hear real disputes between adverse parties—no hypotheticals, advice, or abstract questions allowed.

05:55 Declaratory Judgments Explained
Courts can issue declaratory judgments—but only when an actual dispute exists based on established facts.

10:23 No Fake Lawsuits Allowed
Courts will dismiss collusive or “feigned” lawsuits where parties aren’t truly adverse to each other.

12:09 Standing: The Core Test for Justiciability
To bring a case, a plaintiff must show injury in fact, causation, and redressability—each element is essential.

13:36 Injury in Fact: It Must Be Concrete and Personal
The Court requires more than vague harms to the public—injuries must be real, particularized, and not speculative.

19:06 Causation: Connecting Injury to Defendant’s Actions
A plaintiff must show their injury was fairly traceable to the defendant’s conduct, not a distant or speculative link.

26:03 Redressability: Will the Court’s Ruling Help?
The injury must be likely to be resolved by a favorable court decision—vindication or punishment alone won’t cut it.

31:34 Constitutional vs. Prudential Standing
After the constitutional test, courts may impose additional judge-made prudential standing requirements.

metadata.title: Thomas Higgins Limited - What Is the Process of Commercial Debt Collection?
metadata.author: Thomas Higgins Limited
metadata.shortDescription:
What is the process of commercial debt collection — and how does it work from start to finish?
In this full video, Thomas Higgins Limited explains the entire commercial debt recovery journey, giving UK businesses a clear and practical understanding of every stage involved in recovering overdue invoices.
If your customers aren’t paying on time, knowing the correct legal and procedural steps can make the difference between successful recovery and financial loss. This video breaks down the full process in simple, actionable terms so you can take control of your credit management.

In this video, you’ll learn the complete debt recovery process:
Internal Credit Control & Payment Reminders

How to chase an overdue invoice politely and professionally
What information to include in reminder communications
When internal efforts should stop and formal recovery should begin

Formal Debt Collection Letters

What types of letters you can send (reminders, final demands, Letter Before Action)
What each letter must contain
How compliant wording increases your chances of being paid

Adding Statutory Interest & Late Payment Compensation

When you can legally add interest
How late payment fees work
Why adding interest can encourage faster payment

Letter Before Action (LBA)

Why an LBA is the final warning before legal action
What legal status it carries
Common reasons why LBAs prompt immediate payment

Issuing a Money Claim in Court

When to escalate and what evidence you need
What happens after a claim is issued
How judgments are made and enforced

Enforcement Options After Judgment
If the debtor still does not pay, this video explains:

High Court Enforcement Officers (HCEOs)
County Court Bailiffs
Charging orders
Attachment of earnings
Third‑party debt orders

When to Use Professional Debt Recovery Services

How outsourcing saves time and increases success rates
The benefits of using a fixed‑fee legal service
When professional support becomes the most effective option


Why understanding this process matters
Commercial debt recovery isn’t just about sending reminders — it’s about following a structured, compliant legal pathway.
Learning the process helps you:
✔ Recover unpaid invoices faster
✔ Protect your legal position
✔ Reduce bad debt
✔ Improve cashflow stability
✔ Avoid common mistakes businesses make when chasing debts

Need help recovering commercial debt?
Thomas Higgins Limited specialises in fast, low‑cost legal recovery services for UK businesses.
We handle everything from early‑stage letters to legal action and enforcement, helping you get paid quickly and professionally.

Visit: www.thomashiggins.com

metadata.title: Invoice Recovery: Mediation Versus Litigation Analysis
metadata.author: Taurus Collections (UK) Ltd
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of Debt Matters, we unpack one of the toughest choices UK finance teams face when invoices go unpaid: do you sit down at the table for mediation or head straight to court? Using Taurus Collections’ guide on mediation versus litigation as our roadmap, we break down how each route works in practice, what it really costs, and how long it typically takes to get money back into your cash flow.
We look at the legal basics around unpaid invoice disputes, from pre-action protocols and Letters Before Action through to what evidence you actually need in place before you escalate. Then we compare the commercial reality of mediation – faster, more confidential and relationship friendly – with the formality of litigation, where you may get a binding judgment but at the price of higher fees, longer timelines and more risk.
Finally, we talk about how to choose the right route for your situation: when protecting a key customer relationship matters more than “winning”, when a hard legal line is unavoidable, and where a specialist collections agency like Taurus can slot in alongside your lawyers to reduce risk and improve recoveries. If you are a business owner, finance director or credit controller dealing with stubborn late payers, this episode will help you pick a smarter path to getting paid.
#DebtMatters #TaurusCollections #DebtCollection #UnpaidInvoices #Mediation #Litigation #CreditControl #CashFlow #UKBusiness #SME #B2B #LatePayment

>> So that really clarifies the immediate
trade-off. With mediation, you're in the
driver's seat. With litigation, the
court is and you have to go wherever the

structure of mediation can actually
bring people to the table.

>> Because they see the alternative. They
realize that if mediation fails, the
next step is a much more expensive, much
more public court battle. Sometimes just
the threat of litigation is enough to
make mediation seem like a very
attractive cost-saving option for them
too.
>> That makes a lot of sense.
>> Okay,
>> let's get into what everyone is probably
thinking about right now. The money. How
much do these two paths actually cost?
>> The difference is pretty dramatic.
Mediation is by its nature designed to
be lower cost and crucially more
predictable.
>> Predictable is a good word when you're
already worried about cash flow.
>> It's a huge deal. With mediation, your
main costs are really twofold. You have
the mediator's fee, which is often split
5050 between you and the debtor.
>> And what does that typically run?
>> It can vary, of course, but you might be
looking at, say, $1,500 to $5,000 for a
full day. And then you have whatever
time your own lawyer spends preparing,
but the total is usually in the low
thousands. You can budget for it.
>> Okay? You can see the expense and plan
for it. Now, litigation,
>> litigation is uh a whole different
universe. The costs aren't just higher.
They can be unpredictable and they can
spiral.
>> How so?
>> Well, you start with an initial retainer
for your attorney. That could be$10,000,
20,000, even $50,000 just to get
started. Then you have the hourly fees
piling up.
>> And it's not just for the courtroom
time, right?
>> Oh, not at all. The real cost driver in
many cases is something called the
discovery phase. This is where the
lawyers spend hundreds of hours
gathering evidence, reviewing documents,
emails, financial records.
>> So, you're paying your lawyer maybe
$400, $600 an hour just to read through
boxes of old emails.
>> That's exactly it. And that part alone
can run into tens of thousands of
dollars before you're anywhere near a
trial. And that's not even counting
things like expert witnesses. If you
need an accountant to testify, for
example, that adds thousands more. It
sounds like the process itself just
creates these enormous costs. Whether
the debt itself is complicated or not,
>> that's a perfect way to put it. The cost
is procedural. With litigation, you're
paying for a guaranteed legal judgment.
Yes. But you're also paying for a
mandatory and often very expensive
process to get there.
>> Okay. So, we've covered the financial
drain. Let's talk about the time drain.
If you need that money for payroll,
every week counts. How fast can you get
a resolution? On this front, it's not
even a contest. Mediation is built for
speed.
>> How fast are we talking?
>> I mean, you could have a resolution in a
few weeks. For a more complex issue,
maybe a couple of months. The schedule
is flexible because you and the other
party are the ones setting it. You
decide when to meet.
>> You control the calendar.
>> You do. If everyone wants a quick
resolution, you can get one. It's
designed to be efficient.
>> And litigation. I think we all have an
idea of what that looks like.
>> It's the definition of slow, a slow
procedural grind. It's not unusual for a
case to take a year, 18 months just to
get through the initial stages. And
that's if things are moving smoothly.
>> And that's before any potential appeals,
I imagine.
>> Exactly. An appeal could add another
year on top of that. The most
frustrating part for many businesses is
that you have absolutely no control.
You're waiting on the court schedule,
the judge's availability. You're just
stuck waiting.
>> And while you're waiting, you're not
just out the money. Your team is tied
up, right? Someone has to manage the
lawyers, pull documents. It's an ongoing
operational headache.
>> That is such a critical point. It's a
hidden cost. Litigation forces you to
run your business while also managing a
lawsuit in the background, sometimes for
years. Mediation lets you solve the
problem and get back to what you're
supposed to be doing.

itself. Beyond just getting paid, what

process?

different. With litigation, when a judge
makes a ruling, it's very rigid. It's
typically a monetary judgment. You are
awarded X dollars. That's it.
>> It's a win or lose situation.
>> It's binary. Yes. A judge isn't there to
craft a creative business solution.
They're though to apply the law. And
another thing, court judgments are
public record.
>> Oh, so anyone could look it up.
>> Anyone. Your dispute becomes searchable
online. And of course, a lawsuit is
basically a declaration of war. that
business relationship is over,
guaranteed.
>> So, if it's a client you've had for 10
years who just hit a rough patch,
litigation means that relationship is
completely severed.
>> It's the nuclear option. Now, contrast
that with mediation. Because you're both
building the solution together, you can
be incredibly creative.

a structured payment plan, or maybe they

>> Meaning, do people actually pay up?

the money.
>> Yeah.
>> Okay. So, to wrap this up, the core

relationship. So, the choice really
boils down to your top priority. Is it

bridge. So before you make that call,

relationship actually worth? How does

It's typically a monetary judgment. You are awarded X dollars. That's it. >> It's a win or lose situation. >> It's binary. Yes. A judge isn't there to craft a creative business solution. They're though to apply the law. And another thing, court judgments are public record. >> Oh, so anyone could look it up. >> Anyone. Your dispute becomes searchable online. And of course, a lawsuit is basically a declaration of war. that business relationship is over, guaranteed. >> So, if it's a client you've had for 10 years who just hit a rough patch, litigation means that relationship is completely severed. >> It's the nuclear option. Now, contrast that with mediation. Because you're both building the solution together, you can be incredibly creative. >> What do you mean by creative? >> Well, it doesn't have to be just a simple cash payment. Maybe you agree to a structured payment plan, or maybe they give you a discount on future services in exchange for forgiving part of the debt. You can find solutions that actually benefit both of you long term. >> Things a court would never order. >> Never. And the entire process is confidential. It stays behind closed doors protecting everyone's reputation. And maybe the most important thing is compliance. >> Meaning, do people actually pay up? >> Right? Because the debtor helped create the agreement, they have a sense of ownership over it. We see a much higher rate of people voluntarily complying with a mediated settlement than with a court order that was forced on them. >> That makes perfect sense. The goal isn't just to get a piece of paper that says you're owed money. It's to actually get the money. >> Yeah. >> Okay. So, to wrap this up, the core trade-off seems to be this. Litigation gives you that ultimate legal power, that statebacked enforcement, but it comes at a very high price in money, time, and flexibility. >> It does. And mediation is the flip side. It's fast. It's cost-effective and it allows for flexible solutions that can even preserve a valuable business relationship. So, the choice really boils down to your top priority. Is it getting absolute legal certainty no matter the cost? Or is it getting your money back quickly, controlling your expenses, and maybe keeping that business connection alive? Understanding that choice, the high cost of certainty versus the value of speed and flexibility is really what helps you make the right call. >> And let me leave you with one final thought. In a lot of places, you're encouraged to try mediation before you can even file a lawsuit. But choosing to sue as your very first move, that's an irreversible step. You're burning that bridge. So before you make that call, ask yourself, what is that professional relationship actually worth? How does its value stack up against your need for an immediate court enforced order to pay? Answering that question can change your entire strategy.

metadata.author: Shergroup TV
metadata.shortDescription:
Send us Fan Mail (https://www.buzzsprout.com/1686079/fan_mail/new) 


IN THIS EPISODE |  Chief Shergroupie, Claire Sandbrook, explains how our Cashflow Solutionss can help you collect in your unpaid invoices, escalate to legal claims, and finish the process by transferring judgments to the Shergroup Legal for enforcement.  Since 1995 Shergroup has been adding value to its function as Sheriffs, and now High Court Enforcement Officers, by helping crediitors with a range of different commercial profiles.  It was our first diversification outside our heritage as Sheriffs and we have enjoyed collecting and litigating on B2B and B2C debts ever since. 

Our process follows the 3 tiers of function of in a logical flow as part of our overall Cashflow Solution.  These tiers are |

  •  Collection
  •  Legal
  •  Enforcement

In the first tier – Collections - we offer a NO COLLECT NO FEE service to help our creditor clients feel comfortable in outsourcing their debts and claims to us.  We don’t want our clients worrying about the cost of doing this.  Our commission starts at 15% + VAT.   There are no hidden extras, or hidden set up fees.  We also encourage our clients to review their terms and conditions of business, so our fees are recoverable from their customer wherever possible.  Why should your business lose a slice of your invoice debt from your late paying customer?  


The Collections process has a standard cycle of 30 days and the last step in that cycle is to send a FREE Letter Before Action (“LBA”) to warn our client’s customer that legal proceedings will be taken if they do not pay or put forward an acceptable offer.  


If the Letter Before Action doesn’t prompt payment we move to the Legal tier of our process. 


Our sister company, Sherwins Limited trading as "Shergroup Legal", carries out this part of the process.  We charge fixed court fees and the court fee to issue as a simple way to move through this part of the recovery process.  Today we can help a business manage its Accounts Receivables function, from start-ups to multimillion businesses.  


The end result of the legal process will be a judgment in our client’s favour.  


Enforcement is the final tier of our process and its where it all started in Shergroup, when we were appointed Under Sheriffs.    Today Writs of Control issued by the High Court give us the authority to enforce payment from people named on this historical document.


Judgments over £600 in value (made up of the debt, interest, costs, and late payment interest), are transferred to Shergroup Enforcement for a High Court Writ of Control to be issued.  An additional fee of £156 is charged to cover the management and court fee for this process.


This uniqueness in our 3 tier process, makes up the cliché of our ONE STOP SHOP.  Only a few companies can enforce payment.  We are the only High Court Enforcement provider that through our history can do the entire process from start to finish in a professional and client-friendly way.


This is the Shergroup way, and we love to look after everyone in our client community with your debts, your claims, and your judgments.  

To find out more email us at 
hub@shergroup.com 
or call us for a chat on 020 3588 4240

metadata.title: What Should I Do If a UCC Lien Has Been Filed Against My Business
metadata.author: Credit Commerce & Currency
metadata.shortDescription:
If a Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) lien has been filed against your business, it's essential to take prompt and appropriate action to address the situation. Here's a detailed description of what you should do:


Review the UCC Filing: Obtain a copy of the UCC filing from the appropriate state or local authority where it was filed. Review the details of the filing, including the creditor's information, the collateral involved, and any other relevant terms.
Understand the Implications: Understand the implications of the UCC lien on your business. A UCC lien grants the creditor a security interest in specific assets of your business as collateral for a debt or obligation. It can affect your ability to obtain financing, sell assets, or engage in certain business transactions.
Communicate with the Creditor: Reach out to the creditor who filed the UCC lien to understand the nature of the debt or obligation and explore options for resolving it. Clarify any discrepancies or errors in the filing and negotiate a repayment plan or settlement if possible.
Seek Legal Advice: Consider seeking legal advice from a qualified attorney who specializes in commercial law or business transactions. An attorney can provide guidance on your rights and obligations concerning the UCC lien and help you navigate the legal process effectively.
Address the Debt: Take steps to address the underlying debt or obligation that led to the UCC lien. This may involve paying off the debt in full, negotiating a settlement, restructuring the debt, or pursuing other options to satisfy the creditor's claim.
Request Lien Termination: Once the debt has been resolved, request that the creditor terminate or release the UCC lien by filing the appropriate paperwork with the relevant authorities. Ensure that the lien is removed from the public record to prevent any negative impact on your business operations.
Monitor Your Credit Report: Keep a close eye on your business credit report to ensure that the UCC lien is accurately reflected and updated once it has been resolved. Promptly dispute any inaccuracies or discrepancies to maintain the integrity of your credit profile.
By following these steps and taking proactive measures to address the UCC lien filed against your business, you can mitigate potential risks and protect your business interests effectively.

Topic: UCC-1 Explained: Debtor vs. Secured Party & the Two Planes of Law

UCC-1 Explained: Debtor vs. Secured Party & the Two Planes of Law

In this teaching, we break down the relationship between the public commercial plane and the private common law/trust plane, and why understanding the difference matters before filing a UCC-1.

This lesson explains the distinction between the debtor entity, the secured party, the role of the security agreement, and why the UCC-1 financing statement is used to place a private commercial relationship into the public record.

We also discuss key concepts like:

Public vs. private capacity
Debtor vs. secured party
Security agreement vs. UCC-1 filing
Attachment and perfection
Constructive notice
“First in time, first in right”
Why filing without understanding can leave you exposed

This is a snippet from a longer teaching designed to help you gain clarity before taking action.

Educational purposes only. This is not legal advice.

metadata.title: What Happens After A Writ Of Execution?
metadata.author: County Portal Law
metadata.shortDescription:
What Happens After A Writ Of Execution?

Following a writ of execution, the sheriff or a designated law enforcement officer is empowered to seize and sell the judgment debtor's assets to satisfy the outstanding debt. This process typically involves identifying and levying on property, which could include bank accounts, vehicles, real estate, or personal possessions. The seized property is then advertised for sale, often through public auction. Once sold, the proceeds are used to pay off the judgment, including court costs and any associated fees. If the sale proceeds are insufficient to cover the entire debt, the judgment remains active, and the creditor may pursue further collection efforts. If there are surplus funds after the debt is paid, they are returned to the debtor.

metadata.author: Receivables Info | Debt Collection News
metadata.shortDescription:
What’s holding back your oversight strategy—bad tools or unstructured data?
In this episode, I’m joined by David Pauken, CEO of Convoke, to unpack how structured data for collections is transforming compliance workflows for credit issuers. We talk about cloud-based media sharing, scalable recovery operations, and why your next audit might depend on your tech stack.
If you want to modernize your approach and stop guessing at oversight—this one’s for you.




Listen now and level up your strategy.


Podcast Website:
https://receivablespodcast.com/videos/structured-data-collections-pauken
Guest Website:
https://www.convokesystems.com/
Guest LinkedIn:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/davepauken/


 structured data for collections,
 credit issuer compliance tools,
 third party oversight platform,
 automation in financial services compliance,
 digital transformation in receivables

#StructuredData
#DavidPauken

Thanks for listening! Follow Us On LinkedIn (https://www.linkedin.com/company/receivables-info/) , Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/ReceivablesInfo/)  & Youtube (https://www.youtube.com/@receivablesinfo)
