Thanks for having me on your program today. >> Well, I got to say you've got one of the most interesting backgrounds I think in the space, and this always is my favorite part of the podcast, learning where people came to the debt collection industry from. For anyone who has not heard this story before, can you tell everyone a little bit about yourself and how you got to the seat that you're in today? >> Sure, happy to tell the story. Graduated college, I was an accountant, went to work for this old accounting firm called Arthur Andersen, was there for a long time, a dozen years, and uh it was time to leave the firm, Adam, and I was looking for a job, and I got a job at a startup that was uh started by a college dropout in Bethesda, Maryland, and it was a marketing services firm. I went there to work there as the chief accountant, and the company took off and it went public on the New York Stock Exchange, and this founder was Dan Snyder, who later acquired the the Washington Redskins. Now that company went public, and at the time, Dan was the youngest CEO ever on the New York Stock Exchange, uh later eclipsed by Mark Zuckerberg. That company uh Snyder Communications took off, uh it grew to billions in revenue, and we eventually sold it to a company called Havas, a French ad agency. He bought the Redskins, he joined he asked me to join him there as the chief operating officer. Uh you know, I didn't grow up as a huge uh sports fan or football fan, but here I I just I fell into this job that people spend their life trying to get, and uh so here I was in sports entertainment. So I was there for six years as the as the chief operating officer, and um learned a lot about It's really a business, contrary to what some people might think. You still have revenue you got to grow and customers you have to serve, and a product that you have to put on the field. So that's where I learned my business chops. And and after some time I left. It was time to do something different, and I wanted to get into technology. And I became the CEO of a local energy technology company here in the Washington area. It was owned by some venture capitalists. Grew that, sold it. And then some investors who had invested into into Convoq asked me to come run this new startup. And the original business model had challenges to it. There were uncertain times in 2010, and me and a couple of my partners eventually bought the business and restarted it into what it's become today. So that's that's how I got to where I am. >> So and you know, Convoq is a really common name across the industry. You're always well represented. You you're always at the shows and the conferences, and it's just a a very common phrase, but I don't know that everybody truly understands the storyline of this organization and you know, the original business model is compared to how you've pivoted. And ultimately, I would like to talk about what you're seeing over the next 5 years because I think you've had a great vision in the time that you've been managing that organization. So I'm I'm curious to see what you're starting to think about over the next couple of years as well. >> So what should I give you the origins and then >> Yeah, let's start let's start at the beginning of the storyline and we'll work our way through it. >> Okay. So the the the origin was there was there was a couple of debt buyers who were collection attorneys and debt buyers up in Michigan. They had a problem getting media, and they were buying debt. And so the idea was, hey, this thing called the cloud was new back then. Can we take the media and put it in the cloud, and whoever has permissible purpose to the account could get access to it? That was fundamentally the idea. So coders were hired, friends and family raised money, and we built a platform where media could go into the cloud, and if you could demonstrate that you owned the account, you could get access to the media. And we were fortunate enough to get uh a very a first customer which was a large bank. And we were able to prove out the model and that it actually worked. Interestingly, so the the original idea was just solving the media problem for debt sales. I can stop there and let you ask a question or just >> So I mean look I was living through it. I was buying debt around the time when giant rider trucks full of documents would show up and we had to bring in someone to scan it. So I mean I was there at the beginning of this and and had an opportunity. I mean that was a that was a major step in the industry going to a new level and being able to manage things in bulk. That's I mean it really the idea of digitizing media changed the debt buying industry forever. It's I remember at that time thinking about it and looking at the challenges of the cloud because at the time nobody trusted really putting anything into the cloud. It was such a new concept. Even the terminology was really new. >> Yeah. >> How you got a a major creditor to pioneer that with you. I think one has really helped to stake something in the ground that said this is a trustworthy service, but I can only imagine how difficult that lift must have been to get that first group on board. >> Yeah, it was it was uh it was very difficult. Uh they fortunately had a big problem and needed a solution. And so they were willing to to take a chance on us. Sometimes you know when the when the pain is bad enough you're willing to maybe look at something you otherwise wouldn't do to make a change and and they did. Um the the challenge we had after that though Adam you may recall back from those years that a lot of credit issuers actually stopped selling debt altogether. And so we and we were struggling there for a while. But then uh the regulators said that credit issuers became responsible for the activities of a third-party debt collector. >> Mhm. >> And that happened I think in 2012. And that created an immediate overnight problem for a credit issuer. How are How are they going to oversee what these third parties are doing if they're responsible? And so what we what we did was we took the product we had were successfully getting media from a credit issuer to a third party. What if we just sort of flipped it on its head and got information from a third party and made it available to a credit issuer? So that that's how we evolved to help solve the oversight problem that the industry faced pretty urgently in the early years. >> You know, in that 2012-2014 time frame is the same timeline that we created Compliarm with the purpose of doing the same thing, but doing it from the perspective of complaints, disputes, and being able to move that data back and forth. We ended up selling that company to Provana in 2019 >> Okay. >> because it was a [clears throat] it was a big problem. I mean, being able to understand now all of a sudden you're responsible for all of these third-party vendors. You can't stop collecting. That revenue is expected in the bottom line and that's, you know, it's in their financial reports and, you know, that that is a direct drive on profitability. So to just cut debt collection or litigation out was almost impossible, but the technologies not only to let's say managing a a legal network, there was a lot of challenges in getting the documentation back and forth between these organizations. So it sounds like you had some of the the right infrastructure technology at the right time to actually be able to execute on. >> Yeah, one one of our strategies that we were trying to bring to the industry was which is very difficult for them to absorb these regulatory changes, providing media, doing oversight. And what we wanted to try to educate our customers on is that, hey, technology can be your friend. We don't have to stop collecting. We can still collect. Let's just bring some technology tools to satisfy the changing regulatory environment. Some collectors stopped, right? Some law firms are not in business or agencies stopped. We all saw that, but we tried to educate that, hey, you can you can still collect. It's okay to do that under this new regime. That brought us into the field of data. So we were good with media and then we started capturing this data and we found ourselves working alongside the recovery management systems of large financial institutions. The large recovery management systems were good at placements and recalls and balance tracking, but all of these oversight and media tools they didn't have. And so we found ourselves working alongside uh these systems. And so the way things have evolved here coming up to 2015, we see credit issuers wanting a modern recovery management tool that allows them to do inventory management, that allows them to track balances, that manages their media, that gets them the information for the oversight in in a one-stop shop. And then now that we're in this area of AI over the last 2023, can I have business intelligence to help me be more compliant, have higher productivity, and better performance, collecting more money? Those three things. Compliance, productivity, performance. >> Centralizing those disparate systems is the only way to structure the data to be able to learn for what's coming in the future. So it sounds like you've taken this natural evolution to really providing an ancillary service to starting to provide the primary software or that consolidation of all of those different data points. Your standard debt collection software wasn't really built for the purpose of managing third parties, right? It was built for collection agencies to manage themselves and banks would deploy something similar for their own collection efforts, but that's not always the infrastructure that you're looking for to be able to go out to third parties and to manage those other relationships, right? Because the flow of litigation data requirements is different than the flow of collections is different than if we were to sell accounts and how all that starts to look from a consulting standpoint. I've I've never worked at the banks, but you know, having worked with some of the banks from a consulting standpoint that was always an issue was that their loan management system built for collections and either they don't have something and they were using spreadsheets and old school technology, but starting to structure all of that data in 2015 is really insightful going into where we are now in 2023 because if the data's not structured, it's not valuable, right? >> It's not valuable. Yeah. It's a good point on the channels that you're bringing up, Adam, because a credit issuer, as you point out, has the three choices ahead of them. They can sell the debt, they can use an agency, they can hire a law firm, or I guess they can work it internally. They've got four choices before them. And we try to be the tool to help them if they want to go external to one of those third parties, debt sales agency or legal, they're in one platform. >> Well, they should always be attacking at least one or more of those cuz if you look back at the old Bill Bartmann days when the banks had limited themselves to only debt sales, they were overly reliant that cash flow through one organization. When that organization didn't exist anymore, they had to go rebuild all of their recovery networks. So I would think that a large creditor should be looking quite closely at having all four of those channels running simultaneously and you should be able to pull your levers and move your volume back and forth and champion challenge, but if you're just collecting internally and you're not comparing yourself to a third party, >> Yeah. >> I've always found that banks are really good at like underwriting and performing loan servicing, but when it comes to debt collection, like it really does require specialized strategies and services. Now look, I I think the line has become blurred because anybody can send out a text message, anybody can send out an email these days, but the differentiator is in the strategies. It's in the content and in the strategies. It's not in the ability to send a text message or email. So being able to specialize portfolio volume in a way in which it's being worked by those with the highest degree of certainty and collecting it, I mean that feels like it's a a natural fit for a a even a mid-sized creditor. >> Abs- absolutely. A mid-sized creditor, uh even, you know, smaller credit unions, you know, any organization that's got past due debt, they have a responsibility to try to collect it. It's it's all part of our credit system here in the US and they need to have tools to be able to do it efficiently and effectively. >> And if they can't collect it, what are the options? They can raise interest rates or they can make credit less available. They've only got two levers to pull. >> That's it. And neither of those are good options. Yeah. >> No, not for the consumer or for the or for the investor or for the bank. >> Yeah, your your point on on champ champion challenger, that's historically been hard to do. It's been sort of a manual data accumulation effort to try to compare one strategy to another. But in in the day and age that we live in today with some of the technologies that exist out there through companies like DataBricks and Click and come under some really modern technologies that are available to companies like Convoq, we can we can now take data much more easily from a third party and present it to a credit issuer so they can do this champ champion challenger and and then make better decisions on how to push through collection of of a given consumer debt. >> Yeah, being able to compare apples to apples workloads and it I'm often surprised by how little people really understand AB testing and you know, limiting to a single variable and being able to measure and test on like one particular thing. I think sometimes we get so excited that we're running an experiment that we try to include too many variables >> Yeah. >> and it really dilutes the end result or the at least the measurement of in in conclusion based on the the end result of the experiment. It's always been a challenge in our space. >> Yeah, and I what I'm excited about for the future is is some of these tools that you mentioned sending sending emails and texts and all of those are available. How how can we use that data and the consumer's behavior in response to that to make better predictions about how to pursue collecting debt? Can we predict oh, you should email this consumer, you should text this one. Here's the time of day you should do that. And maybe it's for this this particular asset class, but on another one, it's something else. >> Mhm. >> And I all the data will I think will guide us there. And that's the really exciting part about the future here. >> I think the fourth dimension of that is the content. I think, you know, it dealing with what to send them or really like is it a text message, an email, the cadence of things, all that to me feels like 3D chess. I think the fourth dimension is when we have to start including in that calculation what content are we sending them. So not only are we trying to pinpoint what, where, when, who, how, but we're now also trying to figure out what what's the message that we're communicating within that individual communication. And and as an industry, we've been very focused on the channels themselves and not so much on how are we going to test and and perfect that content. But that content, I believe, will be one of those major differentiators between organizations in the coming three to five years. Just like I would say to people, and you hear me say it fairly often, that those organizations that don't start deploying some machine learning and starting to test artificial intelligence a year from now, maybe two years from now, it's going to be five years to never in terms of opportunity to catch up again. So staying on that wave and not letting it crash over you, I I think is really solid advice for the whole >> It's a it's a really important point, Adam. I was I was with a group of technology CEOs last night here in Washington and with some private equity investors along in the meeting. And what they're seeing now, it's it's somewhat pattern matched to when the internet came in the late '90s. Remember all the excitement about the internet company? Well, there's similar excitement about native AI companies. So you've got all kinds of native AI companies being created, some of them in our industry that are going to be very innovative. So that's one track. Some of those guys will be successful, some others. Then there's companies like Convoke where we were not traditionally native AI, but we have to move in that direction, which is your point. Like we we have to do that. And so there's so many of us in the industry that are been around five, ten, fifteen years, we now have a job to do to transform ourselves. >> The larger the data set, the more that's required. >> Yeah. Yeah. >> The larger the data set, the harder it is to recognize patterns, but the easier it is for the machine to do it. So the more that we can start to look at these large data sets and unleash some learning capabilities there to identify at least breadcrumbs towards the insights that we're looking for will make a big difference. >> Yeah. And look, our our job at Convoke is to try to do this in a way that's safe because PII is involved, efficient, and actually better than a credit issuer can do on their own. The credit issuers are spending a lot of money on technologies and innovation as and as you pointed out earlier, they're they're often most of that time and energy is spent on either underwriting or servicing, maybe less on the back end. Where so there there's opportunities for companies in our our space, in the arm space to bring real tools to the to the credit issuers. >> Agreed. There there's a lot of opportunity with the credit issuers right now. As you start thinking about what the next five years looks like, we're going to go through this the great AI race over the next probably two years, maybe three. But what do you think the next five years starts to look like as we think about how rapid the world is changing today? >> Well, certainly it's it's along the the theme that we've been talking about where since you have these data sets and they're large data sets, what AI machine learning tools can you bring to that data to help make better decisions so performance goes up, productivity goes up, and compliance goes up. And I think also bringing in external data that might be useful in that. So I think I think that that will be a big part of the next five years. Then the then the other the other element I think is it's important to spend time tying into some of the credit issuer systems. They're now more many more of them are digitally engaging. They're looking at you have data from pre-charge off behavior. I think you can bring all of that into the into the mix mix as well. And I think these tools will help lower head count on collections, audit costs cuz it it can be done by a machine. We can just leave aside for the second the issue of what's happening to the labor force, okay? That's that's a real thing that affects real people that we need to be sensitive to. But the reality is some of this technology is just going to make costs go down, accuracy go up, efficiency climb, and collect more money. >> It's a diversification opportunity for collection agencies and looking at customer service and some of the other things that do require that more labor intensive, but then you've always got that overflow skill set. As a collection agency, you're trying to build this like culture and team around you that has a a particular career craft, let's call it. >> Yeah. >> And it's hard because as you start looking at the account to collector ratios are going up, the profitability per, you know, per collector is also going up. >> Yeah. >> Now you have to figure out how how do you start to diversify and use that workforce in new and interesting ways to provide additional value because it is a craft and it's a valuable craft that I don't think will be replaced by AI anytime soon, although we may start to see more of the administrative things, it's an opportunity to start to grow the minds of the team around you and starting to move in that direction, which as I've started deploying artificial intelligence across my organizations is always my focal point. Grow the people around me and teach them how to use the tools. >> Yeah. Well, look, even if even if you look over the history of Convoke over the last 15 years, there there used to be a lot more human involvement in delivery of media. Now >> Good statement. >> We're we're moving millions and millions of documents around and no human ever touches it, right? That this analogy will continue into this AI machine learning world. And I I think >> connections. >> Those all those data connections. And somebody was telling me recently about some interesting technologies where if I've got a foreign accent, there's technology that'll smooth that out so I sound like I'm from You know, it's how do I allocate capital on where I want to spend my R&D efforts? >> Mhm. >> Cuz there's this element where I You ask me, what's the future like? Well, I can maybe say broadly, but do I really know? Hard Sometimes it's hard to know. >> It's real hard to know right now. It's It's becoming more difficult to predict because of the speed in which we're dealing with challenges. I think a lot of it I I've identified and I I've written an article about six use cases of artificial intelligence in debt collection. That's not to say that that's specific to debt collection, not including HR and accounting and all of these other places where you're going to start to see that type of technology deployed. But pretty much every Like everybody keeps talking to me about their use cases internally, and I keep putting them into those same six buckets. And understanding that structured data that I call it scoring and and kind of treatment, but it's really talking about like workflows and workflow engineering, I think is really where we're going to start to see that evolution over the next five years. It's going to be about how are we going to move these things through processes and how can we smooth out those processes and human manage the exceptions until we can learn how to automate those too. But that process of continuing to manually manage those exceptions, I think goes on for a long time. And when you talk about AI from a compliance standpoint, for example, being able to listen to 100% of calls instead of 5% of calls, and then a live person listens to the 5% that are actual exceptions is a perfect example of using artificial intelligence and the technology at hand the right way to enhance and to refine, not to replace. Because we're not going to replace all the people, but we are going to be able to refine the processes and have the people's minds focus on those areas in which they add the most value. >> Yeah. And look, on some of those examples you just rattled off, our our role in it is to is to get that information from the agency and law firm, and we get it every day, and present it in this business intelligence model that's easy for a credit issuer to digest and use. >> Well, data's not worth anything unless you can visualize it. If you want to show me reports that are just big long spreadsheets full of numbers, it doesn't actually help me. Looking at a dashboard, being able to visualize the information behind it quickly identify the anomalies that require my attention, like that's what I'm looking for. >> Yeah. Yeah. I mean, I'm I'm I'm excited to see the day when somebody's typing in in a in a natural language inquiry, hey, compare this particular credit card from this lawyer to this lawyer on this vintage on the first 30 days. Just be able to type that in and get a presentation. >> I've spent the last 20 years compiling a database just like that, but I can't query it in that way, right? I'm still in the world of reports and trying to understand, but I agree wholeheartedly with you that I believe from a data analytics standpoint and as more structured data comes together, those things will become more and more possible in the near future. >> Yeah. I guess the other thing that I would add is we we work hard uh Adam to stay focused. >> Mhm. >> We we are we are particularly focused on the needs of a credit issuer. We've often been asked, could a debt buyer or a agency or law firm use some of our services, and it just hasn't been designed for that. And we, at least at this point in our history, we want to stay focused on the credit issuer. There's plenty of other great technology companies that can serve others. So we do we do try not to be all things to all people and and stay in our lane, which we think is has been helpful to us and our customers over the years. >> I respect that. I definitely respect that. Being able to focus like that and to to grow your success in a particular channel and not be distracted by taking on every challenge or every opportunity that's presented, I can definitely appreciate and respect that focus. >> Yeah, over the years like people will say, hey, okay, I've captured the audio call, so somebody can listen to it. Can you build technology to listen to that technology? Actually, I couldn't because there's audio listening technology where people spend $100 million building it. I could never create anything that good. So let let's go rent that from them. So we we try to do things that other people actually can't do. >> I like that. I I like that a lot. Dave, I got to say you this has been an inspiring conversation. I really do appreciate you taking the time and energy to come on here and share your insights. I've learned a lot about Convoke and your storyline and kind of how things have come together. Have any additional questions you'd like to ask Dave or myself, you can leave those in the comments on LinkedIn and YouTube and we'll be responding to those or if you have additional topics you'd like to see us discuss, you can leave those in the comments below as well and hopefully I can get Dave back at least one more time to help me continue to create great content for a great industry. But until next time everyone, really do appreciate your time and attention. We'll see you all again soon.

metadata.title: Debt Collection Data Waterfalls: Testing, KPIs, and Continuous Improvement | Ep. 264
metadata.author: Receivables Info | Debt Collection News
metadata.shortDescription:
What is a debt collection data waterfall, and why should it never be “set it and forget it”?

In this episode, Adam Parks talks with Will Turner of TEC Services about building and managing waterfall strategies across compliance scrubs, recovery scoring, and skip tracing. They cover the KPIs that matter, how to avoid common mistakes (like single-threading one vendor), and how to test improvements using retroactive analysis or champion-challenger experiments in production.

Receivables Podcast Website: 
https://receivablespodcast.com/videos/debt-collection-data-waterfalls-turner 

Guest Website – TEC Services: 
https://www.linkedin.com/company/tec-services-group

Guest LinkedIn – Will Turner: 
https://www.linkedin.com/in/willturner/

There's so many different data sources. But I think that's an interesting kind of brings to a an interesting point is with all of these different data sources that are available to us and the the level of complexity and energy that goes into testing, I guess hiring a concierge such as yourself to kind of walk the journey with you would make a lot of sense. I mean, even in what we're talking about in the basics here within the skip tracing, there's going to be potentially five, six, seven, eight steps of their waterfall and which data sources belong at which levels of that stair step. >> Yeah, that's >> order of operations will change everything. >> 100% and that's part of what's fun about this, Adam, is obviously our customers know their business better than anybody and fortunately, you know, we know the data side really really well both because we have a number of customers across a bunch of different markets all providing performance data to us. So we have about 120 different data sources connected to our platform today, but we have performance data that's helping us inform how those data vendors are performing and then how to sequence those vendors, how to configure those products to get the most out of them. Um so it's a combination of our customers knowing their business better than we do and us knowing the data piece better than most and you put those two together and there's something that happens. It's the 1 + 1 = 3 scenario. >> Well, the just even engaging in that process, I think is a great start for most organizations, but I think people get scared like I don't have a data scientist. I don't know how to measure not only the value of the data, but the value of that investment in comparison to other potential data investments. And if the number one thing in mathematics is the order of operations, then the order of operations of adding and subtracting data to the waterfall process is ultimately going to have a pretty significant impact. And then if you think about all the different reasons that two waterfalls are never the same because of the level of complexity that we're talking about, I mean, look at all the consulting I've ever done and I know you've been in far more shops than I have, I've never seen two organizations running identical waterfalls because depending on your product, your location, your strategies, I mean, there's so many different variables that go into it. Talk to me a little about the uniqueness that you see between these different types of waterfalls at different organizations. >> Yeah, so so one of the things I find interesting, Adam, is so we get the question a lot, you know, which data vendor is the best? And so that's a >> It's a loaded question. >> It is a loaded question. It's a hard one to answer because it's relative to your business, your budget, your tolerance for risk, um what you define success as. And what I find interesting is that we do a lot of AB testing or champion challenger testing. >> Mhm. >> And you can take five different data providers and run them different a different order or sequence and get very different performance outcomes with the exact same vendors. So you asked me about the uniqueness of a data waterfall. And so I'd start with the customer. >> Mhm. >> The customer in itself is unique. They're unique in the their budget, they're unique in their risk tolerance, their philosophy. They're unique in the type of consumers that they work with. The portfolio itself varies, right? What's the makeup of this portfolio? What type of debt is it? How old is that debt? Has it been worked before? Is it prime? Is it non-prime? What are the characteristics of the consumer? How good is the data within that portfolio? Is it accurate? Is it incomplete? >> How many times has it been worked? >> Exactly. And we haven't even talked about, you know, the third-party element, the external data, but just the customer in itself. And so that's where I think part of the uniqueness is saying, okay, what is the business challenge or use case that we're trying to solve? What's the cost of fixing that or not fixing that? So what's the financial or performance gain or loss if we fix that problem or we don't fix that problem? How are we going to measure that? What does success look like? And then once we know that, then it's time to start assembling sort of the ingredients, the third-party data providers that we're going to use in our waterfall fashion to to solve for this. So, I talked about the customer and the portfolio and the uniqueness of that. Now we're getting into the third-party data providers or external data and what's the uniqueness of them. And so, sort of on the surface the the simple test that a lot of people do is, you know, they'll take a small sample of accounts, they'll run the same file of accounts out to, you know, a handful of different data providers. They'll look at what data is unique, what data overlaps. Um, and that just gives you kind of a a quick and dirty understanding of do they have the depth of coverage? How unique is their data? And that's typically where a lot of the data testing stops and I think that's really where ours starts. >> Okay. I mean that that makes [clears throat] a lot of sense cuz as we start thinking our way through building out this data waterfall and really where people are generally stopping is before they can actionably move that data set into an intelligence. So we can bring all this data or all these signals together, but we're going to have to convert them into some sort of actionable intelligence that allows us to move things down the path here. But as we think about how unique they are, so we've talked about how the different organizations themselves are driving what's unique about their waterfalls and all of those different data sources that are coming in. But each one of those data providers and each one of those vendors is also going to have a whole other set of data products and now you're comparing different data products sourced without truly understanding where they're coming from. So what kind of KPIs are you able to start looking at from a data quality perspective to understand the value attributes of these different sources as they're available? >> Yes, so as far as KPIs, so going back to the uniqueness of the customers and what they're trying to solve for, it could be a lender or a debt buyer or a servicer. You know, in the case of a servicer, you may have just within the same customer they may have a portfolio where liquidation rates are fairly high, but maybe their profitability isn't where they wanted to be. So their goal is to maintain their liquidation rates but improve the profitability of this portfolio. They may have another portfolio where they're competing on customer scorecards and they're chasing, you know, market share awards. >> Mhm. >> So maybe the speed at which they get to a right party contact and a payment are important metrics for them to compete on their client scorecards. And so when it comes to KPIs, I think going back to what specific problem are we trying to solve and then how are we going to measure success? And we break those success metrics or KPIs out into sort of two buckets. So I'll use a phone waterfall because it's just really simple. >> Okay. >> In the case of a phone waterfall, when we're using external data to verify what information is correct or enrich or append data to get to the correct information, we look at things like how many dial attempts were made on this account, what was the result of those dials? Did it Was it a right party contact, a wrong party contact? So sort of the dialing metrics themselves are important to inform uh not only how the data is performing but how is the client actually using the data that they're purchasing. And then on the payment side, of course, did this person pay or not? Uh what percentage of the balance did they pay? What's the average payment amount? What are your gross dollars collected? What are your fee dollars collected? What is the ROI on that information? You know, what is the liquidation rate or excuse me, the liquidation dollars per account? So we kind of break it out into operational metrics from, you know, dialing, sending SMS text messages, emailing, whatever the channel communication is. How is the customer working that data and what are the performance performance metrics there? And then then there's more the money metrics around liquidation rates, dollars collected, ROI, etc. >> And it feels like there's these measurements or at least some predictive measurements within each one of those. And you know, as you're talking about the phone number one and then I start thinking about some of the skip tracing that has to be done post judgment and really like just how different the needs of the different disciplines of debt collection really are when we think about debt buyers versus agencies versus law firms and what that looks like. Just how truly different is all of that. I would think that their data needs themselves are wildly unique. >> And you're referring to, you know, maybe a lender versus a debt buyer versus a collection agency at early stage versus a legal strategy. Yeah, wildly different data needs. And even within any of those categories, right, Adam, each customer can kind of have unique unique goals. Is it Is it performance? Is it revenue? Is it profitability? Is it chasing scorecard metrics? But yeah, certainly a data waterfall or wash for a legal debt collection strategy is going to look a lot different than, you know, early stage collections for a first party collection agency, for example. >> Yeah, investment capability, like how much am I willing to spend early stage versus later stages and how much money am I willing to throw after bad money? Now, with all of these different data sources that you've been playing with over time, I have to assume that measurement, you know, testing and and evolving the waterfalls for your clients is one of the big things that you're spending a lot of your time on. How do you get a organization to set those parameters in advance of a test? It's been my experience as a consultant that when you go in, if you don't set those if you don't put those yardsticks on the field, then goal post always seems to move further away. How do you go through the process of getting everybody on board in advance to make sure that we're all speaking the same language before we're spending dollars on data? >> Yeah, so I think I know what you're driving there. Um, so we we typically start with a complementary data assessment, and we look at First, we talk about the organization's goals, their priorities, how they measure success, and then we look at their individual data strategies that they have in place, the data vendors that they use, the reporting that they have in place or don't have in place place to track key performance indicators. And we make observations and recommendations that say, you know, hey, you told me that your goal was X, Y, and Z, yet your process today appears So maybe the goal is, let's say, revenue, you know, growing revenue. But the data strategies that they have in place are really more based on data cost and ROI. Those two mean that the data strategy they have in place isn't necessarily aligned with what their performance goals are. And so having a dialogue around that to get alignment on these are your goals, here are the success measurements, we we agree on those, and then we then we have a trust then we talk about what is the test testing methodology that we're going to use to prove out a new data strategy, whether it's performing better or worse than their current data strategy. >> Okay. And so for an organization that feels like they have their data waterfall in order, they've been working through it and all of that, how often should an organization be revisiting that data strategy? >> I love this question because we take the philosophy and our clients that have the highest performance have the philosophy of continuous improvement. So you never sort of arrive at this ultimate data strategy. So we would recommend that there's always um a portion of your inventory that's in a AB testing type environment. But if I were to answer it as far as periodic testing, I mean no less than quarterly. Again, we're not advocating nor are we building, you know, set it and forget it type data waterfall strategies. Um, you know, all of us are operating especially our customers in very competitive environments and you know, I I think and everything is in flux, right? The market is in flux, consumers' lives are in flux, our customers their customer environments are are in flux. And so I think for data strategies to really perform, they require refinement over time. And the way that we know how to do that is through, you know, a AB testing and trying out new data sources and new data strategies. And then you know, we achieve success today and then we say, okay, now how can we do that better tomorrow? >> I I like that approach. How do you recommend testing new data sources or treatment paths without disrupting the current production? Because we're talking about testing again quarterly and constantly going through this process, but how do you structure some of those tests so that you can continually run this testing, continually push the boundaries but without interrupting the business at hand. >> Yeah, great question, Adam. So a couple of ideas come to mind or approaches that we take. So one is doing retroactive testing where you know, you grab a pool a sampling of accounts that have known performance outcomes. And then you take those accounts and you bounce them across um a data vendor or a or a waterfall a group of data providers. And you determine if this account if you didn't know what the performance data was and you ran this account at time of placement, what what would the data vendors have have appended? And then you match that up to the performance results and so it's a way without any operational impact to identify you know, hey, is there something here with this data provider that could add value? The other way is through production champion challenger testing where you take a small percentage of your inventory and then run your champion challenger on that. And that way the bulk of your accounts are running your existing strategy and so it's a lower risk way on production accounts to to run a strategy but not impact the whole population. >> So that you're you're testing it in real time but you're testing it within a isolated sample population to avoid any deeper disruption but if you've already built out that waterfall your risk level should be pretty minimal there. So as you see all these organizations that are going through the constant evolution of improving their data waterfalls what's the big mistake that you're seeing organizations make again and again and again as a consultant you get such visibility into so many different landscapes. Is there a recurring theme that you're seeing in terms of a mistake or a challenge that organizations are creating for themselves? >> Yeah, so in no particular order there's a few that come to mind. >> particular order. All right, we've got a list. I love it. >> Oh. So I think overconfidence is is one of the main ones you know thinking that you have all the things that you need data vendor wise and the strategies in place with the reporting in place. It's more that sort of that static mindset of maybe it worked when we tested it and we put that in place and then assuming that that is still working would probably be a pretty bad assumption because against the all all the flux that I talked about. Number two would be being single threaded putting your all of your eggs in one basket using one primary data provider would be a mistake in most situations or for most use cases and there was a third one I was thinking of um I think for a servicer and this would apply to a lender too is assuming the data that the consumer provided the original creditor is good. We talked at the start of of this podcast about the rate at which consumer data becomes inaccurate or stale. And it's somewhere between 30 and 40% per year. And so a lot of times I hear especially from collection agencies at hey, we don't skip trace. We think that's too risky. So we only use the data that came from our customer, you know, the creditor. You know, again, after two years, 60 to 70% of that consumer data is not correct. And so that in itself can be risky, right? So those are the three big ones that come to mind, overconfidence, being single-threaded, and then assuming that that the consumer data is the best. >> So the advice that I hear there is remain diversified, continue to push the boundaries like a velociraptor testing the fences. Like we always want to be pushing those boundaries and see what we're capable of doing there. But as the world continues to change around us data professionals, what do you see looking forward in the application of artificial intelligence? Clearly data is required to run those models, to run those tool sets and to find the success but behind AI itself. But that aside, how do you think artificial intelligence will ultimately impact your role, like your world, so to speak, in terms of testing, understanding data and being able to apply it? What do you think that looks like over the next five years? >> Two things come to mind, Adam. So for data companies themselves, you know, they're starting to use artificial intelligence to gain additional insights. Now they're building products that you know, are using hundreds of different data sources to come up with these products. And artificial intelligence is now starting to be be used to get insights into that data to figure out how to how to better piece that data together to solve a particular business problem. And then also on the reporting and analytics side, drawing insights from that data for the customer using artificial intelligence. And then the second way that I see it being applied is as you know, Adam, our customers are starting to use things like AI powered virtual agents >> Mhm. >> to communicate with consumers in a 24/7 environment. And so there's a whole new channel of communication that's happening between our clients and consumers using artificial intelligence that come with a whole set of new key performance indicators. It's a little bit more complex now, right? Because it used to be that, you know, somebody would send a letter, pick up the phone and make a phone call and those are the two channels of communication. Now we have, you know, a whole a whole bunch of ways that consumers can interact and engage with our customers. And so with that comes a whole new set of key performance indicators and metrics that need to be understood, I guess to maximize the investments that our customers are making in third party technology tools like artificial intelligence. >> I I think you're right on the the AI use case. I think when it comes to the data is yeah, it's going to be to say combine the data and maybe operationalize some of the data that's coming into organizations, getting it into their CRMs, identifying the signals from their communication channels, but it's that conversion to actionable intelligence when we can take all of these data sets. But we also read, you know, articles and things around I was reading the other day it's like 250 bad documents can corrupt an entire AI model. And like that's really all that it takes for that to happen. So I think the curation, the sommelier of data ultimately still needs to be there to refine what is being fed into it because I think there's some value attributes from an artificial intelligence standpoint, but it's so specific and the more data that we can feed it obviously the more insights or correlations that we can find in the data. But I think that's the big use case over the next five years and how we're going to start activating some of that from a data collection standpoint to like actionable intelligence where we can drive next behavioral action. >> Percent agree, Adam. >> Well, it sounds like the future is now because we're starting to see some of that stuff start to happen. But Will, as we think about data waterfalls and kind of our whole discussion today, is there anything that I didn't ask you that that you thought I would ask you today? >> You didn't ask me which was the best data source, which I thought was good. >> Yeah, well, because that's a ridiculous question. >> It's a ridiculous question. Um >> Use cases are everything. >> No, I don't think so. Maybe what type of performance lift we typically see. >> To that see to me that's too specific of a question because whatever number you give out is going to apply to one specific client that you were working on yesterday and not, right, all of the people. And that's why I try to like formulate the questions the way that I do because I want to make sure that we provide an accurate representation to the industry of of kind of what's happening here. But Will, I know I'm going to have more questions for you in the next couple of months just looking at everything that's happening in the economy. And once the 2025 TransUnion debt collection industry report rolls out in February, I know that we're going to have to have another discussion here. But for today, I really do appreciate you coming on, sharing your insights, spending a little time with me. This was fun. Clearly there's a lot that I can continue to learn from you. So I look forward to our next adventure together at whatever conference that happens to be. >> Hey, thanks for talking to Adam. Always enjoy talking to you. Appreciate the opportunity. >> Absolutely. For those of you that are watching, if you have additional questions you'd like to ask Will or myself, you can leave those in the comments here on LinkedIn and YouTube and Will be responding to those. Or if you have additional topics you'd like to see us discuss, you can leave those in the comments below as well. And I'll get Will back here at least one more time to help me continue to create great content for a great industry. But until next time, Will, thank you so much. I appreciate you. >> Thank you, Adam. >> And thank you everybody for watching. We'll see you all again soon. Bye everyone.

metadata.shortDescription:
Visit our website for more info on small claims court, including sample forms: 
https://dcba.lacounty.gov/small-claims/

segments.text: in this video we'll cover
filing an acknowledgement of
satisfaction and judgment
acknowledgement of satisfaction form
sc-130 notice of entry of judgment
[Music]
sc-290 acknowledgment of satisfaction of
judgment
and ej 100 acknowledgement of
satisfaction of judgment
when the creditor the party who won the
judgment is paid in full
the creditor must immediately submit to
the court one of the following three
forms
or
if the creditor does not file an
acknowledgement of satisfaction of
judgment with the court within 14 days
after receiving a written demand by the
debtor the party who owed the judgment
the creditor may have to pay the debtor
damages and a penalty
let's review each of these forms to help
you decide which one to use
when the court awards a judgment a form
notice of entry of judgment is mailed to
all parties in the case
page one of the form lists the date the
judgment was entered the party who was
awarded the judgment and the amount of
the judgment
[Music]
on the back page of this form is an
acknowledgment of satisfaction of
judgment
for the creditor to sign and mail to the
court when the judgment is paid in full
the form should be used when payment has
been received and the creditor
has not placed a lien against the
debtor's real property real estate by
recording an abstract of judgment with
the county registrar recorder
or filed a notice of judgment lien with
the california secretary of state
[Music]
when the court enters a judgment against
multiple debtors
the judge will specify how much each
debtor owes
the judge may indicate that each debtor
is only responsible for his or her
portion of the debt
but often a judgment against multiple
parties
will likely be jointly and severally
liable
meaning that each debtor will be 100
responsible for paying the award
on the form sc-290
the creditor is able to select the
option that the judgment is satisfied
against all debtors
or the option that only specific debtors
have satisfied the judgment
it is very important that the creditor
acknowledge which individual debtors
have paid what is owed
just like the form sc-130
this form should be used when payment
has been received and the creditor has
not recorded an abstract of judgment or
filed a notice of judgment lien
[Music]
the form
ej-100 must be used when the judgment is
fully satisfied and the creditor has
placed a lien against the debtor's real
property real estate
or filed a notice of judgment lien
against personal property owned by a
business
through the california secretary of
state's office
if a lien exists the creditor must have
the form notarized before filing it with
the court
the creditor must also provide a
notarized original of the form to the
debtor to file at the county registrar
recorder's office
where the abstract of judgment was
recorded
to release a notice of judgment lien the
creditor must file a judgment lien
change form jl3 with the california
secretary of state
this form is obtained from the
california secretary of state
in addition to using the form ej-100
to file full satisfaction of judgment
this form is also used when the creditor
reports that partial payment has been
received from the debtor
thanks for watching
if you would like additional information
about the small claims process visit our
website
dcba.la county dot gov
forward slash small dash claims

metadata.title: 💼 A Final Judgment With No Reserved Jurisdiction — Vacating It Under Rule 1.540(b)
metadata.author: Florida Trust, Real Estate, Probate, & Foreclosure
metadata.shortDescription:
Salamandre, Inc., etc., et al. v. Parc Place Development LLC | Case No. 3D13-3244 | Third District Court of Appeal

Counsel for the appellants asks the court to vacate a final judgment along with the writs of execution and possession issued on it, and structures the argument around four points. The lead one is jurisdictional: the judgment was entered without the trial court having retained continuing jurisdiction over the settlement. Counsel argues the governing rule is plain and that the trial bar has followed it for years — you put the settlement agreement before the trial court.

Key issues addressed:
- Whether the trial court retained continuing jurisdiction to enter judgment enforcing a settlement agreement — Paulucci, as argued
- Placing a settlement agreement before the trial court as the condition of later enforcement
- Motion to vacate a void judgment under Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.540(b), and why the thirty-day window does not control
- Whether damages can be liquidated from the face of a lease that fixes them by percentage
- Conditions the landlord had to satisfy before judgment could be entered
- Writs of execution and possession issued on the challenged judgment

🔗 Florida Rules & Legal Resources: www.floridarules.net

#Rule1540 #VoidJudgment #SettlementEnforcement #CommercialLease #LiquidatedDamages #WritOfPossession #ThirdDCA #FloridaAppellate #CivilProcedure #FloridaAppeal

metadata.title: Vacating a Consent Order or Settlement Agreement in New Jersey
metadata.author: Jacobs Berger, LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn from our divorce attorneys on how and if the terms of a consent order or settlement agreement can be vacated. 

Additional information: https://jacobsberger.com/vacating-a-consent-order-or-settlement-agreement-nj/

segments.text: hi Sarah Jacobs here today we're talking
about consent orders unsettlement
agreements and how and if the terms of
those documents can be vacated
we know that each case is unique and
fact sensitive but it's important to
start with the premise that if the
consent order or settlement agreement
was entered into consensually on the
terms were legal to begin with
the court is more than likely to enforce
those terms and that the terms cannot be
vacated
however and I'm sure you expected this
there are circumstances in which consent
orders and settlement agreements can be
vacated first if the agreement or
consent order was unconscionable which
means the terms were so skewed to one
party's favor that a reasonable person
would not have entered into the deal the
court can vacate the consent order or
settlement agreement or that specific
provision of this consent order or
settlement agreement
second if there was a fact or mistake of
fact made that substantially Alters the
outcome of the agreement for instance if
the value of a house or bank account or
brokerage account was incorrectly stated
and all of the calculations flowing from
that were incorrect the court can vacate
that provision to make sure that the
calculations in the future are correct
third if there was coercion or duress
which means that one party in the
relationship who may have more power
than the other either entices or forces
the less powerful party to enter into
the agreement or consent order the
entire document or certain provisions of
that document may be vacated
also if there was a knowing
misrepresentation by one party or a
knowing mistake and there was no
transparency or no communication letting
the other side know that there was a
misrepresentation or a mistake and later
the party who didn't know discovers it
that agreement can be vacated
applications to vacate pieces of a
consent order agreement or entire
consent order or agreements can be
complicated they need to be well
documented supported by the law and
detailed it's imperative if you believe
that you meet the criteria to vacate
certain Provisions or entireties of
orders or agreements that you speak to
an attorney experienced in family law
specifically in this area to help you
navigate the facts and circumstances of
your case it's really important to
present the application to the court in
a thorough Manner and a good attorney
will partner with you and let you know
if you have a case
we've helped many families like yours
gain relief from oppressive or unfair or
legally or factually deficient consent
orders or settlement agreements and have
succeeded in vacating many of them
we're ready to help you on your next
PATH and we look forward to talking to
you

metadata.title: How This Guy Started an $80k / Month Debt Collection Service
metadata.author: Hard Hat Economics
metadata.shortDescription:
Even in recession there are certain industries that continue making really good money. Take for example collection agencies, whose job it is to collect on past due invoices and debt of all sorts of companies. .   

Back in 2017, Avi Grunwald is one entrepreneur who decided to start a debt collection company called Fair Capital without any prior knowledge of the industry. Today, Avi’s company works with more than 600 companies and brings in more than $80k per month in revenue. 
 
In today’s business case study, I'll break down what you’ll need to start a debt collection service of your own, how to find customers, and how to get paid. Let’s get into it.  

To give you some perspective on how big the debt collection industry actually is.. An estimated 28% of the United States has some debt in collections right now. According to Consumer Reports, 43 million Americans are contacted by collection agencies for medical debt each year. And of course there is a massive industry built around collecting on these obligations. 

In case you’re not familiar, here’s how debt collection companies work: 

Imagine there’s an ABX telephone company out there with 1,000 accounts more than 6 months overdue on their bills. Of course, the company already tried to get paid on this debt in the normal ways by sending email reminders, mailing letters, and making courtesy calls. 

At this point, the ABX telephone company might give up on trying to collect any money. This is where a debt collection agency could come in. 

From the perspective of ABX telephone company, getting a little bit of money from these past due customers is better than getting no payment at all.. As a result, ABX telephone company decides to work with a collection agency to do the work of calling and mailing people to pay their bills. 

According to Avi these are the two most common ways that a debt collection company gets paid: 

The first is called a contingency-based model. This means you only get paid when you successfully collect on a debt and is the approach Fair Capital used to build their business. 

The average debt collection fee is 20% - 40% of debt owed. This means you’ll get $20 - $40 for every $100 you’re able to collect. 

To use another example, if you were able to get connected with a landscaping company where outstanding bills could range from $1,000 - $10,000, you could see how this business model would be quite lucrative if you’re able to scale the business and take on a lot of clients. 

The second way debt collection agencies get paid through a flat-rate fee. This means you’ll negotiate how much you’ll get paid with another company to collect payments. This allows you to get paid regardless of the number of accounts you’re able to convert into payments. 

Mentioned in Video: 

https://www.thefaircapital.com/post/collection-agencies-fee

https://www.capitalrecovery.net/blog/important-debt-collection-statistics-to-know-in-2022/

https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/debt-collection-faqs

https://www.consumerfinance.gov/compliance/compliance-resources/other-applicable-requirements/debt-collection/debt-collection-rule-faqs/

https://www.consumerreports.org/money/debt-collection/fight-when-contacted-by-a-debt-collector-for-medical-bill-a8932597676/

Form an LLC for $49 + State Fees: https://mobile-cuisine.com/zen-llc-review/

This is the business database I use to see the revenue numbers and tools of 3,000+ businesses: https://www.starterstory.com/subscribe?via=fte

Sign up for a paid subscription to Starter Story and I'll even give you a free personal consulting session for joining.

law account if you haven't already done

for this service simply use your SCU edu
email address and click on the new user
page on Bloomberg for those of you that
have already created your account and
are ready to get started the second step
is to click on the tab for litigation

dockets and our assignment we are
looking for trademark dilution actions

that search by restricting our search

enter in the state name there Bloomberg
risk is going to offer me some
suggestions at the bottom of the list is
the US District Court for the District
of Oregon once I've selected a court

in the bottom half of the screen among
those include a cause of action so you

infringement click on search
number of results here we can restrict

of infringement click on search
click on the entry and this will pull up

Bloomberg from pacer that's why the link
here says view rather than request is
because Bloomberg has kept a cache copy
if we click on View and then the actual
complaint itself
you'll see that this is a complaint
which does allege trademark dilution

metadata.title: How to Search Federal Court Dockets for Free with CourtListener
metadata.author: Tommy from DocketDrafter
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to search federal court dockets and filings with CourtListener’s free RECAP Archive—and how to make that research easier with Claude.

In this tutorial, I walk through CourtListener’s advanced RECAP search, explain the difference between CourtListener and PACER, and use The New York Times v. Microsoft/OpenAI docket as a practical example. Then I show how our free CourtListener plugin lets Claude search dockets, download available filings, build a persistent local research library, retrieve cited opinions, and help with attorney-controlled cite checking.

Install the free CourtListener plugin for Claude:
https://youtu.be/yw3V6mhgk1U

Search CourtListener:
https://www.courtlistener.com/

Questions, feedback, or help installing the plugin for you or your firm?
tommy@docketdrafter.com

Learn more about DocketDrafter:
https://www.docketdrafter.com

CHAPTERS
00:00 What you can do with CourtListener and Claude
00:42 Searching federal dockets in the RECAP Archive
01:26 Filtering by court and filing date
02:35 Finding and reading docket entries
03:53 CourtListener, PACER, and the RECAP extension
05:22 Finding The New York Times v. Microsoft/OpenAI docket
07:04 Why docket searching can be difficult
07:28 Searching and downloading filings with Claude
09:23 Building a persistent local research library
10:01 Finding cited opinions and checking citations
12:45 How to install the free CourtListener plugin

metadata.title: How To Find Bankruptcy Court Records?
metadata.author: County Portal
metadata.shortDescription:
How To Find Bankruptcy Court Records?

To find bankruptcy court records, the primary digital resource is PACER (Public Access to Court Electronic Records). This federal service allows you to search for cases filed in U.S. Bankruptcy Courts nationwide, requiring registration and typically charging a small fee per page viewed. For an effective search, you'll need the individual's full name, the court district, and ideally the case number or filing date. If the case isn't found on PACER, or for older records, directly contact the clerk's office of the specific U.S. Bankruptcy Court where the case was filed; they can assist with physical record retrieval or guide you to local access terminals. For very old, closed bankruptcy cases, particularly those predating electronic systems, records might be archived at the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). Additionally, various third-party public record search websites exist, but these often charge a fee and may not offer the same comprehensive or current information as direct court sources.

🔎 Helpful Links & Resources
• Video Link: https://youtu.be/IDWN8CuNtfA
• Channel Link: https://www.youtube.com/@CountyPortal/?sub_confirmation=1


⚠️ Disclaimer: County Portal provides information for educational purposes only. We do not guarantee accuracy or timeliness. This is not legal, financial, or medical advice. Use at your own risk.

are held by the federal court system.

records is Pacer, which stands for
public access to court electronic
records. Think of it as the official
online filing cabinet for all federal
court cases, including bankruptcy.
To get started, you'll need to go to the
Pacer website, which is
pacer.uscourts.gov,

documents, typically around 10 cents per

waved. So, for casual searching, it's

case locator. To find a specific case,

petition, the list of creditors, motions

discharge order that officially closes
the case. But what if the case is very

the records are likely archived. Your
first step is to contact the clerk's
office of the specific bankruptcy court

provide you with the information needed
to request the records from the National
Archives and Records Administration or
NAR. This process is slower and involves
different fees. While you might see
thirdparty websites offering to pull

are generally just using Pacer
themselves and charging you for the
convenience.
It's almost always cheaper to do it
yourself directly through Pacer. Keep in
mind that while these are public
records, sensitive personal information
like full social security numbers or
bank account numbers will be redacted
for privacy.
So, to recap, use Pacer for modern cases
and contact the court clerk for older
archived cases. It's a powerful tool for
accessing important public information.
Thank you so much for watching. If you
found this video helpful, please give it

Rich Mayer & The Default Investor Association
754-210-3754
7151 Pembroke Rd.
Pembroke Pines, FL 33023

About Default Investor Association:
Default Investor Association is dedicated to helping real estate agents become investors. Our program has already helped thousands of real estate agents from around the country and we have a reputation for producing successful real estate investors.

Based on the teachings of real estate investing mastermind Richard Meyer, we offer best-in-class training, products and services designed to help our agents take control of their financial futures, escape the rat race and join the financial elite on the fast track to success.

Through various channels that include live courses, online training, mentoring programs, and multi-media products, Default Investor Association provides an innovative training model that imparts skills and knowledge in real estate investing, financial instrument investing (stocks, bonds, etc.), entrepreneurship and personal finance.


About Rich Meyer
After college, Rich worked his way up the corporate real estate ladder to become the broker and owner of ERA Prestige Realty. For the next few years he grew Prestige to a formidable 4 office operation with over 250 full time agents and exceeding $45M in annual sales each year in business. This of course is when $45M meant something.

After a divorce, he sold the real estate offices and went to work for a leading foreclosure law firm where he studied the legal aspects of real property law, the election of remedies and foreclosure litigation.

In 1993 his expert understanding of the consequences of default lead him to begin investing in foreclosure and tax deed auction properties. Currently he has participated in the acquisition and sale of over 1800 (and counting) properties.

In 2003 Rich’s business model became more focused on an off-the-beaten-path-investment in defaulted mortgages and notes. All in all, he’s purchased 1000’s of non-institutional first and second mortgages and institutional second mortgage notes.

Lastly, he remains extremely active in the field of (defaulted consumer debt) judgment collections. Rich currently receives over $12,600.00 per month in passive income resulting from monthly settlement payments from various judgment debtors.

Rich is a member of Real Estate Owned Managers Association of California (REOMAC), a member of the National Tax Lien Association (NTLA) and a platinum member of Broward Real Estate Investors Association (BREIA).

 Rich’s experience and real-life examples in the field of default investing creates a powerful yet enlightening narrative that has been enjoyed by real estate investors of all interests and levels of experience.

metadata.title: How to Improve Your Judgment Recovery Success Rate with Joe Dickerson
metadata.author: Hanna Hasl-Kelchner
metadata.shortDescription:
Judgment recovery is not as easy as asking “show me the money” after you win a lawsuit. Getting a judgment in a court of law gets you a piece of paper and the right to now go and collect on it. It doesn’t mean you’ll necessarily be successful AND if you’re not successful if feels like getting victimized all over again.

So if you want to know how to actually recover what’s rightfully owed to you, you’re going to love today’s guest. He’s the nation’s leading financial forensic expert and he’ll explain what you need to do to successfully enforce and recover a legal judgement in the United States.

What You’ll Discover About Judgment Recovery:

Why building a better relationship with the local sheriff’s department is a smart idea.

Why deposing the debtor immediately after the verdict isn’t the smartest thing to do.

How to avoid the debtor’s delays and stall tactics.

The financial forensic research you need to do before engaging in judgment recovery.

The best strategy for locating assets the debtor hides.

The mistake lawyers often make when seeking judgment recovery.

And much more.

This video is from the Business Confidential Now with Hanna Hasl-Kelchner podcast. 

If you find this video helpful, please consider giving it a like and leaving a positive comment.

To access the show notes that contain the guest bio, related links, and a transcript, please visit https://businessconfidentialradio.com/improve-your-judgment-recovery-success-rate-with-joe-dickerson

Business Confidential Now always aims to give you smart, practical, and timeless tips focused on helping you see things hidden in plain view that matter to your career and bottom line.

Transformational. Educational. No nonsense & Fun.

Subscribe on your favorite podcast app or YouTube and never miss an episode.

It’s the stuff they don't have time to teach you in business school, but that you need to succeed!

FOLLOW ON YOUTUBE!
https://www.youtube.com/c/HannaHaslKelchner

VISIT https://BusinessConfidentialRadio.com

LET’S CONNECT
https://facebook.com/businessconfidentialnow
https://www.linkedin.com/showcase/business-confidential-now-with-hanna-hasl-kelchner/

metadata.shortDescription:

5:02 Notices: deadlines worked out for you
5:59 Recovery: the money ledger and reversals
7:15 Coercive Measures: travel bans and detention orders
8:17 Wrap-up

that already exists.
There is nothing left to argue. So,

one location. Search for commercial
execution,

says it plainly, cases created under
this mapping enforce an existing

changes the shape of the form and of
every case created under the mapping.

not disabled. They are removed outright,
and anything entered in them is cleared.

sending settings you can no longer see.

does not convert existing cases.
It decides how cases are created from
this point on.
Back on the grid, the execution case
column is hidden by default.
Switch it on through edit columns.

and a litigation mapping with hearings
turned off both show a hearing type of
none.
This column is the only place the
difference is visible.
Now, registering the case.
There is nothing new to learn here.

have,
picking the case type and location.
Because that mapping is marked as
execution, the case opens as an
execution file.

Here is our case, commercial execution
in Dubai.

measures.

emails work exactly as they do on any
other case.

card is added alongside the usual ones.
Four tiles, assets, how many found out
of how many classes searched, realized,
the total collected so far,
notices, how many are live,
and coercive measures, how many are in
force.
Beneath the tiles, an alerts rail lists
only what needs attention.
Here, an active travel ban with its

counting down.
Every tile and every alert is a
shortcut. Click it and you land on the
tab it came from.
The assets tab is the debtor's asset
register.
When it opens for the first time, Case
Engine seeds a checklist. Every asset
class marked auto seed becomes a pending
row.
So, instead of an empty grid, the lawyer
starts with a list of what to search
for.

many are found, how many are under
attachment, and the total realized.

offers the step that is actually
available. This trade license is

Not found is not a dead end either.
Run the investigation again later and

as you see here.
The stage is the same, only the

And money realized on this tab is what
the recovery tab counts, so the two
always agree.

Case Engine adds the notice types
response window to the served date.

progress is recovered as a share of
claimed.

is grouped by where it came from. So,
you can see what each attachment

Recorded a payment that did not clear?

once each.

Coercive measures are pressure applied
to a person, not to the file. Travel
bans, detention orders, and the like.
Four statuses.
Requested, waiting on the court,
active, in force, lifted, and rejected.
Active is shown in red on purpose.
A measure running against a person is
something to keep an eye on, not an
achievement to tick off.
This travel ban carries an expiry date

are closing.
Read the note at the bottom. Leverage
only. No payment is recorded here.
If a debtor pays to have a band lifted,

Record it there, then lift the measure
here.
Keeping the two apart is what stops the
same money being counted twice.
That is the execution module.
One toggle on the case mapping.
Registration exactly as before.
And a case view built for enforcement.
Assets traced. Notices served. Money
recovered. And measures in force, all
summarized on the overview.
The four tabs are driven by four
masters.
Asset classes. Notice types. Coercive
measure types. And recovery payment
types. So, set those up first. And the
checklist builds itself.

only what is a garnishment garnishment
is when money is legally withheld from
your paycheck and sent to another party

debts such as unpaid taxes monetary
fines child support payments defaulted
student loans and Consumer Debt the
consumer credit protection act CCPA
prohibits an employer from firing an
employee whose earnings have been
subject to garnishment if a debt

against you the debt collector could
garnish your bank
account under the CCPA wage garnishment
for Consumer Debt is generally the lower

income if the individual's disposable

amount or the amount by which the
individual's disposable income is
greater than 30 times the federal weekly
minimum wage let's look at this in more
detail disposable income is gross income
minus legally required deductions such
as federal state and local taxes and
Social Security deductions for example
if the federal minimum wage is
$725 an hour and an individual earns
disposable income under
$27.50 per week which is 30 times the F
federal minimum wage there can be no
wage
garnishment if the federal minimum wage
is $725 an hour and an individual earns
between
$27.50 and $290 per week the amount
above
$27.50 can be

$290 or more per week a maximum of 25%

orders time is of the essence if you're

metadata.title: 20 Real Estate Exam Questions On Liens - Must Know Questions To Pass  The Real Estate Exam!
metadata.author: Real Estate Exam Questions
metadata.shortDescription:
Real estate liens are legal claims against a property, typically used as security for the repayment of a debt or obligation. They give creditors an interest in the property until the debt is paid off or the obligation is fulfilled. Liens can be placed on real estate by various parties, including lenders, contractors, taxing authorities, or judgment creditors.

Here are some common types of real estate liens:

Mortgage Liens: When you take out a mortgage to buy a property, the lender usually places a mortgage lien on the property. This lien gives the lender the right to foreclose on the property if the borrower fails to repay the loan according to the terms of the mortgage agreement.

Mechanic's Liens: Contractors, subcontractors, or suppliers who provide labor or materials for improvements to a property may place a mechanic's lien on the property if they're not paid for their work. Mechanic's liens provide these parties with a way to seek payment by forcing the sale of the property if necessary.

Property Tax Liens: If property taxes are not paid, the government may place a tax lien on the property. This lien takes priority over most other liens, including mortgage liens, and gives the government the right to seize and sell the property to collect the unpaid taxes.

Judgment Liens: If a property owner loses a lawsuit and is ordered by the court to pay a monetary judgment, the creditor may place a judgment lien on the property. This lien ensures that the creditor has a claim to the proceeds if the property is sold.

HOA (Homeowners Association) Liens: Homeowners associations can place liens on properties for unpaid dues or assessments. These liens typically have priority over other liens, except for property tax liens.

Liens can affect the ability to sell or refinance a property, as they encumber the title. To clear a lien from a property title, the underlying debt or obligation must be satisfied, usually through payment or fulfillment of the terms.
